stories.Headline: Singapore warns of privacy dangers as personal AI agents like Meta's Muse gain consumer access
stories.Summary:
Singapore's Cyber Security Agency, the Government Technology Agency and the Infocomm Media Development Authority issued a joint advisory on Nov 6 to help consumers use personal AI agents safely. Unlike chatbots that mainly answer questions, these agents can act on a user's behalf, such as browsing websites, managing emails and making bookings. The advisory follows the launch in Singapore of Meta Muse, which the company describes as the first personal AI agent built for consumers and which can connect to services such as Gmail and Google Calendar. CNA listed other examples of agents, including Dots, Hermes, Grok Bot and OpenClaw. The authorities warned that depending on the access granted, agents may expose sensitive information, make mistakes or act beyond what users intended.

The advisory sets out five precautions. Users should connect only necessary apps and accounts, avoid giving agents access to banking, government or healthcare accounts, check with employers before linking work accounts, and never share credit card details, passwords or one-time passwords. They should begin with limited or read-only permissions, require approval before sending messages, deleting or sharing files or posting publicly, and prefer one-time approval over an "always-allow" setting. Permissions should be set through app settings, since chat instructions may not be followed consistently, and users should regularly revoke unneeded permissions and check activity records. For Singpass services, CNA reported, consumers should default to passkey authentication, complete it themselves and avoid approving unexpected requests.

The authorities stressed that users remain responsible for how they use AI agents, including the actions agents take for them, and may be held liable depending on the circumstances and applicable laws. They said agents should not be treated like human assistants given broad access and implicit trust, and that users should grant narrowly scoped permissions, keep control of consequential actions and know how to revoke access. They also advised users to check what data providers collect, who receives it, how long it is kept and whether it trains AI models or personalises advertisements. Because many agents keep persistent memory and can build profiles of users and their contacts, inaccurate or unwanted stored information should be deleted.

On security, the advisory warned that scammers can hide instructions in websites, emails, calendar invitations, documents or images to push agents into making purchases, moving money or revealing personal data. The authorities said the best protection is to limit what an agent can see or do, and users should watch agents as they browse, restrict who can instruct them, use strong authentication and download agents only from official sources. If something goes wrong, users should stop the agent, disconnect affected accounts, look for unexpected payments, changed settings or email forwarding rules, save activity records before deleting suspicious items and notify anyone affected. Users were also asked to consider the people whose details appear in their emails and files, to say when a message was sent by an agent, and not to ask an agent to bypass paywalls or login requirements.

stories.Headline: Anthropic is rapidly accelerating AI development amid slowdown calls, outside research group says
stories.Summary:
The nonprofit Model Evaluation and Threat Research, known as METR, released an analysis on Thursday finding that Anthropic is developing its AI systems about twice as fast as it was a year earlier. The Berkeley, California group reviewed internal data the company provided over roughly 11 weeks, from mid-August through late October, and also interviewed employees. Anthropic invited the review as it prepares for a Wall Street debut, with a public offering planned for later this month that could be the biggest ever. The findings arrived at a time of debate over whether AI models could slip out of human control, and they matter because most details about the technology have come from AI companies that the Trump administration has encouraged to police themselves. METR said Anthropic has made as much progress on benchmarks in the past year as it did between October 2023 and October 2025, which The Verge described as roughly two years of historical progress in one.

The group said it could confidently rule out growth in training computing power as the cause, and it concluded that most of the acceleration as of October came from AI itself. Employees using Anthropic's most capable internal model reported being about 12 times as productive as they would be without AI help, around double what staff reported a few months earlier. METR also found no clear bottlenecks, such as limits on computing power or data, that would hold back even faster progress. It listed three unreleased models, codenamed Model 2, Model 3 and Model 4, that finished training in July, August to September, and September to October. The report carried several caveats.

METR said it might be overstating the result if the speedup applies only to well-specified tasks that can be graded automatically, rather than messier ones, or if Anthropic understated its earlier progress. Anthropic's redactions limited how METR could share more detailed estimates, and the group's own team had some internal disagreement and uncertainty, though it still believed the rate had doubled. Anthropic was permitted to redact parts of the final report under its agreement with METR, and The Verge said it appears to have used that power liberally. Anthropic did not immediately respond to requests for comment from The Associated Press. The central worry METR raised is that using AI to improve itself could compound the acceleration.

It said AI cannot yet make highly significant, fully autonomous contributions to the most important parts of model training, but Anthropic researchers described meaningful signs that this could happen soon. CEO Dario Amodei raised the same concern in a Sept. 12 essay, which fell during METR's assessment period. In it he urged the industry to slow the pace at which it improves model capabilities so that safety measures can catch up. He wrote that recursive self-improvement, meaning AI's growing ability to build the next generation of AI, could outrun human ability to understand and control these systems if left unchecked. He also backed placing outside evaluators inside leading labs and named METR as a suitable one, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he supported the idea of independent evaluators with employee-like access.

stories.Headline: AI data-center stocks slide, renewables rally after Democratic US midterm sweep
stories.Summary:
Data-center stocks fell on Wednesday and clean-energy shares rallied after Democrats took control of Congress in the US midterm elections, Reuters reported on November 4. The result includes wins in Republican strongholds and in the data-center hubs of Texas and Georgia, and it brings divided government to Washington. Investors responded by repositioning for tougher scrutiny of the AI boom and a change in policy priorities. A second report, from Tom's Hardware, described the vote as a comprehensive defeat for AI data centers, with 45 measures on the ballot and Americans overwhelmingly voting against developments.

Among data-center operators, Applied Digital fell 8.8%, CoreWeave dropped 9.5% and Cipher Digital slid 21%. Power and equipment suppliers tied to the buildout also came under pressure, with GE Vernova down 11.5%, Constellation Energy down 9.2% and Vistra down 15.4%. Large US cloud companies bucked the trend, as Amazon and Microsoft each jumped 6% and Alphabet rose 4.6%, because investors bet a slower construction pace would raise the value of existing assets and curb Big Tech's heavy AI spending. On the clean-energy side, First Solar gained 8.4%, Sunrun added 6.9%, Enphase Energy rose 8.8% and NextEra Energy climbed 4.6%, while in Europe Vestas rose 2.9%, Orsted 4.6% and EDP Renewables 2.8%.

Other sectors moved too. Trump Media & Technology Group dropped 13%, SpaceX fell 3.5% and Tesla lost 3.3%, and defense stocks declined as investors reassessed expectations for President Trump's proposed $1.5 trillion budget, with Northrop Grumman down 3.7% and RTX, Lockheed Martin and L3Harris losing between 3% and 6%. Hospital operators and insurers rose, with HCA Healthcare up 8.5%, Universal Health Services up 6.8%, Centene up 7.3% and Molina Healthcare up 6.3%. Private prison operators GEO Group and CoreCivic fell 3.8% and 2.1%.

Analysts offered several explanations. Mark Malek of Siebert Financial said the AI buildout would become more expensive rather than disappear, with fewer tax incentives and more responsibility for power and water costs squeezing returns, and he judged borrowers to be more vulnerable than the biggest spenders. Art Hogan of B. Riley Wealth argued that hyperscalers already have their data centers, so those assets are worth more if overbuilding is avoided, though slower construction would also mean slower capital spending. Kathleen Brooks of XTB said the result casts doubt on a possible SpaceX and Tesla merger, since Congress could slow it with extra scrutiny, and she noted Musk had given hundreds of millions to the Republican Party.

On context, the data-center boom sparked public backlash this year, and analysts doubt any legislation could meaningfully stall construction, though a Democratic Congress makes more hearings and investigations likely. Democrats could also use the Congressional Review Act to challenge rules that ease sales of gas-powered trucks and SUVs. Morgan Stanley analysts said Congress now has more room to pursue Democratic healthcare priorities, such as restoring enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies or reversing parts of the GOP's Medicaid cuts, but they still see meaningful changes as unlikely before the next presidential election cycle. Lale Akoner of eToro warned that a difficult debt ceiling negotiation could delay defense spending increases.

stories.Headline: AS ELECTION CAMPAIGNS GATHER MOMENTUM, ONANUGA URGES CAUTION IN USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
stories.Summary:
Bayo Onanuga, the Special Adviser to the President on Information and Strategy, called on Thursday, November 5, 2026, for responsible and cautious use of Artificial Intelligence as political campaigns ahead of Nigeria's 2027 elections pick up speed. He spoke in Beijing, China, where he delivered a paper titled "AI and the Future of Global Communication" at the 7th World Media Summit. The summit was organised by Xinhua News Agency and the People's Government of Beijing Municipality. He said that although AI has brought real benefits, guardrails are now needed to protect democratic institutions and public trust.

Onanuga noted that social media platforms such as X, Facebook and TikTok are flooded with AI-generated videos and images, used both to promote political interests and to entertain. He described the present moment as the thick of the political season, with campaigns underway for the 2027 general elections, in which new leaders will be chosen at the national and sub-national levels. In his words, AI has become a powerful tool in electoral contests for politicians and their supporters, for good and for bad. Some political actors use it to spread falsehoods, some use it for satire, and some use it to highlight what candidates have achieved. He argued that this growing influence makes it necessary for political actors, media organisations and the general public to take greater responsibility when creating and sharing content.

The remarks were made public in a statement signed by Abiodun Oladunjoye, Director of Information and Public Relations at the State House, and were reported by the State House, Leadership and ThisDay. Onanuga did not present his message as a rejection of the technology. He acknowledged its contributions to medicine and mathematics, calling it an indispensable tool for improving human life, and said it now touches daily activities such as warning drivers of their surroundings and mapping the fastest route to a destination. He added that the world can no longer ignore AI's far-reaching impact, most of it beneficial, unless it wants to return to the Stone Age.

Onanuga said he is optimistic because individuals, scientists and governments, including the United Nations, share concern about the direction AI is taking and are pushing for necessary controls. He urged the international community to move quickly, warning that the world must act before it becomes too late and calling for guardrails to be built fast to save humanity. The articles do not describe any specific rules, laws or enforcement steps that Nigeria plans to introduce for AI use in the campaigns. The call comes as the build-up to the 2027 general elections continues.

stories.Headline: Nvidia, Micron, 8 Other AI Stocks Just Broke Below a Key Technical Support
stories.Summary:
Ten of the largest artificial intelligence stocks, together worth about $8.8 trillion, fell below their 200-day moving averages in just four sessions this week, according to Benzinga. All ten had traded above that line last Friday, and by Thursday every one was below it. The group includes Nvidia, Micron, Taiwan Semiconductor, Advanced Micro Devices, Cisco, Qualcomm, Dell, Arista Networks, Cloudflare and Marvell. Most of the damage came after Tuesday's midterm elections, in which Democrats won both chambers of Congress and key governorships. Investors quickly priced in the risk that data center construction would slow, especially in Texas, where much of the next wave of AI capacity is planned.

The individual moves were steep. Marvell broke first, falling 12.7% on Monday to $171.41, below its 200-day average of $184.80, after investors pushed back on its deal to buy Lumentum, and it now sits 25.4% below that line. Nvidia closed Wednesday at $200.13, under its average of $204.67, then fell another 8.4% on Thursday to $183.27, which is 10.5% below the line and erased about $564 billion of value over two days. Micron slid 15.9% to $669.03, 11.4% below its average of $755.33, even though Counterpoint Research said global DRAM revenue rose 369% year over year in the third quarter. AMD dropped 15.9% to $411, just under its average of $415.03, while Qualcomm fell 13.7% after earnings and Dell fell 13.9%.

The selling reached the broader market as well. The Nasdaq 100 fell 5.4% on Thursday to 26,909.96, which is 3.8% below its 200-day average of 27,977.94, and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF dropped 10.3%. The S&P 500 remains 1.2% above its own line despite a 3.6% decline. Dennis DeBusschere of 22V Research said his team had flagged the threat to 2027 AI spending from Texas before the vote but underestimated it, and he described a clear pivot to a growth world less driven by AI. His colleague John Roque said he had spotted bubbles in AI, semiconductor and memory stocks in June and expects those groups to keep performing poorly.

A separate Trefis piece published Friday offers fundamental context on two of the names. It noted that Micron trades at 9.2 times earnings against 23.4 for Nvidia, and that Nvidia said in August that soaring memory prices had forced it to reset its gross margin expectations. Nvidia guided fiscal third-quarter revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, while Micron guided fiscal first-quarter 2027 revenue of $60 billion to $63 billion. Benzinga cautioned that a break below the 200-day average is a signal about trend, not a forecast, and that many of these companies still report record demand. The next test comes November 17, when Nvidia reports earnings, and Micron reports in December.

stories.Headline: AI takes on more decision-making roles
stories.Summary:
Shanghai-based startup StartLux has pushed a new kind of artificial intelligence, models built to make decisions rather than generate text, into the spotlight. According to results the company published itself, its StartLux-Decision v1.1 27B Instant model ranked first among 174 entries on the Decision Index 0.3.2 leaderboard hosted by Hugging Face, the US-based platform for sharing AI models and datasets, with a score of 69.12. The company has also released and open-sourced StartLux-Prism, an inference engine built for the decision model. Separately, on Nov. 6, ABB launched ABB Ability Augmented Operator, an AI-enabled software suite for industrial control rooms, as part of its participation at ADIPEC 2026 in Abu Dhabi.

StartLux says its decision models differ from general-purpose large language models because they pick from predefined options and return the probability tied to each one. That makes them suited to jobs such as customer service routing, web operations and running code for AI agents. In the company's own tests, its first 27-billion-parameter model beat a rival model called Jev in 31 of 38 benchmarks under Decision Index 0.2.1. In another evaluation it averaged 91.82 percent accuracy across seven Intern-Decision test suites, against 88.74 percent for Jev, though the article notes results depend on evaluation methods and testing conditions. ABB's software, meanwhile, spots anomalies earlier, shows how similar situations were handled in a facility's past, forecasts critical process variables and simulates the outcome of a change before it is made, and it is aimed at chemicals, oil and gas, power generation, water and other industries.

Chuan-Wei Kuo, StartLux's co-founder and chief technology officer, said decision models could cut computing costs and raise efficiency. He expects more than 80 percent of AI demand to be handled locally within the next one to two years, and said China's AI talent density is comparable to North America's, while computing resources and infrastructure remain challenges. Gao Chengyuan, head of the Influence Academy, said the commercial potential of decision models is underestimated and that local deployment could appeal to government, financial and industrial customers who need data security, low latency and cost control. At ABB, Gino Hernandez, head of global digital business in the Energy Industries division, said AI must earn its place in control rooms and that operators need to understand and trust the tools they use. He said Augmented Operator explains its reasoning, draws on a facility's own experience and lets operators test a change first, keeping humans in the loop while moving toward more autonomous operations.

The competition is growing. After US-based startup TypeSafe AI launched Jev, companies and research bodies including OpenAI, Cloudflare, Amazon and the Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory have introduced related models or research. Reuters reported that AI PCs made up 44 percent of HP Inc's personal computer shipments in the second quarter of its 2026 fiscal year, up from more than 35 percent the quarter before. ABB's launch comes amid a skills gap, with the International Energy Agency counting 2.4 energy workers nearing retirement for every new entrant under 25 in advanced economies. StartLux plans to launch a consumer-facing local AI agent soon, followed by enterprise solutions next year, and Gao pointed to usage-based fees, local-deployment licensing and industry-specific solutions as possible business models.

stories.Headline: NPCI launches new tech subsidiary for AI, blockchain
stories.Summary:
The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) announced on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, that it has set up NPCI Tech Solutions Limited (NTSL), a new wholly owned technology subsidiary. NPCI described the company as the technology and innovation arm of the group, created to build capabilities beyond its core payments mandate. Vishal Kanvaty, who has been with NPCI for nearly a decade and has led the development and commercialisation of several market innovation platforms, was named its managing director and chief executive officer. One report says he was previously NPCI's chief technology officer.

NTSL will concentrate on artificial intelligence, blockchain, digital financial infrastructure and Global Capability Centre (GCC) services. It will also provide technology services for digital public infrastructure programmes, including eKYC Setu and the Unified Ticketing Platform (UTP). According to NPCI, several of the platforms Kanvaty helped build now fall within the new company's focus areas. NTSL is NPCI's fourth wholly owned subsidiary, joining NPCI International Payments Limited (NIPL), NPCI Bharat BillPay Limited (NBBL) and NPCI BHIM Services Limited (NBSL).

NPCI said the company was formed with the approval of its board and the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). Dilip Asbe, NPCI's managing director and CEO, said technology has been central to NPCI's journey and its contribution to India's digital transformation. He added that advances in AI and other emerging technologies are opening new possibilities across digital infrastructure and financial services, and that NTSL was created to pursue them and strengthen the group's technology capabilities. Asbe said he was pleased to have Kanvaty lead the subsidiary and was confident that his experience and leadership would guide its growth and future direction.

NPCI was established by the RBI and the Indian Banks' Association and runs India's retail payment and settlement infrastructure, including the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), RuPay, IMPS, NACH, the Aadhaar Enabled Payment System and National Electronic Toll Collection. The new subsidiary follows other recent technology moves. At the Global Fintech Fest in September, NPCI launched AiNxt and AtOM, platforms that help enterprises build AI agents and automate workflows across the payments ecosystem. NPCI also has a multi-year research partnership with IISc, announced in March 2024, focused on AI and blockchain development. The articles do not set out specific next steps or timelines for NTSL beyond its stated areas of focus.

stories.Headline: Vultr launches 20 MW AI supercluster in Chennai, eyes 1 GW India capacity
stories.Summary:
Vultr, a privately held US-based cloud infrastructure provider, has launched a 20 MW artificial intelligence supercompute cluster in Chennai, the company said at a recent launch event reported on 5 November 2026. The cluster is powered by more than 10,000 AMD Instinct MI355X graphics processors alongside AMD EPYC central processors, and is built for large-scale AI training and inference. Vultr described it as its second-largest supercompute deployment worldwide, behind its facility in the United States. One report cited Tamil Nadu minister Keerthana, who called the launch an important milestone for the state's AI and digital infrastructure.

Alongside the cluster, Vultr India signed a memorandum of understanding with StartupTN, the Tamil Nadu Startup and Innovation Mission, to give eligible startups in the state cloud credits and preferential pricing. Early-stage startups can receive US$2,500 in credits plus a 20% discount, while eligible startups beyond the early-stage funding threshold can receive US$45,000 in credits along with the same discount. A separate report from 3 November says Vultr expects to make the Chennai cluster operational by March 2027, which suggests the capacity will come online in stages. Vultr also plans to bring newer generations of GPUs and CPUs to India over time, and it intends to scale its Indian AI capacity to 600 MW by 2028 and 1 GW by 2029.

Kevin Cochrane, Vultr's chief marketing officer, said India is not only consuming AI but is where the buildout is happening, pointing to its engineering talent. He said the company made its first strategic investment in India because of its base of platform engineers, cloud-native architects and developers, and because it is a major centre for engineers working on open-source AI models. He added that Vultr is scouting sites across India for the multi-stage expansion, so future capacity will not all sit in Chennai. Keerthana said the state is committed to developing technologies that shape the future and to making Tamil Nadu an important centre for them under Chief Minister Vijay.

State officials stressed that the benefits should reach smaller businesses. MSME Minister P. Mathan Raja said access to computing could help firms with product design, software testing, inventory management and efficiency, adding that the true measure of technology is the opportunity it creates. Atul Anand, additional chief secretary in the IT and Digital Services Department, noted the state has about 16,000 startups and urged Vultr to offer accessible pricing, especially to Tamil Nadu firms. Singai G. Ramachandran, chairman of the startup mission, said infrastructure should be judged by its impact and not only by megawatts.

Vultr began operating in India in 2022 with data centre regions in New Delhi-NCR, Bengaluru and Mumbai, first using AMD EPYC processors and later adding AMD Instinct GPUs including the MI300X, MI325X and MI355X. The company runs across six continents and says it has been building its developer relations work in India through open-source support, hackathons and access to compute. The reports do not give an investment figure, the exact site in Chennai, or details of power and cooling arrangements. Further detail on those points would have to come from Vultr or state authorities.

stories.Headline: What to know about the labor market amid AI bubble concerns
stories.Summary:
U.S. stocks fell sharply on Thursday, November 5, 2026, as a broad sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks combined with new uncertainty after Tuesday's election. The tech-heavy Nasdaq took the biggest hit, dropping more than 5.5%. Headlines in the coverage also put the S&P 500's decline at 4.4%, and Thursday was the worst day for that index since President Donald Trump's tariffs rattled markets in April 2025. Nvidia shares were down about 7.5%, to $181.60, and the CBOE Volatility Index jumped nearly 70%, to 28.18.

Investors appear to be worried that the election results could slow or complicate the construction of AI data centers. One question raised is whether Democratic victories could bring more scrutiny or delays for those projects. Voters in many communities backed proposals aimed at limiting or restricting data center construction, and there were 41 separate ballot initiatives on the subject. NBC News also reported that the U.S. added 165,000 jobs in October, with the unemployment rate falling to 4.1%, though the articles do not tie that report directly to the market moves.

Michael Armstrong, a financial advisor with Armstrong Advisory Group, said the big single-day swings and heavy volatility are not unusual when a revolutionary technology is developing quickly. He said the price movement did not look logical or healthy, and argued the reaction may be about more than which party won, pointing to the data center ballot measures. He urged investors not to panic, saying no good decisions come out of panic, though he added that anyone holding a concentrated portfolio could reasonably take a second look at it. He noted that stocks have historically tended to recover after downturns and cautioned against reacting to a single day's losses.

Armstrong also said affordability was a major driver for voters, with the price of gas front and center in people's minds this year. With the war in Iran continuing, he advised consumers to plan their winter budgets carefully, since prices may not fall quickly and he does not think anyone will fix the affordability problem overnight. The Yahoo Finance report described the story as still developing. A calendar on the page listed more labor market data due Friday morning, including unemployment, nonfarm payrolls and a preliminary University of Michigan sentiment reading.

stories.Headline: Blue Wave, New AI Rules? What Democratic Control of Congress Means for AI Regulation - The National Law Review
stories.Summary:
Democrats won majorities in both the House and the Senate in the November 2026 midterms, a result a Foley & Lardner attorney says will bring the biggest shift in federal AI policy since generative AI went mainstream in 2022. In an analysis dated November 5, 2026, Peter Z. Stockburger wrote that when the 120th Congress convenes in January 2027, Democrats will hold the committee gavels, the hearing calendar, subpoena power and the legislative agenda. He expects oversight to come first, with hearings, document requests and executive testimony on AI safety incidents, model testing, competition and data practices starting in early 2027. Separately, a Central Asian outlet reported that leaders from Central Asia, Jordan and Azerbaijan met in Astana on November 6, 2026, for an Aqaba Process meeting on how AI is changing the meaning of security.

On the legislative side, the analysis points to several specific proposals. House Democratic committee leaders have already asked five frontier AI companies to report misalignment and safety incidents to Congress within 48 hours of detection. Senator Maria Cantwell of Washington, positioned to chair the Senate Commerce Committee, has released a six-principle framework calling for enforceable safety standards developed by NIST, independent pre-release audits and mandatory incident reporting. Representative Lori Trahan of Massachusetts has a discussion draft, the CLAIM Act, that would create a federal cause of action against developers when AI systems cause harm through conduct that would be unlawful if a person did it, without overriding state law. Democratic leaders on the tax-writing committees have also named AI and data center taxation, including rolling back bonus depreciation, as priorities.

The analysis argues that a push in Congress to preempt state AI laws is now far less likely to succeed, because Democratic proposals generally treat federal rules as a floor rather than a ceiling. State laws in California, New York, Colorado, Texas and Illinois would therefore keep setting the compliance baseline. It advises companies to prepare for oversight, catalog past safety and security incidents, and keep up state compliance, especially the January 1, 2027, effective dates for the California and Colorado automated decision-making technology laws. It also recommends reviewing indemnities and liability clauses in contracts and aligning governance with NIST frameworks, and with standards such as ISO 42001 and AIUC-1.

The author cautions that the blue wave has limits. President Trump keeps the veto pen and the executive branch's enforcement and litigation arms through January 2029, and his administration has opposed binding AI safety mandates. Most bills still need 60 votes in the Senate, Democrats disagree among themselves on licensing, chartering, liability and taxation, and attention will soon turn to the 2028 presidential cycle. Bipartisan measures such as kids' online safety and chip export controls, along with bills like the FRONTIER Act and the AI Kill Switch Act, have the best odds. He notes that 66% of registered voters in an October survey wanted more AI regulation, and that a poor Republican showing could lead the administration and congressional Republicans to reconsider their resistance, opening the door to compromise.

stories.Headline: Kyndryl, AWS Partner on Agentic AI Modernization Solution
stories.Summary:
Kyndryl, a New York-based provider of mission-critical enterprise technology services listed on the NYSE as KD, announced on Nov. 5, 2026 an integrated agentic modernization solution built with Amazon Web Services. The offering pairs Kyndryl Agentic Modernization, delivered as services-as-software, with AWS Transform. Its aim is to help customers modernize applications quickly, lower transformation risk and set up technology foundations ready for AI. Kyndryl was a launch partner for AWS Transform and says it has worked with AWS to move customers past project-based modernization toward a repeatable approach.

The solution combines Kyndryl's AI-enabled workflows and engineering expertise with AWS Transform so organizations can assess, plan and execute modernization at scale. Services-as-software is built on the Kyndryl Agentic Framework and scaled through Kyndryl Bridge, using pre-built agentic workflows to run complex programs on much shorter timelines and at significantly lower cost. Customers also get access to Kyndryl's skills in cloud, security, compliance, FinOps and mission-critical operations, with governance, resilience and business continuity maintained. Stated goals include establishing a continuous approach to modernizing applications, infrastructure and core systems, building resilient and AI-ready architectures, and reducing technical debt while improving operational efficiency.

Shawn D'Souza, Kyndryl's Global Modernization Leader, said many organizations still treat modernization as a destination when it should be an ongoing business capability. In his view, companies that can modernize continuously will be better placed to adopt AI, adapt to change and create long-term value, and Kyndryl is working with AWS to help customers build that capability at scale. He pointed to findings from Kyndryl's first global modernization report. Nearly 50% of respondents said they are behind schedule on modernization goals, while early adopters running agentic AI in production for modernization did better, with 67% saying they are ahead of or on track, compared with 51% of other organizations.

A report from Simply Wall St on Nov. 6 said the launch came alongside the opening of a Cyber Defense Operations Center in Paris, which will serve European customers with a focus on cybersecurity, AI operations and threat intelligence. That report framed the AWS offering as part of Kyndryl's effort to turn its role running core IT into repeatable, automated modernization services. It said the key test is whether these launches show up in signings and profit metrics over the next few quarters, especially in Kyndryl Consult and revenue tied to large cloud providers. Investors can also watch whether management holds its fiscal 2027 guidance of constant currency revenue flat to down 2%, while seeking better earnings and cash generation from newer AI-led services. Kyndryl describes itself as the world's largest IT infrastructure services provider, serving thousands of customers in more than 60 countries.

stories.Headline: Claude Code sends your email address to websites
stories.Summary:
A GitHub bug report opened on November 5, 2026 by a user named taylor-edwards says that Claude Code, Anthropic's AI coding agent, exposes the user's email address to outside websites. According to the report, the email address appears in the User-Agent header that the tool sends when it carries out web searches. The user says they now receive dozens of scam emails every day as a result, and that this happened without their permission. The report was filed against the anthropics/claude-code repository as issue number 107757, and it lists the affected platform as macOS, Claude Code version 2.1.318, running inside tmux.

The reporter does not want a setting that can be switched on or off. They argue that the behavior should be taken out of the tool altogether, saying it helps no one, does nothing for services that dislike agentic traffic, and does not protect anyone's anonymity online while giving scammers a useful list of addresses. They also say they are moving their company to a different tool called Pi, running through OpenRouter, because they no longer trust Anthropic to protect their privacy. The issue was labeled by GitHub's automation as a bug, with tags for security, tools and macOS. At the time of the snapshot it showed 449 thumbs-up reactions, along with dozens of laughing, eyes and rocket reactions.

Responsibility rests with Anthropic, which builds and maintains Claude Code, and the issue is still open. The articles do not include any reply from Anthropic. The comments shown are from other users, and several are sarcastic about whether the company cares about privacy, with one saying that corporations care about privacy and another asking if people thought Anthropic cared. A few users disagreed with the criticism, as shown by thumbs-down reactions on those comments.

For context, a separate article published the same day on CIO.com, a sponsored piece from CrowdStrike, discusses how companies should govern Claude Code. It describes the tool as running on employee workstations with the developer's own permissions, able to reach source code, credentials and cloud systems. It says Anthropic provides centrally managed settings and hooks for controlling the agent, but argues these see only what the agent intends to do, not what happens afterward. That article does not mention the email address report, and nothing in either piece says what Anthropic will do next about the issue.

stories.Headline: Stocks tumble as AI concerns rattle markets; financial advisor urges investors not to panic
stories.Summary:
Technology stocks suffered a steep selloff on Thursday in the United States, with the Nasdaq falling more than 5.5 percent and about $3 trillion wiped off the value of S&P 500 companies. The slide came days after Tuesday's midterm elections, in which Democrats did well, and investors feared the result could mean tougher regulation of artificial intelligence and a slower build-out of data centers. Thursday was the worst day for the S&P 500 since tariffs rattled markets in April 2025. Wall Street's volatility "fear gauge" soared, and the turmoil triggered margin calls and rattled retail investors and hedge funds alike.

The damage spread across Asia on Friday, according to Reuters. Japan's Nikkei dropped 6 percent, its deepest one-day fall since April 2025, while benchmark indices in South Korea and Taiwan plunged more than 8 percent after the opening bell before trimming losses. Taiwan's market closed down 4.5 percent, and its weekly decline of 12.2 percent was the biggest since 1991. Samsung Electronics fell nearly 6 percent, SK Hynix 9.4 percent and TSMC 4.7 percent at the close, while Kioxia and SoftBank Group each slid 11 percent. CoreWeave, an AI cloud computing provider, dropped 10 percent and its five-year credit default swap spreads widened to a record.

Authorities in Asia moved to calm the selling. South Korean Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il temporarily eased rules on retail investors' leveraged investments, and several people told Reuters that Taiwan's Ministry of Finance told senior executives at state-owned banks to support the market. Investors sought safety in bonds, the US dollar, the yen and the Swiss franc, and the US 10-year Treasury yield sat at 4.838 percent, near its lowest since September 9. The 10-year Japanese government bond yield fell as much as 9 basis points to 1.795 percent, the lowest since June 30. Christopher Forbes of CMC Markets called the episode a disaster, saying clients who were long stocks were carried out and that margin calls and complaints poured in.

Financial advisor Michael Armstrong of Armstrong Advisory Group urged investors not to panic, saying big swings are not unusual with a revolutionary technology and that no good decisions come out of panic. He suggested the reaction may owe as much to the 41 ballot initiatives on data center construction as to which party won, and said anyone with a concentrated portfolio could reasonably take a second look. Steve Sosnick of Interactive Brokers said the market may be oversold in the short term but the underlying questions cannot simply be wiped away. Allen Huang of Mega Financial Holding argued the selling may be near its final stage, noting that TSMC briefly hit its daily limit-down circuit breaker. Masahiko Loo of State Street Investment Management described it as a reassessment of AI policy risk rather than of the AI cycle itself.

The political worry adds to doubts about returns on huge AI infrastructure spending, and analysts said markets have yet to fully weigh local opposition to data centers. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa said the state will introduce laws to protect residents from data center impacts, citing rural communities. At the time of the Reuters report, Nasdaq futures were up 0.8 percent while European stock futures were down 1 percent, a sign that sentiment remained fragile. Armstrong noted that stocks have historically recovered after downturns.

stories.Headline: Airbnb is building an AI travel agent
stories.Summary:
Airbnb said on Thursday, November 5, 2026, that it is building its own AI travel agent and plans to release it in the first half of 2027. The company shared the plan in its third-quarter shareholder letter and on the earnings call that followed, saying it intends to build an "AI-native Airbnb." The agent is designed to help users research, plan and book trips on the platform. It is separate from Airbnb's AI customer support assistant, which is already running.

The company says the agent will not be a plain chatbot. It will draw on a library of hundreds of travel-specific interface elements, including maps, photos, comparisons, calendars and itineraries, and assemble them in real time to fit each request. If a user wants a car rental, for example, the agent would generate a custom display for it, and it will also help invite co-travellers. After a booking is made, the agent is meant to help with changes to a reservation, payment problems, refunds and rebooking, and to offer 24-hour safety support, though Airbnb did not say what that support will involve. Over time, Airbnb wants it to plan a whole trip in one place, across homes, hotels, services and experiences, and CEO Brian Chesky said it will be able to go outside Airbnb's own listings while staying within travel.

Chesky explained the thinking on the earnings call. He said current AI agents such as Muse and Instinct handle simple routine jobs like restaurant reservations and appointments, but that travel is different because discovering where to go and stay is part of the experience. He cited a figure that 80 percent of travelers say they enjoy researching trips, and said people want to look at photos, compare homes and decide together with their companions. In his view, general-purpose agents are not the best tool for that, which is why Airbnb is making its own. He described the interface as "post-chat-based," with less text, though it will keep a chat element.

The announcement came with strong results. Revenue rose 19 percent to about $4.9 billion in the third quarter, with net income of $1.9 billion, and Airbnb raised its 2026 revenue growth forecast to the high teens from the mid-teens. Chesky said it was the company's fastest revenue growth in more than three years. The company also said it shipped more than 50 products and features in the quarter, nearly 70 percent more than a year earlier, and that its existing AI support assistant resolved around 40 percent of customer support issues without human agents, up from roughly 30 percent the previous quarter. Airbnb had previously said only that the agent would arrive within the next year, so the first-half 2027 window is a firmer commitment.

stories.Headline: Congresswoman Calls for AI Superintelligence Ban as Democrats Prepare to Take Control of Congress
stories.Summary:
Rep. Yassamin Ansari, an Arizona Democrat, posted on X on 4 November 2026 that the top of the Democratic agenda on day one should be a pause on advanced AI development, regulation of what she called an out of control industry, and a ban on artificial superintelligence. She wrote the post after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the November 2026 midterms. The call was not new, since she had made a similar appeal at a September press conference in Phoenix. Coverage noted that her post expresses her own priorities and does not reflect an existing Democratic Party policy or any federal prohibition now in force.

Her demands connect to the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act of 2026, which she helped introduce as one of its original lawmakers. Rep. Greg Casar formally introduced the House version, H.R. 10538, on 24 September, and Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the Senate version, S. 5493, on 23 September. Both bills would create a Department of Artificial Intelligence with authority to oversee advanced AI development and enforce safety requirements. Under the House bill, an advanced system is generally one trained with at least 10^25 integer or floating-point operations, and a proposed Secretary of Artificial Intelligence would adjust that threshold each year as training efficiency improves.

The pause would last until the new department is fully staffed and has set the required safety rules, and during that time covered systems could not be trained, modified or fine-tuned, including through recursive self-improvement. One account said violations could bring up to 20 years in prison, a penalty that coverage has compared with those for unauthorized nuclear-weapons development. Neither bill has become law. The House measure was referred to the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, and the Senate measure went to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

The proposal arrives against a different approach from the White House, which has treated advanced AI as part of strategic competition with China and has relied on voluntary commitments. Its Ratepayer Protection Pledge secured company promises on power supply, infrastructure costs and community investment, but it created no binding safety regime for frontier models. Roughly 45 data-center ballot measures appeared in communities during the midterms, and about 33 restrictive ones passed, according to tracking cited by Tom's Hardware. Those votes were driven mainly by utility bills, noise and infrastructure strain, not opposition to AI research itself. Analysts say the bill still has to solve several problems, including a legally defensible definition of artificial superintelligence, Democratic unity behind such heavy penalties, Senate procedural hurdles, and the risk that a pause without an international agreement could cede ground to rivals.

stories.Headline: New program looks to prepare Northern Kentucky students for Artificial Intelligence workforce of tomorrow
stories.Summary:
Northern Kentucky University, the Northern Kentucky Chamber of Commerce and We Lead CS have teamed up to launch a program called "AI for Every Future," aimed at preparing local students for a workforce shaped by artificial intelligence. The program places 20 high school students with regional employers to work on real workplace problems using AI tools. Participating industries include logistics, healthcare and manufacturing, among others. WCPO reported on the effort on Friday, noting that it is meant to prepare students both in the classroom and on the job.

The students are expected to use AI to tackle practical challenges that companies face. We Lead CS CEO Alicia Sells offered one example, in which an advanced manufacturer has a complicated manual that line workers must understand. Students could run that manual through several AI systems, test it, summarize it and look for clearer ways to communicate its contents. Businesses that want to take part can attend a virtual employer information session on Nov. 19, from 9 to 10 a.m. EST, and a registration link was provided with the original report.

Students said the hands-on experience is the main draw. Rylan Harper, a student at Allen County High School, said he is excited about going out into the real work field next semester and gaining real work experience. He described that kind of experience as important for someone who is still learning. Sells and the organizations behind the program see the real-world pairing as the core of what makes it useful for young people.

The effort also responds to a broader regional need. A report released by BE NKY in April found that job growth in the region may not be enough to support its economy over the long term. Over the past 10 years, the region gained 3,600 new residents each year but only 1,800 new workers. NKY Chamber of Commerce President and CEO Brent Cooper said the program could give the region an edge over competitors both nearby and across the country. He said the hope is that businesses will sign up, bring students into their pipeline and create new jobs and opportunities, which he described as the point of the whole effort.

stories.Headline: A brutal sell-off for AI stocks sends Wall Street reeling, and the S&P 500 tumbles 4.4%
stories.Summary:
Wall Street suffered a sharp sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks, with the S&P 500 index falling 4.4% in a single session. The Associated Press described the drop as brutal and said it left the market reeling. The articles identify the trigger as worries about AI stocks rather than any single company or announcement. The report was published on November 5, 2026.

The selling did not stay in the United States. A second Associated Press report said benchmarks across Asia declined after the rout on Wall Street, with shares trading lower on the same AI worries. That points to a wave of selling that moved from New York to markets in the Asia-Pacific region as the next trading day began. The excerpts supplied do not list the individual Asian indexes or give figures for them.

Neither article, in the portions available, names a specific person or institution as responsible for the decline, and neither includes statements from company executives, regulators or analysts that can be paraphrased. The text that came through is mostly the Associated Press website's navigation menus and headlines, so the detailed explanations the full reports likely contain are not available here. For that reason, the only firm figures are the 4.4% fall in the S&P 500 and the date of publication. Details such as the size of the losses in dollars, the biggest individual decliners, or the moves in other U.S. indexes cannot be reported from this material.

The wider context offered by the page is limited, though other headlines on the Associated Press business section point to a busy news period, including midterm election coverage and tariff and inflation reporting. The articles do not say what comes next for markets, whether the sell-off is expected to continue, or whether any official response is planned. Investors will likely watch how stocks open in the following sessions to see whether the AI-related worries deepen or ease. For now, the clear facts are that U.S. stocks fell hard on November 4 into 5, that Asian markets followed lower, and that concern about AI companies lay behind the move.

stories.Headline: This week in the big AI data center buildout.
stories.Summary:
The Verge's roundup on the AI data center buildout opens with a link to a Bloomberg piece, which is the first announcement its headline points to. The Verge, in a post by Jay Peters dated November 4, 2026, pointed to Bloomberg's report that the AI data center boom is set for upheaval after the Democratic rout in the US election. The roundup itself gives only that headline and notes that AI data center projects keep appearing across the US, often meeting opposition from locals worried about their impact. The substance behind the Bloomberg headline comes from coverage of the same election by Investing.com, which reported that Democrats swept the midterms on Tuesday and captured majorities in both the Senate and the House.

According to Investing.com, the result triggered a selloff in AI data center stocks, as investors braced for tighter regulatory oversight, possible rollbacks of tech tax incentives and heightened antitrust scrutiny. Democrats flipped traditionally Republican-leaning states including Texas and Kansas. Texas and Georgia, which together account for roughly a third of all AI data center spending and projects, both saw Democratic wins at the governor level. In premarket trading, CoreWeave fell as much as 3.2%, Applied Digital fell 3% and Nebius dropped 1.3%, while Oracle, which recently priced a combined $20 billion stock and debt offering, was down about 1.2% after gaining 5.85% on Tuesday.

Analysts at Evercore ISI, led by Amit Daryanani, said a more restrictive environment for data center development could create incrementally more negative sentiment for AI infrastructure names. They added that the initial reaction would likely be to sell AI stocks, and that the real question is how far the political shift alters fundamentals and whether other factors such as inflation and yields offset it over time. Several Democratic governor-elects have already voiced support for more AI regulation. Any Democratic legislation would still need President Trump's signature to become law, a check analysts say limits near-term legislative risk, though it does not fully remove the threat of executive branch regulatory action or the chilling effect that uncertainty can have on capital spending.

The political change adds a federal layer to pressures that were already building. Data Center Watch found that in the second quarter of 2026, at least 45 data center projects worth $68 billion were disrupted by local opposition. The broader AI trade was also weakening before the vote: the Goldman Sachs Broad AI basket fell 15% in October and had dropped more than 24% from its peak heading into Wednesday's session. The Verge's roundup also lists local fights, including a scuttled $1.6 billion project in a small Wisconsin city and a delayed data center in San Diego. Neither article lays out specific next steps, so what the new Congress does on data center rules remains to be seen.

stories.Headline: Global media discuss mass communication in AI era - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
A sub-forum of the 7th World Media Summit in Beijing on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, brought together representatives of media, think tanks, government departments and other institutions from China and abroad. They called on media organizations to use intelligent technologies to deliver reporting that is accurate, fair, authoritative and trustworthy. The breakout session was titled Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Chinese Modernization and centered on the theme of AI Plus and a new consensus on global communication governance. Participants discussed how media can adapt to change, seize opportunities and meet challenges together in the AI era.

The event also included several firsts and launches. The world's first bionic humanoid robot news anchor made its official debut there. The sub-forum held a signing ceremony for the Xinhua News Agency AI Industry Alliance (Beijing Base), along with a launch ceremony for a research project on mobile news image technology and authenticity standards. Participants urged their media colleagues to build consensus and to promote dialogue among civilizations through openness and inclusiveness. The summit itself runs from Nov. 5 to 9 and draws nearly 500 delegates from nearly 330 mainstream media outlets, think tanks, government departments and international organizations across 112 countries and regions.

Two speakers were singled out in the reports. Huo Xiaoguang, vice president of Xinhua News Agency, said traditional mainstream media around the world are generally going through major transformations as AI develops. He said China's mainstream media are carrying out systematic reforms to secure new competitive advantages in the emerging communication ecosystem. Xinhua, he added, is willing to work with all parties to safeguard media credibility, promote the inclusive sharing of technological achievements, and strengthen mutual understanding and friendship among different civilizations.

Bayo Onanuga, the Nigerian president's special adviser on information and strategy and his spokesman, said the profound impact of AI can no longer be ignored, and that much of it is positive. He argued that, unless people were willing to return to the Stone Age, they must face the trend and treat it seriously. The summit is co-hosted by Xinhua News Agency and the People's Government of Beijing Municipality. Ahead of the gathering, Khalid Mahmood, chairman of the Board of Governors of the Institute of Strategic Studies Islamabad and a former Pakistani ambassador to China, told Xinhua that the summit would give news organizations worldwide an important platform to explore how technological progress can serve the public interest. He noted that AI has made it possible to access, process, analyze and distribute information at unprecedented speed, and he planned to attend.

stories.Headline: Seattle schools to block AI tools, limit screen time
stories.Summary:
Seattle Public Schools announced at a special board meeting on Wednesday that it will block student access to Gemini AI, Minecraft and other generative artificial intelligence tools starting Monday. The block also covers Google Search AI summaries and applies to students from kindergarten through 12th grade. YouTube will be blocked for students in kindergarten through fifth grade, and Minecraft will remain available only when it is part of a teacher-led lesson. Superintendent Ben Shuldiner said students had found a way to reach Google's AI through search and use it to get to things they should not. Parents also rallied outside district headquarters that day, calling for a pause on AI in classrooms.

The new guidance also cuts back on device use in elementary schools. Students in kindergarten through second grade no longer get individual assigned devices and are limited to up to 30 minutes of screen time per day. Starting in January 2027, the same approach expands to grades three through five, with no individual devices and a limit of up to 60 minutes a day. District and state tests do not count toward those limits, and teachers may not use devices as rewards, incentives or free time. Families can still check out computers so students have internet access at home.

Shuldiner said the problem began during the pandemic, when the district handed out laptops to everyone and then stopped closely controlling what students could access. He said the district is now being thoughtful and critical after starting from a position of being overwhelmed by technology. Assistant Superintendent of Academics Mike Starosky said devices should be used for education and not as incentives. The superintendent also said he welcomes parent suggestions about other games to block, and that the district is training students and educators on AI and the guidance around it.

Parents and a watchdog group said the changes are only a start. Seattle Families for Intentional Tech asked the school board to pause student-facing generative AI until products are reviewed for safety, legality and educational value for minors, and to notify families if AI is used to assess student work. The group also wants an advisory committee of caregivers and teachers, a public list of classroom apps with their privacy policies, annual caregiver consent before students' personal information is collected, and paper-based alternatives on request. District parents Ashley Worobec and Danica Novle voiced concerns about children being led down dangerous paths by AI, misinformation, and the use of classroom data for commercial purposes. Shuldiner said middle and high schools are next, though the approach there will differ because older students take coding, career and technical education, and AP computer science classes that require screens.

stories.Headline: US midterm aftermath: Can Democrats put the brakes on America's AI data centre boom?
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday's midterm election day, voters in 10 states decided 41 local ballot measures about data centers, as Forbes reported and Fast Company relayed. Ohio had 21 of them, Illinois seven, Maine four and Kansas three, while California, Florida, Nevada, New Jersey, North Dakota and Wisconsin had one each. Of the measures with reported results, all but one went against data center development. More than 80% of voters in Ashville, Ohio, rejected an agreement tied to two proposed data centers, though that vote does not itself stop construction. Emporia, Kansas, approved a ban on high-impact facilities, Ottawa, Kansas, barred those drawing more than 25 megawatts, and Boulder City, Nevada, turned down a plan to allow them in the Eldorado Valley Transfer Area.

The one exception was Harwood, North Dakota, where voters rejected a measure that would have required extra review of certain industrial projects, data centers included. Democrats also won governorships after campaigning on slowing construction. Gina Hinojosa ousted Greg Abbott in Texas, becoming the state's first Democratic governor in more than 30 years, and has called for an immediate moratorium on new data centers, while Amy Acton in Ohio and Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia also ran on slowing builds. CoreWeave's unsecured bonds due in 2031 fell as low as 79.5 cents on the dollar, with its 2030 and 2032 debt near distressed levels and yields above 15%. The company's shares had already dropped about 40% over the prior month, and it reports third-quarter results on November 10.

Representative Ted Lieu of California, vice chair of the House Democratic Caucus, said Democrats will hold public hearings on AI and pass reasonable guardrails next term, and will also consider limits on new data center construction. He faulted Republicans for failing to regulate the industry while they ran Congress. Shakeel Hashim wrote in Transformer that the odds of strong AI legislation had jumped, noting that a Democratic gain from 54 to 56 Senate seats would leave the party needing only four Republicans to beat a filibuster. He predicted Congress could pass something tougher than the bipartisan FRONTIER Act within months, including mandatory testing and approval of the most powerful models and tighter limits on federal preemption of state laws. Representative Robert Garcia of California, the incoming House Oversight chair, posted "LAWYER UP" as the results came in.

Markets first wobbled, then rallied, with the S&P 500 closing 1.6% higher on Wednesday. Taiwan Semiconductor fell 1.5% and SoftBank 3.2% in early Asian trading before those fears faded, and South Korea's KOSPI ended up 0.6%. Analyst Ben Thompson argued that the last constraint on the AI buildout is political, and that opposition to data centers is not a partisan issue, since both parties see it as a winner. Elon Musk spent roughly $474 million on the midterms, and 44 of the 106 congressional candidates he backed lost, including Ken Paxton in Texas, who lost to James Talarico by 12 points. Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz gave $116 million and Greg and Anna Brockman $50 million, mostly to Republicans, and several candidates who ran against data centers beat them.

stories.Headline: AI decision models gain traction for enterprise agents
stories.Summary:
Sarvam AI has launched Prism, an open-weight decision model built on its 105-billion-parameter foundation model, Sarvam 105B. The launch was reported on November 4 to 6, 2026. Unlike a typical language model that writes out text, Prism is fine-tuned to make structured choices, such as routing a customer-support query, moderating content, running fraud checks and screening for security problems. It looks at the available options in one processing pass and returns a probability for each.

Sarvam reports that Prism averaged 71.8 across three evaluation indices, with a median response time of 44 milliseconds on an Nvidia B200 GPU. The company says this was the highest average among the 25 decision models it tested that responded in under 100 milliseconds. It also reports that Prism gave consistent results across 2,000 questions after a fixed ordering mechanism was applied, so that the order of the answer options did not change its decisions. Its observed error rates were lower than predicted across the confidence thresholds tested, including in Indian languages. The weights are released under the Apache 2.0 licence, which lets developers adapt the model and run it on their own infrastructure, and Prism is also available through an API.

Beyond Sarvam's own figures, outside developers have offered mixed readings. Sandipan Kundu, a developer relations and AI engineer, wrote on X that the model looked capable but questioned whether the 44-millisecond claim holds in real use, citing a p95 latency of 420 milliseconds in his tests. He also raised the cost of self-hosting a model of this size. Faizan Shaik, a software engineer at Atlan, shared results from the company's Decision Bench, where Prism scored 91.5 per cent across 1,071 decisions on 36 public datasets, placing 12th among 22 models, with a median latency of 65 milliseconds on a B200 GPU. Ananthanarayanan S, managing director for India at Articul8, said Sarvam's launch adds to the range of general-purpose models, while his company's Bivia is aimed at different enterprise needs, such as abstaining when evidence is thin.

The launch puts Sarvam alongside other builders of decision models. Kerala-based ConvAI Innovations made Laya, an open-weight model meant to run locally on devices, and PurpleTalk's Sthānika AI lab in Hyderabad built Sieve, a family of models that return probabilities for a fixed set of answers. The category gained visibility with Jev, the first public model from TypeSafe AI, and Microsoft and Perplexity have since introduced their own offerings. Articul8 is developing Bivia, a multimodal decision model for evidence-backed decisions across text, images, documents, audio and video. The articles note that Sarvam's figures are company-reported, and that independent testing across comparable workloads will be needed to show how Prism performs in production.

Only one article was provided, and it covers a different deal from the one named in the headline. It reports that Oracle has ended a $7 billion contract to lease artificial intelligence chips to Tencent, according to a report from the Financial Times that other outlets repeated. The deal, which was revealed in September, would have given Tencent access to about 100,000 high-end AI processors through Oracle data centers in Southeast Asia. The article says Oracle dropped the arrangement after U.S. officials raised concerns about it.

The contract ran for five years and was billed as the largest foreign chip leasing deal Tencent had signed. It was said to include an upfront payment of around 30% of its estimated value. The article says U.S. officials were worried about Chinese access to sophisticated computer technologies, and that Oracle backed out after being asked about the pact. It does not say whether Oracle will keep any advance payments, or how the cancellation will affect the company's financial forecast.

The articles supplied contain nothing about Microsoft winding down an Oracle deal to rent AI cloud capacity, so that part of the story cannot be confirmed from this material. Neither Oracle nor Tencent is quoted directly in the piece, and the account rests on the Financial Times report as relayed by GuruFocus. The cancellation is described as cutting off a significant source of contract revenue just as Oracle is investing heavily in more AI computing power. The article adds that it raises questions about whether other overseas customers could face similar limits.

The article describes the episode as evidence of regulatory uncertainty facing cloud providers that use offshore facilities to serve Chinese technology companies. The next development to watch, it says, is whether Oracle discloses the financial impact and whether it can replace the lost capacity with commitments from other customers. Beyond that, no further steps are laid out, and the Microsoft connection in the headline is not addressed. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Parents sue Google after discovering what daughter was doing with AI on school Chromebook
stories.Summary:
The parents of a 13-year-old girl identified as Emma filed a lawsuit against Google on Monday 2 November in a court in California. They allege that she used Google's AI technology on a school-issued Chromebook to plan a possible suicide and her funeral. The case is believed to be the first to accuse Google of negligence over AI-powered search features reached through a school laptop. Another report describes the 104-page complaint as coming from parents in North Carolina, and says it centers on the Gemini chatbot.

According to the complaint, Emma could not open Google's Gemini app or OpenAI's ChatGPT at school, since both had been blocked, but she could still use Google's search engine and its AI features. The family says she had no history of mental illness, yet within months of using the search tools she fell into what the filing calls a quiet spiral into a severe psychological crisis. The other report says that as her chats grew more frequent through January and February 2026, the AI convinced her she had major psychological disorders and that suicide was the only escape. On 17 March, the school's monitoring software flagged a document titled "Funeral" and alerted her parents. Her mother then found her writing a farewell letter, and her father stepped in.

Andrew Liddell, one of the family's attorneys, told AFP on Thursday 5 November that schools should switch off search until Google removes AI mode from search or can ensure every student is safe while using AI. Google says its AI Mode has safeguards against self-harm and works to stop people from bypassing them. Company spokesperson Jose Castaneda told AFP that Google is reviewing the claims and takes them very seriously. The articles do not report any ruling or response in court.

The suit adds to growing legal pressure on technology companies over harms to young people. OpenAI faces several wrongful death lawsuits, including one from the parents of 16-year-old Adam Raine, who died by suicide after allegedly getting harmful advice from ChatGPT. In January, Google and Character.AI agreed to settle several lawsuits brought by families of teenagers out of court. Meta was recently ordered to pay New Mexico $25 billion after a jury found it liable for deceiving users about privacy and content moderation. Separately, Google, TikTok and Meta sued California on Wednesday to block a law, signed by Governor Gavin Newsom in September, that bans addictive social media features for users under 16 and is due to take effect on 1 January 2027.

stories.Headline: GitLab 19.5 integrates agentic development, enhances AI governance
stories.Summary:
GitLab released version 19.5 of its DevOps platform on October 15, building agentic software development and governance directly into the product. The headline change is that the GitLab Model Context Protocol server is now generally available. That lets compatible tools such as Claude Code and Cursor reach GitLab's wider tool catalogue and call GitLab Duo Agent Platform agents and flows. A separate announcement reported on November 5 added capabilities for workflow automation, supply chain security, credential management and AI cost monitoring, aimed at helping organisations govern AI-generated code as it moves from development to production. GitLab said active users of agentic development on its platform grew 200% year over year over the last three months.

The release adds several controls for external agents. Security teams can see which agents are in use, by whom and against which projects, and administrators can choose which MCP toolsets are exposed, a simple form of least-privilege design. On GitLab.com, MCP rate limits are 60 requests per minute for Free users and 600 for Premium and Ultimate users, with reconnects and retries counted. Externally connected agents such as Claude Code, Cursor and Codex can be brought into AI governance through the GitLab CLI, with qualifying sessions recorded by user, agent, project and timing, and audit events can be streamed to a SIEM system. The Duo CLI also gains an auto mode, off by default and controllable at instance, group and project levels, which lets agents run tools without approval for each command, while anything marked "Always Deny" stays blocked.

GitLab Secrets Manager, built on OpenBao, is now generally available, uses existing group and project permissions, scopes secrets to the jobs that need them and generates audit events. GitLab says it can save up to 50% compared with hosting a separate vault, and it is due on GitLab Self-Managed with the 19.5 release. GitLab Artifact Central is in beta on GitLab.com, with Self-Managed availability planned for later this month, and the company claims it can cut total cost of ownership by up to 50% against alternative tooling. GitLab Dependency Firewall, in early access, checks packages against organisational policies on age, vulnerability severity, malicious package detection and licence compliance before they enter a build. The /goal command is also generally available, letting developers describe an objective and have GitLab Duo hand implementation and verification to a governed flow.

All of these claims and figures come from GitLab itself, as reported by TechGig and ET CIO, and the company says the changes connect development stages through shared workflows, policies and audit records. It argues that organisations often use separate tools for coding, issue tracking, CI/CD, security, artifact management and deployment, which makes consistent identity and policy controls hard to maintain. The company also reported that over the same three months secure repositories grew 100%, user namespaces rose 80% and CI/CD pipelines grew 40%. It is expanding security configuration profiles too, so organisations can centrally set excluded paths, analyser images and full-history scans for Secret Detection and SAST.

The release arrives as the wider conversation about agentic AI shifts toward governance. A CIO.com piece sponsored by HCLTech cited a survey in which 87% of participating enterprises use generative or agentic AI in IT operations, and research from Omdia in which respondents expect about 43% of major AI initiatives to fail. It argued that governance should be built in from the outset, with human oversight kept for high-stakes decisions. The ET CIO article said GitLab also plans to make Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5 and 5.1 available, though the text provided cuts off before further details.

stories.Headline: CloudBolt Adds New AI Agent Governance Capabilities to Its Cloud Management Platform
stories.Summary:
CloudBolt Software, based in Rockville, Maryland, announced on November 5, 2026, new agent governance capabilities in its CloudBolt CMP cloud management platform. The features let AI agents provision and manage infrastructure under the same policies, permissions and limits that already apply to people. Platform teams decide which actions agents may run and which credentials and authentication they can use, and CMP enforces those choices every time an agent acts. The company said the capabilities are available now to all CMP customers, and teams new to the platform can try them through a no-cost plan.

Under the new setup, OAuth support maps each AI agent to a named user in CMP, so the agent inherits that person's groups, environments, rights and limits rather than relying on a shared service account. Agents can see only the blueprints administrators have published in the governed catalog, and policy pre-fills fields such as cluster, network and cost center. A request that would normally need 20 inputs to provision on Amazon EC2 may need only two or three. Administrators can require a maximum lifespan so agent-built resources do not run indefinitely, and approval workflows, budgets and quotas apply to agents just as they do to people. Each CMP action also carries its own AI setting, so routine work like power, snapshot and resize can be opened to agents while deleting a server stays limited to people, and a hidden action does not appear to agents at all.

CMP checks every agent action against the user's permissions and policies when it runs, regardless of how the request was worded or which AI model sent it. Agent requests land in the same order history and job records as portal requests, giving teams one audit trail across people and agents. A new agent dashboard records each session, including the tools called, the orders placed and the user the agent acted for. Yasmin Rajabi, chief operating officer at CloudBolt, said customers keep asking how to allow AI agents to do real infrastructure work without losing control, and that the same catalogs, approvals and cost policies customers built over the years now apply to every agent. Co-founder Alexandre da Rocha said that because every interface is becoming a chat window, the guardrails are what must be unified, and that CMP decides whether a given agent may act whatever the prompt says.

The company pointed to a gap between adoption and oversight, citing Deloitte's 2026 State of AI in the Enterprise survey of 3,235 business and IT leaders. In that survey, 74% expected their companies to use AI agents at least moderately by 2027, but only 21% said they have a mature governance model for agentic AI. The new capabilities build on Model Context Protocol support CloudBolt introduced in May and the natural-language interface that arrived with the CMP redesign in August. The announcement comes as other vendors also add agent controls, with Google Cloud extending governance tools across its agent runtimes and Smartsheet adding oversight features to its work platform.
