stories.Headline: 3 charged in scheme to use AI to impersonate CEOs and attorneys to steal $129 million
stories.Summary:
Three people have been indicted in a scheme that used artificial intelligence to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys in order to steal about $129 million, prosecutors said Thursday, November 6, 2026. The charges are wire fraud and aggravated identity theft, and the indictment was filed in a U.S. District Court in New York. The defendants, Jacob Soall, 41, Sharon Hazan, 54, and Guy Sheetrit, 42, were arrested between June and September. Prosecutors also charged them with money laundering.

Over more than a year and a half, the group targeted thousands of companies around the world. Their victims included hospital systems in Missouri and California, a bank in Rhode Island, a financial technology company in the United Kingdom, a mutual fund company in Massachusetts and a pet food company in Florida. The scheme usually began with an email that appeared to come from a chief executive, asking an accounting employee for help with a confidential transaction. The group then arranged a phone or video call in which AI copied the executive's voice and sometimes image. The defendants then directed employees to contact an attorney at a major law firm, a role the group also impersonated, often using attorneys from the United Kingdom.

According to court documents, the impersonated attorney told employees to wire large payments to bank accounts around the world. The money was then converted into cryptocurrency to conceal its origin before being distributed to the three defendants and others involved. Soall was described by prosecutors as having used a handwritten script titled "Lawyer Call" to seem like a real attorney. The defendants come from Spain, the United Kingdom, Israel and the United Arab Emirates. Their lawyers did not immediately respond to requests for comment, and it was not clear whether Hazan had an attorney.

James C. Barnacle, Jr., an FBI Assistant Director in Charge, said in a statement that criminals are increasingly using emerging technology to commit large-scale fraud and that the bureau is adapting to disrupt them. Each wire fraud charge carries a maximum sentence of 20 years, while aggravated identity theft carries two years, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office. Hazan had been convicted in 2008 in a New York court of conspiracy to commit bank fraud. The case is ongoing, and the articles do not say when a trial will begin.

stories.Headline: Consumers Are Now Worried About an AI Bubble, Michigan Survey Says
stories.Summary:
The University of Michigan released its preliminary November 2026 consumer survey on November 6, 2026, and it found that average households were voicing concern about a possible AI bubble. Survey director Joanne Hsu described the mood as "growing anxiety," though the survey attached no percentage to the idea. The headline Index of Consumer Sentiment rose to 51.0 from 48.0 in October, a gain that only returned it to its November 2025 level. Stock-owning households with the most wealth grew gloomier by 5%, while lower- and middle-wealth households became more upbeat.

The split matters for investors in the AI-heavy Nasdaq fund. QQQ fell 13.41% over the past month, while the broader S&P 500 fund SPY fell 5.39%. NVIDIA alone made up about 7.6% of QQQ as of June 30, and that concentration leaves the fund more exposed to AI spending. SPY also holds companies such as Berkshire Hathaway that do not depend on AI spending. Hsu linked the wealthier households' decline to a turbulent period in markets.

The survey also shows that high prices remain the dominant household worry. About 57% of consumers said, without prompting, that high prices had reduced their living standards, up from 46% in February. October's reading was the second-lowest on record, and the November figure is the highest since August. Interviews ran from October 20 to November 2, so the survey missed the midterm elections and a sharp market selloff on November 5, when the S&P 500 fell 4.36%.

Inflation expectations are another limit on relief. Year-ahead expectations fell to 4.3% from 4.7%, and long-run expectations slipped to 3.4%, still above the 2024 range of 2.8% to 3.2%. Analysts cited in the coverage argue that such elevated expectations leave lower interest rates with little room to soften a tech selloff. The next tests are the October CPI report, due November 10, and the final November sentiment reading, due November 20.

stories.Headline: LA Council seeks citywide data privacy policy amid AI, ALRP tech
stories.Summary:
On Friday, November 6, 2026, the Los Angeles City Council voted unanimously to approve a motion calling for a standard data privacy policy that would apply across the entire city. The action was prompted by concerns about how data is kept, how long it is retained, and what privacy rights residents have when artificial intelligence and automated license plate reader technology are involved. The motion was introduced by Councilwoman Monica Rodriguez, and the vote was unanimous. Reporting on the vote came from several outlets that day, including the Daily News, MyNewsLA.com and the Daily Breeze. The motion directs the Information Technology Agency and other relevant departments to return with recommendations for a citywide policy and supporting policies.

These would set standards and safeguards for how data is collected, stored, retained, accessed, shared and disclosed. Departments are also expected to report on cybersecurity measures and protection against unauthorized access or security breaches. The reports are to cover appropriate and prohibited uses of city technology and data, along with transparency, accountability, oversight and auditing requirements, among other things. The articles do not give specific deadlines or dollar figures for these reports. Rodriguez, speaking at the council meeting, said the city has an overarching responsibility to keep residents' privacy and personal information protected.

She argued that departments should not operate under different standards when collecting and sharing sensitive data, whether the tools involved are license plate readers, artificial intelligence or other new technologies. She also noted that the Los Angeles Police Department has faced significant scrutiny over its technology use, and said the same level of scrutiny and protections should apply to every city department. Rodriguez said that if the city is serious, these standards should become routine in how each department adopts new technologies. The articles describe the motion as a response to growing public and council concern about surveillance tools and data handling, with the LAPD's use of automated license plate readers as a central example. The articles do not say when the departments' recommendations are due or when a final citywide policy might be adopted, so the next step is the departments' reports back to the council.

stories.Headline: Google faces scrutiny over student suicide planning with AI chatbot
stories.Summary:
A lawsuit filed in California state court on Monday accuses Google of failing to protect a teenage girl who used its Gemini chatbot to plan her own death. The parents of the girl, identified only as "Emma," say she began using Gemini on her school-provided Chromebook when she was 13. According to the complaint, she discussed different methods of suicide with the chatbot, planned her own funeral, and received help hiding her feelings from her family. Google moved the case to a federal court on Wednesday.

The parents say they learned of the situation after school software flagged a document Emma wrote about her funeral plans. Their lawsuit claims Google wove Gemini into all of its products without warning parents or schools, as part of a race to grow the chatbot's user base. It also alleges that Google knew the version Emma used, Gemini 3 Flash, was unsafe and mishandled mental health issues raised by users. The suit seeks monetary damages. Reporting does not say how much the parents are asking for.

José Castañeda, a Google spokesperson, said the company is reviewing the claims. He said Google has worked extensively with medical professionals and academic experts to build features that help young people find critical support and trusted resources. Google has also said it will turn off Gemini by default for student accounts at schools. Schools that want students to keep access to Google Search, however, will still have to accept AI features such as AI-generated summaries.

The case adds to growing scrutiny of how technology companies protect young users from harmful content, and the articles note a related settlement involving Snap over teen social media addiction. The articles do not report how the court will rule or whether the claims will be proven. They also do not say whether Google will change Gemini's safety design beyond the default setting change for students. The case will proceed in federal court, where its outcome will be decided.

stories.Headline: Filing: Airbnb discloses that it has the option to invest in and license tech from CEO Brian Chesky's stealth AI lab; source: Chesky has self-funded it so far (The Information)
stories.Summary:
Airbnb has disclosed in a quarterly SEC filing that it sold intellectual property to a private AI lab founded and controlled by its CEO, Brian Chesky. The transaction took place in November 2026, and the company said it generated $7.1 million in cash for the IP and expense reimbursements combined. Chief technology officer Ahmad Al-Dahle also holds a stake in the lab, and both executives work for that entity. A separate filing item, reported by The Information, says Airbnb has the option to invest in and license technology from the lab, and that Chesky has self-funded it so far.

The filing does not describe the specific intellectual property that changed hands. It also does not explain how the price was valued or separate the purchase price from the expense reimbursements. Shareholders therefore have little detail about what the company actually received for its money. The arrangement was reviewed under Airbnb's related-party rules, and a special committee of independent, disinterested directors approved it.

That committee structure is designed to address conflicts when executives are on both sides of a deal. The responsibility for the arrangement rests with the company's board and its executives, since the special committee signed off on the transaction. Chesky and Al-Dahle are the people with direct ownership stakes in the lab that bought the IP. The articles provide no direct statement from either executive about their reasons for the deal.

The filing itself is the main source of what the company has said publicly. The context is that the deal links a public company's assets to a private venture controlled by its leadership, a pattern that draws scrutiny from investors. The articles do not say what the lab plans to build or whether Airbnb will exercise its option to invest or license the technology. Any future decision on that option would appear in later company filings, and the articles give no timeline for it.

stories.Headline: AI boom runs into US voter backlash
stories.Summary:
In the midterm elections held this week, Democrats won control of both houses of Congress, and in many places voters also turned against local datacentre development. Voters in at least 38 jurisdictions backed restrictions or outright bans on datacentres, according to The Washington Post. Redbud Consulting, a polling firm that tracked ballot initiatives, counted 44 measures across 10 states seeking to restrict datacentres, of which 38 had passed so far, many of them moratoriums and bans. In Hubbard, Ohio, more than three-quarters of voters backed a total ban, with resistance crossing party lines. Only one measure passed that allowed a datacentre to proceed, and even that one, in a North Dakota city, required developers to pay for independent reviews and hold public hearings.

The biggest shift came in Texas, which accounts for more than a quarter of all planned datacentre capacity. Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican governor Greg Abbott after campaigning for a moratorium on new builds, making her the first Democratic governor there since 1990. James Talarico beat Ken Paxton in the Senate race, flipping the state Democratic for the first time since 1988. Axios reported that Texas was expected to supply more than 41 percent of added datacentre capacity in 2028, and Bloomberg said about 13 gigawatts of capacity is now exposed. Democrats also won governor races in Arizona, Georgia and Ohio, and Ohio's governor-elect, Amy Acton, backed a conditional moratorium and proposed that developers cover their own power and water costs.

Industry figures and critics read the results very differently. Adam Kovacevich, a former Google executive who runs the tech trade group Chamber of Progress, said the results show little evidence of a mandate against AI or datacentres, noting that Democratic gubernatorial candidates who opposed bans won more often than those who backed them. He urged people not to mistake an anti-Trump wave for an anti-tech one. Alejandra Montoya-Boyer of The Leadership Conference's Center for Civil Rights and Technology called it the first true AI election, citing NBC polling that showed three in four voters opposed datacentres. Brad Carson of Americans for Responsible Innovation said voters had sent a clear message that they want rules, while Libby Cantrill of PIMCO expects more delays, permits and concessions even without statewide moratoria.

Analysts said the effects will mostly reach future projects rather than those already under construction or approved through 2027. Only 11 percent of Americans say they would welcome a large facility nearby, and developers have been accused of rushing projects, lobbying local politicians and hiding behind NDAs. Developers may now face longer waits for permits and grid connections, fewer tax tips, and more concessions to communities, and some projects could move to states like Louisiana or Georgia. North Dakota's Harwood, where three-quarters of voters rejected restrictions on industrial development, shows that some places remain welcoming. Trump can still veto federal legislation, so Democrats would need substantial Republican support to override him, and the debate over the race with China continues.

stories.Headline: Aligning MLLMs with the Latent Structure of Human Cognition via Behavior-Derived Semantic Dimensions
stories.Summary:
A research paper posted to arXiv by Ning E, Changde Du, Yizhuo Lu and Huiguang He describes a new way to align Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) with human cognition. The authors noted that it was unclear whether these models' internal representations and decision criteria match the latent structure of human thinking, even though the models perform well on many reasoning tasks. Their approach builds on an earlier behavior-derived semantic embedding space in which objects are represented along 66 interpretable dimensions. Those dimensions were derived from 4.70 million human Odd-One-Out judgements. The paper was listed on doi.org on November 7, 2026.

The framework works by taking each triplet of objects and inferring the most salient decision dimension behind a human's choice. That dimension is then converted into a linguistic rationale grounded in the dimension, so the model learns both the final pick and a justification that fits the inferred criterion. According to the abstract, this improves the model's consistency with human similarity judgements while keeping competitive performance on standard multimodal benchmarks. The authors also report that searchlight Representational Similarity Analysis on an independent fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset showed increased representational alignment between the model and humans. They present these results as evidence for a data-driven way to bring human cognitive structure into MLLM alignment.

Separately, a second paper on arXiv, titled Memorilla and authored by Adibvafa Fallahpour, Parsa Idehpour, Vignesh Kothapalli, Nikita Mounier, Shirley Wu, Shayan Pardis and Jure Leskovec, addresses a different limitation of language models. It introduces a memory system that gathers information from a whole document collection into a fixed number of query-dependent memory tokens for a frozen LLM. The paper states that the first version was submitted on October 15, 2026, and that the latest revision, version three, was posted on November 3, 2026. Using only 16 memory tokens, the system outperformed baselines including Mem0 and MemoRAG on five of eight benchmarks. On FactKG it reached 84.33% accuracy, compared with 80.43% for full-context inference, while using 108 times fewer tokens to represent the source documents.

The Memorilla authors also tested the system in a TextWorld environment, where it reduced an agent's tendency to revisit rooms it had already explored. Its average success rate rose from 18.6% with full-history in-context learning to 24.2%. The paper presents this as a step toward continually learning AI systems that accumulate and use knowledge across long interactions. The articles do not describe any deployment plans or next steps beyond these experimental results and the publicly available code and project website.

stories.Headline: Thomas College Secures $3 Million Federal Grant to Bring AI Into Every Academic Discipline
stories.Summary:
Thomas College in Waterville, Maine, has received a $3 million federal grant to bring artificial intelligence into every academic program, train its faculty and give students hands-on experience with AI tools. The award comes from the U.S. Department of Education's Title III Strengthening Institutions Program and will fund a multi-year project called "Building the College of the Future." The college says the goal is to help students build practical, critical and ethical AI skills before they enter the workforce. Faculty members will be central to the effort, and the college plans to update its curriculum to fit the needs of each discipline. Officials have also framed the project as part of a broader push to prepare graduates for workplaces where AI is already in use.

The grant will pay for several parts of the plan, starting with the hiring of an AI Specialist in Residence who will work full-time for two years. That specialist will help professors in fields such as English, biology and business understand how AI is changing their professions. The money will also cover software subscriptions, curriculum revisions, new staff positions and a learning space equipped for applied technology work. Students there will be able to work with fabrication, robotics, automation, data collection and computer-aided design equipment. Thomas College has said the project will affect all students and could also lead to new majors as demand for AI-related skills grows.

Thomas College President Jeannine Uzzi has said that faculty members need help understanding changes that have happened since they completed their own education. She gave the example of a biology or English professor who earned a PhD ten years ago and never studied how AI would affect medical research or publishing. Uzzi has also said that individual professors, not administrators, will decide whether students must use AI in their courses and how it fits into assignments. Provost Jeremy Qualls described the grant as aligned with the college's focus on career-driven education. The college has also said it will address academic honesty, student privacy and overreliance on AI tools.

The announcement comes as colleges across the country debate whether students should be allowed to use AI for schoolwork. Some institutions have banned the tools in certain courses, while others are looking for ways to teach responsible use. Thomas College has taken a middle path, building AI education into its programs while leaving classroom rules to faculty. The college has also pointed to a 99 percent job placement rate for its graduates and said it expects that record to hold as employers adopt AI. Central Maine Growth Council President and CEO Garvan Donegan said the grant could help local businesses, especially small companies, find workers who understand how to use AI well.

stories.Headline: Gary Marcus Warns OpenAI Could Become ‘WeWork Of AI’ — And Nvidia May Pay The Price
stories.Summary:
Gary Marcus, an NYU professor emeritus and longtime AI critic, told CNBC's Fast Money that OpenAI could become the "WeWork of AI," a comparison he had made before. The remarks, made in an interview published on November 6, 2026, drew on OpenAI's repeatedly delayed plans for an initial public offering. He noted that WeWork, the once high-flying office-sharing company, never completed its IPO, while OpenAI keeps pushing its own listing back. Stocktwits reported the interview on November 7, 2026.

Marcus said the larger worry is what happens if OpenAI cannot sustain its current valuation and has to sell at a discount, for example to Microsoft. He asked what the effect on Nvidia would be if the company, which he called the poster child of the AI trade, took a big hit. He also argued that Nvidia is well run and that its chips are strong, but questioned whether demand for them is unlimited and whether the buyers can turn a profit. He singled out neocloud companies, which rely heavily on outside financing, as the most vulnerable, noting that their borrowing costs are rising. Marcus cited a Bank of England study of roughly 10,000 decision-makers that, in his reading, found only limited productivity gains from AI so far.

The articles do not identify any formal regulatory or contractual change; the central claims are Marcus's own assessments. Responsibility for those views rests with Marcus himself, who framed them as warnings rather than predictions, and who said that shifts in investor confidence could matter as much as financial fundamentals. The reports include no response from OpenAI or Nvidia. On the day of the interview, the S&P 500, Nasdaq-100 and Dow ETFs were all modestly higher in after-hours trading, and retail sentiment on Stocktwits toward the S&P 500 ETF was bearish. The articles do not say what will happen next.

stories.Headline: Facing Backlash, Meta Pulls Down Terms of Service That Pushed New AI Media Strategy
stories.Summary:
Meta has indefinitely paused proposed changes to its terms of service for business account users, which would have allowed the company to scrape content from those users' websites to support its AI products. The company posted a notice in its Business Help Center on a Thursday, saying the update, which had been set to take effect November 20, 2026, was now paused and that existing terms remain in effect. Earlier in the timeline, the new terms were first reported by Nieman Lab on October 15, and they were initially due to take effect October 30 before being pushed back. Critics said the update would have also shifted responsibility for errors produced by faulty AI onto customers.

Opposition came from news publishers in the United States and Europe, who argued that the terms would force them to supply their content free of charge to AI products that could compete with them for readers and advertisers. Democratic Senator Adam Schiff of California wrote to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg urging the company not to implement the terms, calling them a serious abuse of its power. Four European press associations sent a joint letter to the European Commission, claiming the plan violated the European Union's Digital Markets Act. The News/Media Alliance, led by Danielle Coffey, asked Meta to withdraw the terms and hold discussions with publishers before any future changes.

Meta's vice president of communications, Andy Stone, said on October 28 that the company wanted to consult with industry groups and leaders before making policy changes, and that implementation could be delayed beyond November 20. A Meta statement to Nieman Lab said the company was pausing the changes while it continued engaging with stakeholders. Courts in Norway and Brazil had already issued preliminary injunctions to block the terms following lawsuits from media organizations in those countries. The United Kingdom's Competition and Markets Authority has also opened a formal investigation into whether Meta was abusing a dominant market position.

The broader context includes a fine Meta received two weeks before this report for illegal use of customer data, along with a layoff of 8,000 employees earlier in the year. The articles do not say when or whether Meta will return with revised terms, though the company has said it will provide a further update when it has more to share. The outcome of the UK investigation and the court cases in Norway and Brazil remains unresolved in the reporting. For now, the company says its existing terms remain in effect for business accounts.

stories.Headline: Military spouse uses AI to help veterans navigate VA benefits
stories.Summary:
Tracy Contrino, a Calvert County military spouse, has launched TheClusterFix, an independent nonprofit that uses an AI assistant called Frank to help veterans find and understand benefits information from the Department of Veterans Affairs and other federal sources. The idea grew out of her own frustration while trying to help her husband, who served 18 years in the Army and National Guard and is rated 100% P&T disabled, navigate the VA system. Contrino says the tool is meant to show veterans where to start and what steps may come next, not to replace the VA or give legal or medical advice. The organization stresses that it is not affiliated with or part of the VA.

Frank is built to draw on publicly available VA and federal information and to answer questions quickly, without appointments or waiting. Contrino says many of the questions it receives so far concern general and education benefits, and the group has begun working with higher education institutions. Hope Bald, the board president, says Frank surfaced information for her own claim that a service officer had not mentioned, and the team is now expanding its guidance on VA education benefits. The nonprofit is free for veterans, relies on grants and community donations, and hopes to add partnerships, a broader resource center and more data collection that does not identify individuals.

Contrino describes getting a disability rating as a tedious process that can take months or even years, and she says denials can leave veterans confused about their next move. She says many veterans feel alone in the process and give up, even though some available benefits can be significant for them and their families. Her stated goal is to save veterans time, possibly days, weeks or months, spent searching websites or waiting on hold, and not to compete with the VA. Bald says she and Contrino want veterans to receive clear answers rather than confusion.

A separate opinion piece on RealClearDefense, written by Rob Schroder, founder and CEO of SteerBridge and a Marine Corps veteran, makes a related argument about federal benefits. It refers to a presidential executive order directing the Department of War and the VA to modernize record sharing, build digital tools and improve transition assistance. Schroder argues that AI should speed up processing by organizing records, summarizing evidence and automating administrative tasks, but that qualified VA personnel, not AI, should decide whether a veteran is entitled to a benefit. He says SteerBridge has helped agencies cut processing times, such as handling education benefits in seconds rather than weeks and screening disability evidence in hours rather than months, and he urges judging modernization by measurable results for veterans.

stories.Headline: Saudi Arabia introduces AI principles for media
stories.Summary:
Saudi Arabia has introduced a national framework that governs how artificial intelligence may be used in media, setting out principles meant to promote transparency, accuracy and accountability. The AI Principles in Media document, reported by the Saudi Press Agency, asks media practitioners and content creators to say when material has been generated or assisted by AI. They are asked to use clear labels, watermarks or metadata so audiences can tell synthetic content from authentic records. The move follows growing use of AI tools to produce text, images, video and audio. Officials cite concerns about misinformation, intellectual property rights and user privacy.

The guidelines lay out eight core principles that cover transparency and disclosure, factual accuracy and credibility, privacy and the protection of public figures, and the prevention of misleading content. They also address accountability across the full life of a piece of content, impartiality and integrity, public awareness and empowerment, and ongoing impact assessment with regulatory compliance. The framework cautions against treating generative AI as an authoritative source of information. It stresses that human verification, deepfake detection and awareness of possible algorithmic bias are needed. Taken together, these points set expectations for how newsrooms and creators should check and label their work.

The Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority, known as SDAIA, worked with the General Authority of Media Regulation to promote responsible use of the technology. The two bodies organized the AI for Impact forum, which brought together more than 250 media professionals, digital influencers and content creators. Participants discussed ethical standards and practical risks at each stage of production, from research and scriptwriting to editing, audience analytics and impact assessment. The forum also marked the launch of the Impact Creators program, which will offer theoretical instruction and practical training in content verification and professional production standards. According to the reports, the program aims to help Saudi creators use AI safely and effectively while strengthening trust in the Kingdom's digital media sector.

stories.Headline: Teaching AI to build scientific models
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Anthropic published a guest post on November 6, 2026, written by Jakob Macke, Daniel Gedon, and Stefan Wahl of the ELLIS Institute Tübingen and the University of Tübingen, about how AI is beginning to change scientific modeling. They recalled that in 1951 the Cambridge computer was out of action for six months, which left Andrew Huxley to solve the equations he and Alan Hodgkin had written for how a squid nerve cell fires by hand, a process that took him over three weeks. The authors use this episode to argue that a model is only useful if it yields understanding, not just a fit to data. Their point is that many different models can reproduce the same measurements, so a scientist needs to know which features make a model work and which set it apart from failures. The post breaks scientific modeling into three steps: building the model, constraining it by tuning its parameters to real measurements, and interpreting what it says about the real system.

Constraining is the step where AI has advanced most, and the authors describe simulation-based inference, a method that runs a simulator many times, for example about 100,000 times for a model like Hodgkin-Huxley, and trains a neural network to return the range of parameters that could have produced a given output. Once trained, that network can analyze new data in seconds, a speed that let researchers point telescopes at colliding neutron stars while the signal was still detectable. The authors also note that the same method has been applied to nerve cell models, where it shows which parameters the data pins down and where another experiment is needed. The authors describe the building step as now partly handled by AI as well, with LLM-based agents writing candidate model code, running it, comparing it to data, and revising until the fit is good enough. They say several such systems have appeared in the past two years, and that until recently designing the model itself was thought to be something only humans could do.

They caution that a model that replicates data does not by that fact provide insight, since different models can explain the same data equally well. An agent that returns only one of those models, they argue, hides the rest, in the same way a single best-fit set of numbers does. The post places this work in the longer history of the Hodgkin-Huxley model, which remains the standard description of electrical activity in neurons more than 70 years later. The authors note that Hodgkin and Huxley shared the 1963 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, and that a later team found a related potassium channel protein with four identical pieces, matching the fourth power the original model had required. The article does not describe a specific next step beyond the continued development of these methods, so it leaves open how far AI agents will take over the building and interpreting of models.

stories.Headline: ‘Triplets of Belleville’ Director Sylvain Chomet Fires Back at AI Accusations Over Dior Film Featuring Robert Pattinson’s Voice: ‘Everything Was Drawn by Hand’ (EXCLUSIVE)
stories.Summary:
Sylvain Chomet, the French animator behind "The Triplets of Belleville" and "The Illusionist," is denying that generative AI was used to make his six-minute Dior short "Christian Dior's Night in Color," which features voice work from Robert Pattinson, Rihanna, Josh O'Connor, LaKeith Stanfield, Louis Garrel and Camille Cottin. The film, produced by Aton Soumache, drew online criticism after some viewers pointed to visual glitches, including a character with six fingers, as signs of AI generation. Dior presented the film as a celebration of traditional craftsmanship to launch its 2026 holiday season, which made the accusations especially awkward for the brand. Chomet and Soumache told Variety that the film was made with traditional 2D techniques, with characters, backgrounds and key poses drawn by artists.

The pair acknowledges that an automated interpolation system helped generate some in-between frames to smooth movement, but they insist generative AI never produced the artwork. Soumache says the film took seven months to make and employed roughly 20 people, including six animators, storyboard artists, designers, background artists, compositors and editors. He describes the interpolation tool as a small part of the process used for repetitive work. Chomet adds that such tools automate the mechanical side of animation rather than the creative work, and he notes that the artists now draw on digital tablets rather than paper.

Chomet also says the criticism is ironic given his long commitment to hand-drawn animation. He recalls that when Disney and others declared traditional 2D dead after the rise of CGI in the era of "Toy Story," he chose to keep making hand-drawn films. He says he has stayed faithful to drawing throughout his career while still willing to use the tools technology offers. Soumache adds that Dior approached them because it wanted Chomet's distinctive drawing style, and he points to his own history of championing 2D work after years in CGI.

The short draws on episodes from Dior's history, including his friendship with Marlene Dietrich, his ties to Hollywood and the 1949 Junon gown. It also takes inspiration from an early idea behind Jonathan Anderson's Cruise 2027 collection, the shift from black-and-white to Technicolor in cinema. In the story, Dietrich, preparing to shoot in Los Angeles, asks for a colorful Dior gown, setting Dior and his seamstresses against the clock. The articles do not report any response from Dior to the accusations.

stories.Headline: A message from President Gold on artificial intelligence - University of Nebraska Medical Center
stories.Summary:
On November 4, 2026, University of Nebraska System President Jeffrey P. Gold, MD, sent a message to faculty and staff about artificial intelligence, and the system then rolled out Executive Memorandum 48 on Thursday, November 5. The memorandum sets university-wide expectations for the secure, ethical and responsible use of AI. The system has also obtained an enterprise license to ChatGPT, and faculty and staff are encouraged to take the Generative AI Security Essentials Training in Bridge. Those who complete it at Kearney, Lincoln, Omaha or the Nebraska College of Technical Agriculture will automatically receive access to an enterprise ChatGPT account, while UNMC is still working to implement that access.

Faculty and staff who use a free or non-enterprise version of ChatGPT for university work are expected to move to the enterprise version by the end of the fall 2026 semester. Most employees should find the baseline account sufficient, though heavy users can request credits for additional use. Faculty may also request enterprise access for students, and all employees already have Microsoft CoPilot. The NU System is also forming a new NU AI Governance Group to carry out the memorandum, with representatives from faculty, staff, the NU AI Institute, and the legal, compliance, ITS, procurement and business and finance offices. That group will decide which tools are acceptable for routine work, which need an approved exception, and how AI use should be disclosed.

President Gold wrote that the university must harness AI's potential while protecting university data, sensitive information and intellectual property, and he acknowledged that moving to approved platforms may be a significant change for people who built workflows around other tools. He also stressed that the memorandum does not decide whether AI should be used in teaching or research, since faculty keep authority over their courses and principal investigators keep authority over their research. At UNMC, Emily Glenn, dean of the McGoogan Health Sciences Library, along with John Windle, MD, leads implementation as co-chairs of the Campus Steering Committee for Healthcare Artificial Intelligence. Dr. Windle was named UNMC's first associate vice chancellor for healthcare artificial intelligence last month by Chancellor H. Dele Davies, MD.

The changes come as AI evolves quickly and universities everywhere face difficult questions about its use. Norwich University, a separate institution, has announced its own Artificial Intelligence Center to offer courses and research on machine learning and related fields, with an emphasis on ethical and responsible AI. Questions about getting started with enterprise tools can go to the NU ITS help desk at nusupport@nebraska.edu or 866-472-3970. The article notes that additional resources and answers to frequently asked questions will be shared in the weeks ahead.

stories.Headline: Prediction: Wall Street Has the Post-Midterm Artificial Intelligence (AI) Trade Completely Wrong
stories.Summary:
Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the 2026 midterm elections, and Wall Street has since been weighing what that means for the artificial intelligence trade. Investors are considering whether tougher regulation could slow the building of AI data centers in the United States, since several candidates campaigned on data centers as a controversial issue tied to rising utility costs. The Motley Fool's Adam Spatacco, writing on Nov. 6, said the market appears to see a silver lining. If Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta were forced to spend less on infrastructure, their free cash flow could improve, and a tighter supply of computing capacity might let existing operators charge more.

Spatacco argues that this view overlooks another possibility, which is that the big cloud companies simply build abroad. He points to projects already announced before the election: Microsoft plans more than $10 billion across the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Kuwait through 2030, and Amazon plans more than $5 billion in Mexico over 15 years. Alphabet has a $15 billion AI infrastructure investment planned for Visakhapatnam, India, between 2026 and 2030, while Meta has committed 13 billion Canadian dollars to a 1-gigawatt data center in Alberta and has a 168-megawatt lease in Jamnagar, India. He notes that overseas building brings its own permitting, energy and U.S. semiconductor export control hurdles, and that Democratic wins may not produce new federal limits, since President Trump keeps veto power and details of any legislation are sparse.

On the corporate side, Meta's president and vice chair, Dina Powell McCormick, told The Wall Street Journal on Nov. 4 that the results could complicate domestic data center development. She said starting new domestic projects may be harder, and she asked whether the company needs to build outside the United States. Spatacco, for his part, doubts the companies would pause expansion for two years while waiting for the 2028 presidential election, and he says that moving spending overseas would not deliver the lasting cash flow gains investors expect. He stresses that a slowdown in U.S. construction is not the same as a slowdown in global AI investment.

Politico, in a piece published on Election Day, described the political risk from a different angle. It reported that Democrats have promised greater oversight of the technology, and that their probes could reach not only the large tech companies but also the financiers behind the boom. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a potential next chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has warned of an AI bubble comparable to the 2008 financial crisis and has asked financial firms for more information on their AI exposure. An unnamed financial industry official expects more scrutiny of how expansion is funded through private credit funds, while JPMorgan Asset Management's David Kelly said policymakers must first decide how to regulate the technology before moving any legislation. Goldman Sachs Research estimates $1 trillion will be invested in AI-related projects worldwide this year, and the Nasdaq Composite had already fallen more than 7% over the prior month amid AI concerns.

stories.Headline: Ramp data shows AI spending stalling despite usage increase
stories.Summary:
Ramp, the spending platform, released data showing that companies are using more AI tools but their spending on them has stalled, flattening out over late summer even as token volumes rose. Token spend grew only 1.5 percent across August and September, after growing 42 percent from June to July. The report's lead economist, Ara Kharazian, told TechCrunch that almost all AI spending comes from venture-backed, high-growth tech companies. He added that a slowdown among the top 1 percent of firms was enough to pull overall revenue down, even with volumes still climbing.

The top 1 percent of firms, which Kharazian described as the most heavily invested in AI, spent just under $10,000 per employee in August and September, below their summer peaks. Median firms spend $12 to $15 per employee each month, while the top 10 percent spend $600 to $1,000. In September, OpenAI cut API prices in half for its GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna models. Anthropic also reduced prices for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, a move the company said in a recent filing cut its revenue growth by about $600 million. October showed an 8.9 percent rebound in token spend from September to October, though Kharazian said the headwinds remain strong.

Kharazian attributed the slowdown mainly to competition rather than weak demand, pointing to price cuts from OpenAI and Anthropic, enterprise offerings from Meta and Nvidia, and cheaper open-source models from China and the United States. He also noted that companies are getting better at controlling AI costs by using default settings that avoid expensive models, setting employee budgets, and routing tasks to cheaper models. Bloomberg reported that Anthropic's potential valuation fell from $2 trillion in early October to between $1.2 trillion and $1.3 trillion, and that OpenAI lowered its proposed valuation from $1.4 trillion to $1.25 trillion. Both companies have also reportedly cut their fundraising goals.

Investors have assumed that new AI uses, such as personal agents, will sustain rapid growth in spending, much as AI coding did. Kharazian is skeptical, saying that personal agents are not as economically productive as coding and may not drive the same level of spending. He said the data suggests the era of hypergrowth in AI spending may be over. The report comes as Anthropic nears an IPO, which raises questions about how investors will view the company's revenue trajectory.

stories.Headline: Salem City Council to vote on clarifying code to halt AI data centers
stories.Summary:
On Monday night, the Salem City Council will hold a public hearing to decide whether the city's current zoning code already excludes artificial-intelligence or hyperscale data centers like the one planned at the Mill Creek Corporate Center. The meeting is set for 6 p.m. on Monday, Nov. 9, at Loucks Auditorium in the Salem Public Library at 585 Liberty St. S.E. It will also be livestreamed on YouTube in English and Spanish. The article notes that residents packed a previous council meeting on the Mill Creek project in July 2026. The question before the council is whether an interpretation of the existing code could bar these facilities in Salem.

If the council finds that the code already excludes them, the interpretation would effectively halt such projects without writing entirely new rules. The articles give no further detail on the specific language being considered. The hearing is a public process in which the council will weigh that interpretation and decide the matter. A separate report from Salem Reporter also says the developer, Verrus, has offered the city a $10 million package ahead of the code interpretation.

The articles do not describe the terms of that offer or how the council has responded to it. The dispute reflects growing local concern over large data centers and their impact on land use and infrastructure. The available reporting does not say what the council will decide or what steps would follow a vote in either direction. Readers should check Salem Reporter and the city's meeting materials for updates after the hearing.

stories.Headline: IREN Says New AI Cloud Customers Are Prepaying 90% of the Chips
stories.Summary:
IREN, the AI cloud operator, said on November 5, 2026 that a new customer will prepay most of the cost of the graphics processors that will serve it. After the quarter ended, IREN signed a five-year AI Cloud contract at about $22 million of annualized revenue per megawatt of IT load. The customer is prepaying about 90% of the related GPU capital spending. The announcement came as the company's shares fell sharply in the regular session, closing at $18.03, down 16.95%, before recovering to $19.95 after hours.

The prepayments could ease IREN's funding needs, since customer money covers much of the hardware that would otherwise require outside financing. Even so, IREN's cash fell to $3.52 billion from $5.90 billion, and its net debt rose to $4.43 billion from $216 million. The company also signed a short-term contract at more than $40 million per megawatt, expanded a deal with a leading frontier AI lab, and signed new contracts for older H100 GPUs at double the earlier pricing. IREN did not name the five-year customer, and it gave no megawatt counts, GPU numbers, total contract value or start dates.

Chief Financial Officer Anthony Lewis said some recent contracts carry prepayments of up to 90% and that IREN targets total GPU financing of 90% of related capex, including prepayments. Co-CEO Daniel Roberts said lower-credit customers tend to make larger prepayments, which complicates the positive reading of the deals. Chief Commercial Officer Kent Draper said the company does not comment on individual contracts. Lewis also said two-thirds of the $20.3 billion backlog, which grew 22%, comes from investment-grade customers including Microsoft and NVIDIA.

The company's target of more than $4 billion in operating annual recurring revenue is now set for January 31, 2027 instead of year-end 2026, and it could slip to the end of February 2027. Roberts said Microsoft asked IREN to rework the network at its 200 MW Horizon 1 site, which he described as a negligible extra capital cost. IREN plans $15 billion of capital spending for the rest of fiscal 2027, of which $9 billion is covered by cash and committed funding, while $6 billion depends on market conditions. Investors are watching whether the capacity target is met and whether the remaining gap is covered mainly by new stock.

stories.Headline: AI Stock Meltdown: Why This May Not Be The Bubble Burst (NASDAQ:QQQ)
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, the Nasdaq 100 fell 5.5 percent, its worst daily drop in about 18 months, pushing the index into correction as an AI stock sell-off spread through the market. The Nasdaq as a whole shed around $2.5 trillion in value in a single session, and Nvidia alone lost about $448 billion, or 9.3 percent, erasing its entire 2026 gain. Semiconductor names took heavy losses too, with AMD down 17.3 percent, TSMC down 10.8 percent, and Broadcom down 10.4 percent. The Techzine report describes the day as the Nasdaq's worst session since April 2025.

Investors pointed to two main worries behind the decline. The first was doubt about the long-term pace of the AI data center buildout, since Big Tech has poured hundreds of billions into facilities that still need to be built or lack enough power. The second was new uncertainty over political support for data centers in the United States, especially in Texas, where Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa wants a moratorium on new data centers. Republican governor Greg Abbott had already halted permits for new data centers in September pending an audit. Analysts also raised questions about how quickly AI hardware loses value, with Michael Burry estimating that hyperscalers understate depreciation through 2028 by some $176 billion.

Tesla and SpaceX also fell, 11 percent and 9.1 percent respectively, which the article links to a so-called Musk effect. Musk spent hundreds of millions of dollars trying to help elect more Republicans, and investors fear his companies could face closer scrutiny under a Democratic Congress. Both companies are based in Texas, so the state's data center policy could make it harder for Musk to pursue his AI ambitions at the same pace. The article notes that the sell-off was not uniform, since Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon rose 3 to 7 percent on Wednesday and Cloudflare recovered after hours on strong quarterly results.

The article argues that the market is punishing the suppliers of the AI buildout while sparing its buyers, and it compares the move with the software sell-off earlier in 2026, which partly reversed. It concludes that the sell-off is a correction driven by doubts over the pace of the buildout rather than by falling demand, since chipmakers are still reporting strong revenue growth. Nvidia reports quarterly results on November 17, and Hinojosa takes office in January, and according to J.P. Morgan most of the at-risk capacity is planned for 2028. Whether the decline stops here, the article says, will only become clear in the coming months.

stories.Headline: IBM, AMD and Oak Ridge pair a 120-qubit Nighthawk with an AMD supercomputer to test quantum error correction
stories.Summary:
On November 5, 2026, IBM, AMD and the Department of Energy-funded Quantum Science Center at Oak Ridge National Laboratory unveiled a joint platform for quantum error correction that links a quantum processor with a classical supercomputer. The setup places IBM's 120-qubit Quantum Nighthawk processor alongside ORNL's Umbra system, which runs AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs and 5th Gen EPYC CPUs. The platform will also connect to the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility. Reporters covering the launch noted that the partners aim to bring more classical computing into the work to speed progress.

The project supports the Department of Energy's Quantum Genesis Mission, which targets 100 logical qubits running 100,000 hard operations by late 2028. IBM says it has run experiments with up to 70 logical qubits and 438 hard operations, so the partners would need roughly a 230-fold rise in hard-operation count to reach the goal. Researchers will compare what each error-correction technique requires in qubits, time, samples and classical resources. They will also test concatenated and space-time codes, algorithm-aware decoders and hardware-aware compilation through IBM's Quantum System API. Today's qubits err roughly once every few hundred operations, while algorithms such as Shor's need billions of error-free operations.

IBM, AMD and ORNL are the organizations behind the platform, and their leaders described its purpose in their own terms. Jay Gambetta, director of IBM Research, said the question is no longer whether error correction will work on quantum hardware. AMD executive vice president Mark Papermaster described the platform as an important step toward scalable, efficient infrastructure for fault-tolerant quantum computing. Travis Humble, director of the Quantum Science Center at ORNL, said solving error-correction challenges is a laboratory priority. IBM also said the results may shape its planned Quantum Starling, its first fault-tolerant machine.

The platform builds on earlier collaborations among the same partners. In 2025, IBM and AMD demonstrated an algorithm that decodes quantum errors efficiently on AMD chips. Earlier in 2026, IBM and ORNL used quantum computers and the Frontier supercomputer to simulate magnetic materials and fusion-fuel candidates. Other companies are pursuing similar goals, with Quantinuum expecting its Nexus system to automate error correction through 2029. The articles do not say when the partners expect the first results from the new platform.

stories.Headline: We're not 'hitting the handbrake' on AI data centers: Affirm CEO Max Levchin
stories.Summary:
Affirm co-founder and CEO Max Levchin said in early November 2026 that the AI data center buildout should continue, pushing back against a sell-off in tech stocks. Speaking on Yahoo Finance's Sozzi Unleashed, he argued that investors were wrong to bet that spending on data centers would stop. The remarks came as markets reacted to fears that a slowdown in data center construction would hurt the profits of the largest technology companies. On the same day, Affirm reported its fiscal first quarter results, which drew separate questions about its own business.

Levchin said the industry will find places to build data centers and must ensure nearby communities benefit rather than bear the costs. He compared halting the buildout to giving up on solutions such as a cure for cancer, and said the industry would not hit the brakes. The articles report that the S&P 500 fell 4.4% on Thursday, wiping out about $3 trillion in market value, while the Dow dropped 1,280 points and the Nasdaq fell 4.8%, with chipmakers and cloud companies such as Micron and Sandisk among the hardest hit. Yorkville Ives partner Dan Ives argued that a Democratic win in the midterm elections would not end the US AI buildout. Stocks traded cautiously on Friday as investors awaited further developments in the tech sector.

Separately, Levchin told analysts on Thursday, November 5, that he expects interest-free installment loans to make up more of purchases as consumers hand shopping to AI agents. Those plans accounted for 28% of Affirm's gross merchandise volume in the September quarter, against 72% for interest-bearing loans. Revenue rose 35% to $1.3 billion, but the share of US loan balances at least 30 days past due rose to 2.9% in September, and Affirm shares fell more than 9% after hours. stories.Headline: Why Gen Z’s Wealth-Building Future Could Be Threatened by AI
stories.Summary:
Gen Z Americans are voicing fears that their saving habits and wealth-building potential may be undercut by artificial intelligence, even though this generation appears to be in better shape than older ones. Many believe AI will weigh heavily on young people's ability to build significant wealth because of its effects on jobs and the broader economy. A TIAA report from October found that AI is adding uncertainty to retirement readiness, alongside rising costs and longer lifespans. Forty percent of those surveyed called AI in the workplace a threat to their retirement plans, and that figure rose to 51 percent among Gen Z respondents.

Compared with older generations, Gen Z appears to be starting earlier on building financial security. A 2025 Northwestern Mutual report found that Gen Zers began working with a financial adviser at 23, compared with 30 for millennials and an average of 49 for Boomers and older. A U.S. Bank survey fielded from June 15 to July 1 among 5,000 American adults found that Gen Z was leading the country in rewriting the rules of wealth building. Younger Americans begin building wealth at 19 on average, compared with 25 for millennials and 29 for Gen X. Even so, 29 percent of Gen Z say debt has affected their plans for long-term goals such as homeownership, more than any other generation.

Economist Teresa Ghilarducci, an expert in retirement security, told Newsweek that AI could either help or hurt this generation's savings, depending on how companies and workers use it. She said that if AI complements workers' skills, Gen Z's high educational attainment and digital fluency could raise productivity and earnings. However, she warned that if employers use AI mainly to monitor workers, intensify their work, or replace them, the gains could go to capital while wages stagnate. Among TIAA respondents, a third said they were very or extremely concerned that AI could disrupt their careers or reduce their earning potential before they could retire comfortably. A Senate report from last year found that 100 million American jobs could be at risk from automation and AI.

Other voices are more skeptical about the scale of the job losses being predicted. Kate Fortmueller, an associate professor at Georgia State University who studies film and television labor, argued that AI is often used as a convenient excuse for CEOs to make cuts that boost shareholder value. Ghilarducci added that differences within a generation may matter more than differences between generations, given the gaps in job opportunities and career barriers facing different Gen Z groups. She also said AI could make basic retirement decisions easier by helping people compare savings and investment options. Whether AI ultimately strengthens or weakens young savers' prospects, the articles suggest, remains an open question.

stories.Headline: “AI Sandbox” workshop allows faculty and staff to put AI through its paces in low-stakes environment
stories.Summary:
A University of Pittsburgh workshop called the "AI Sandbox," run through the Faculty and Staff Development Program, gave faculty and staff a low-stakes chance to test how AI handles basic writing tasks and whether it is worth using. The session was led by J. D. Wright, an English faculty member who also consults for the University Center for Teaching and Learning. Participants practiced writing prompts, refining them to get different versions of a document, and judging whether the results helped them. The article was published on November 6, 2026.

Wright told attendees that longer and more detailed prompts generally produce more complete and accurate output, and he urged people not to accept the first answer. He described AI as more like a conversation with a colleague than a source of single correct answers, and as a tool for generating options rather than final truths. In one exercise, students asked an AI to draft a social media invitation to a department event, and reactions varied: some were pleased with the layout, tone, and extra details, while others found it made assumptions they had not requested. Wright noted that asking for 100 paper titles takes little more effort than asking for five, and that a few of them may be strong. He also suggested asking the AI to point out what a user might be overlooking, predict how an output could be misread, and recommend a workflow for future tasks.

Wright was candid that his own use is limited, saying he rarely uses AI to create full documents, though he recommends it for first drafts that can be revised. One participant said she likes the tool but does not fully trust it, since she still has to check its work and is unsure it saves her time. Wright's central test for any use was whether it saved time or produced a better result than the user would have on their own. The article reports these views without describing any broader institutional policy.

Separately, a Nebraska Public Media report dated November 5, 2026, describes a different approach at the University of Nebraska, where President Jeffrey Gold announced university-wide expectations for AI use in a Thursday message. The executive memorandum bars using institutional and research data in personal AI subscriptions, prohibits tools that claim ownership of user data or use it to train other models, and makes users responsible for checking outputs, facts, and citations. The university is providing an enterprise ChatGPT license that faculty and staff must complete training to access, with Gold asking everyone to move to it by the end of 2026, and faculty can request enterprise access for students. Copilot is already available system-wide, and a new NU AI Governance Group with faculty, staff, and units such as the NU AI Institute, legal, and finance will help implement the memorandum. Gold said faculty and staff still decide whether AI is used in their courses or research, and that the rules are meant to keep pace with fast-changing technology.

stories.Headline: WashU Expert: Preparing workers for the age of AI
stories.Summary:
AI is reshaping the workforce, and Jason Jabbari, an associate professor at the Brown School at Washington University in St. Louis, has laid out how education might respond. He argues that training must pair current technical instruction with durable skills such as critical thinking, adaptability and collaboration. His view comes from a recent book chapter, "Rethinking Human Capital Development in the Age of AI," published in October in the Wiley book "Learning Curves." The chapter looks at how workforce training organizations are adapting to AI, a subject Jabbari studies through policies, programs and practices that can strengthen human capital and promote social mobility.

Jabbari says the change is happening quickly, with experienced workers using AI for tasks that once went to newcomers and some coding work becoming less essential. Fundamental knowledge still lets people use technology well, though English may be becoming the most common computer science language. Because AI is a general-purpose technology, workers will need to fold it into their workflows well beyond technology sectors. If coding is an early signal of broader labor trends, he suggests, economic mobility will depend on learning new skills quickly and learning advanced skills earlier, whether formally or informally.

Jabbari's chapter examines LaunchCode and Per Scholas, two education providers in technology that are adjusting to an AI-driven labor market. Both work directly with employers, which lets information about in-demand skills reach their programs far faster than in traditional education. Per Scholas now also upskills, offering courses to alumni so earlier graduates can keep pace with new demands. LaunchCode, through its Hire Human initiative, aims to match people with roles where AI makes them more efficient rather than replacing them, and in both cases the gap between employer needs and classroom content is shrinking.

Jabbari adds that technical skills may age quickly, so students need to learn how to keep learning, which LaunchCode describes as learning how to learn to code. Technical skills still matter for a first job, but they may soon give way to more advanced ones, and durable qualities such as adaptability and a growth mindset may be what let workers absorb each new set. He also argues that higher education is well placed to act now, since AI is changing both how and what is taught, and it can personalize learning around individual career goals. Institutions have the infrastructure to scale, while the faster methods of LaunchCode and Per Scholas show how to adapt, and combining them could spread AI's gains more widely rather than letting the already advantaged capture most of them.

stories.Headline: Faculty 100 Q&A: Ankit Shah on AI and cybersecurity
stories.Summary:
IU Today published a Q&A on November 6, 2026, profiling Ankit Shah, an assistant professor of operations and decision technologies at the Kelley School of Business who joined Indiana University in 2024. The interview is part of IU Bloomington's Faculty 100 initiative, which launched in fall 2022 and has brought more than 70 new tenured or tenure-track faculty to campus, with a goal of reaching 100 by 2027. The article notes that Faculty 100 scholars have contributed to nearly 300 proposals seeking more than $230 million in new external funding, with nearly $40 million awarded so far. Shah's hire falls within strategic areas that include microelectronics, artificial intelligence, quantum science and health sciences.

Shah's research sits at the intersection of artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, operations research and information technology, with a focus on AI-enabled cyber defense, multi-agent AI systems, reinforcement learning, adversarial AI and secure, reliable and resilient AI. He said his work aims to help organizations and mission-critical systems identify, respond to and adapt to emerging threats while keeping autonomous AI systems dependable. Before coming to IU, he directed the Artificial Intelligence Research Laboratory for Secure and Efficient Systems and conducted research at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory and George Mason University's Center for Secure Information Systems. He also reported more than nine years of experience in information technology and security industry roles, including software engineering and executive leadership.

In the interview, Shah described a current project on multi-agent AI systems for tactical cyber defense, in which autonomous agents coordinate and adapt to fast-changing threats. He said the work is supported by multiple defense research organizations, including DARPA and the U.S. Army. He also said he hopes to collaborate with colleagues in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing and Engineering, the Center for Applied Cybersecurity Research, the Luddy Artificial Intelligence Center and across the Kelley School. Describing the initiative's effect on his view of IU, he said Faculty 100 has shown him a university where interdisciplinary research can grow across traditional boundaries. The article is part of a series profiling Faculty 100 scholars, and it does not report any further developments beyond the interview itself.

stories.Headline: Can Privacy Become Gag Order? Data Protection Law And Investigative Journalism
stories.Summary:
The Digital News Publishers Association, which speaks for the digital arms of 21 major Indian news organisations including The Indian Express, The Hindu, India Today, NDTV, Network18 and the Times Group, has gone to the Supreme Court against India's data protection law. It is challenging several provisions of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025. On 27 October 2026, a Bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana issued notice on the petition. The Court declined to grant an interim stay without first hearing the Union Government, and the matter is next listed on 17 November 2026.

The petition targets Sections 7, 17(2), 18, 19, 27, 29, 36, 37 and 44(3) of the Act, along with Rules 16, 17 and 23 of the Rules. One main objection is that the notice and consent framework under Sections 5 and 6, and the legitimate uses listed in Section 7, make no room for journalism as a basis for processing personal data in the public interest. Section 17(2), which exempts purposes such as research, archiving and statistics, is challenged for leaving journalism out. A second objection concerns Sections 18, 19 and 27, which govern the constitution, composition and powers of the Data Protection Board. The petitioners say these hand major adjudicatory and enforcement functions to an executive-controlled body without enough safeguards, and Section 29 on penalties is challenged alongside them.

The Act and Rules are being brought into force in phases. The institutional provisions, Sections 18 to 26, and the amendment to Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act under Section 44(3), took effect on 13 November 2025. The substantive provisions on processing personal data, Sections 3 to 17, together with Sections 36 and 37, are due to start on 13 May 2027, as are Rules 16 and 23. Rule 17, on appointing the Board's Chairperson and Members, commenced earlier.

The association's case is that the framework ignores how journalism works, since information of public interest often has to be gathered, checked and reported without the consent, or even the knowledge, of the person concerned. The article gives the example of an inquiry into a public official's assets or irregular government contracts, where having to notify the subject or seek consent could defeat the investigation. The petition therefore asks whether a law meant to protect informational privacy can place a disproportionate burden on press freedom and the public's right to know. The articles do not carry any response from the Union Government.

The challenge has a legislative backstory. The Personal Data Protection Bill, 2018 expressly recognised journalistic purposes and offered an exemption under Section 47, and a similar protection appeared in the 2019 Bill, which a Joint Parliamentary Committee examined. That Committee accepted the importance of free expression to the media while also wanting to prevent misuse of personal information in the name of journalism. The exemption vanished from the Draft Digital Personal Data Protection Bill, 2022 and was not restored in the 2023 law, and no alternative safeguard replaced it. The Supreme Court's hearing on 17 November 2026 will be the next step.

The two firms are reportedly asking some potential buyers to take stakes of up to $500 million before the formal syndication process begins. The multi-tranche financing is said to keep debt off SpaceX's balance sheet and is described as the largest arrangement of its kind for graphics processing units on record. Reuters said it could not independently verify the report. Goldman Sachs declined to comment, while Apollo Global and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests.

SpaceX said in October that an affiliate of Apollo Global Management would buy AI chips and server hardware and lease them back to the company in a transaction involving about $40 billion in principal payments. The leases are set to run for a little over five years from the date the equipment is delivered. That delivery is expected in the first half of 2027. The arrangement is meant to fund the growing computing needs of SpaceX's AI business. Its structure lets the company expand its computing capacity without taking the full cost onto its own books at once.

Responsibility for structuring and marketing the financing rests with Goldman Sachs and Apollo Global Management, according to the Bloomberg account. SpaceX confirmed the lease arrangement in October but did not respond to questions about the investor solicitation. Goldman Sachs declined to comment on the report, and Apollo Global did not immediately reply. The reporting relies on people familiar with the matter, and the figures have not been independently verified by Reuters.

The deal reflects the heavy spending that major technology companies are making on computing power to build artificial intelligence products. Financing it through leases and outside investors is one way to spread that cost across several parties. The articles do not say when the formal syndication will open or how many investors will take part. The first hardware deliveries are expected in the first half of 2027, which will be the next concrete milestone.

stories.Headline: EU court adviser: AI chatbots that replace reading the news may breach publisher rights
stories.Summary:
On 3 November 2026, Advocate General Szpunar of the EU Court of Justice delivered an Opinion on whether AI chatbots that use online news may infringe press publishers' rights. The Opinion concerns Like Company v. Google Ireland Limited (C-250/25), a case about Google's Gemini chatbot and articles published by a Hungarian news business. It addresses press publishers' related rights rather than authors' copyright, and the judges have yet to rule. The Opinion separates two activities that are often lumped together.

Training a model on material is treated differently from retrieving an article to answer a user's question, and the Advocate General sees no need for the Court to decide the training question in this case. He also distinguishes a factual summary of a source from a recognisable reproduction of its protected expression. Lost website traffic alone is not enough to show infringement, and paraphrasing does not escape liability if the original expression survives. Facts themselves are not protected, and very short extracts and individual words fall outside the right. Responsibility is treated as turning on system design, safeguards and evidence rather than on the user's prompt alone.

The Advocate General does not propose automatic liability for providers whenever a user prompts an infringing answer, but says pointing to the user is not enough where the business model facilitates reproduction or reasonable safeguards are missing. Publishers are advised to record what a chatbot accessed and returned, while a claim that a service makes content available to the public would require systematic reproduction across related queries, not one unusual answer. On the facts of the Hungarian dispute, the Advocate General doubts infringement, noting that effective access restrictions and recognisable expression appear absent and that Google seems to have adopted appropriate safeguards, subject to the national court's findings. The Court typically follows an Advocate General's Opinion, but it is not bound to, and the wider legal framework for AI, copyright and related rights remains unsettled. Even so, the Opinion signals how access controls, output design, evidence and licensing may matter in future disputes.

stories.Headline: European Parliament President Metsola warns against using AI to draft laws
stories.Summary:
On November 5, 2026, the European Commission said in its annual simplification report that it has begun using artificial intelligence to draft new laws and to simplify existing ones. The report, presented that Wednesday, described new digital tools that help staff spot overlaps, inconsistencies and duplicates across legal acts. The Commission is also strengthening legal training and staffing so that new rules are not overly complicated. The changes form part of a wider plan to cut red tape and administrative costs for businesses across areas such as tech, agriculture, migration, environmental protection and taxation.

The Commission reports that it has produced 12 so-called omnibus packages to revise and simplify existing legislation, which it estimates will save the EU economy €22.3 billion in costs. It also launched 874 infringement procedures between August 2025 and July 2026, which the report describes as the highest number in the last 10 years. The Commission is pressing member states to stop "gold-plating," the practice of adding extra requirements when turning EU law into national law, and it expects to sign a pact against gold-plating with governments by the end of the year. Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis, who oversees simplification, called for a joint effort with member countries. He warned that some omnibus proposals may end the legislative process with much less simplification than the Commission proposed, because governments keep weakening them during negotiations.

Responsibility for the simplification drive rests with the Commission, which is led by Ursula von der Leyen, who has made simplification a central part of her second term. Dombrovskis said the agenda is already changing daily life for small business owners, who now spend less time on forms. Separately, European Parliament President Roberta Metsola has urged lawmakers to be careful about adopting AI in decision-making. Speaking to MEPs, she said AI can help draft amendments but cannot replace debate or the critical thinking that complex legal decisions require, and that elected representatives must remain personally responsible for their decisions. She wants Parliament to be open about its AI use so citizens can hold their representatives to account.

The articles show that the institutions are moving in parallel, with the Commission leaning into AI for drafting and review while Parliament works on guidelines. Parliament's administration is preparing rules based on transparency, keeping confidential documents off public platforms and checking all AI output carefully. Staff have been required to disclose AI use since 2024, but MEPs are not yet bound by that rule for speeches or amendments, and binding it would likely require a change to Parliament's Rules of Procedure considered by the Committee on Constitutional Affairs. Parliament is also building an internal platform called EPGenAI Hub for sensitive data. The articles do not say when the rules for MEPs will be adopted.
