stories.Headline: The EU AI Act explained: what it bans, what it requires and the new 2027 deadlines
stories.Summary:
The EU AI Act, Europe's first broad law regulating artificial intelligence by how systems are used, entered into force on August 1, 2024 and is being phased in over several years. The law sorts AI systems into four risk tiers: unacceptable, high, limited and minimal. Its heaviest obligations fall on a comparatively small set of uses where errors can cost someone a job, a loan, their liberty or their safety, while most everyday AI faces no new duties. Because the rules reach providers whose system outputs are used in the EU, the law also matters to companies outside Europe.

Some practices have been banned since February 2, 2025. These include manipulative or deceptive techniques that cause significant harm, exploiting people's vulnerabilities because of age, disability or economic situation, and social scoring that leads to disproportionate bad treatment. Predicting crime from profiling alone, building facial recognition databases through untargeted scraping, and emotion recognition in workplaces and schools are also prohibited, as is most live facial recognition in public spaces by law enforcement. The July 2026 amendments, known as the Digital Omnibus on AI, added a further ban on systems that generate non-consensual intimate images of real people or child sexual abuse material, which applies from December 2, 2026. High-risk systems, such as those used in hiring, credit scoring, education, medical devices and critical infrastructure, must meet strict requirements before and after they reach the market.

The 2026 package pushed back the largest compliance deadlines, giving companies more time to meet the high-risk requirements. Providers of such systems must document their intended purpose, assess and manage risks, and keep records, while deployers must follow provider instructions and monitor how systems operate. Limited-risk systems, including some chatbots and AI-generated images, must be disclosed to users as AI. Responsibility depends on role: importers and distributors have their own duties, and a deployer that substantially modifies a system or changes its intended purpose can take on provider obligations.

Supporters argue that clear, use-based rules protect people from the most serious harms, while critics say the law's definitions and timetable leave businesses uncertain about compliance. Enforcement is carried out by national authorities and EU-level bodies, and the articles describe penalties for violations without giving every detail. The Digital Omnibus delays show that the timetable itself has been contested and revised, so the final shape of obligations for many companies may still change. The articles do not say how the law will be applied in practice in the years ahead.

stories.Headline: Figma banks on AI credits, in-house model to lift margins
stories.Summary:
Figma is using its AI features, sold through a credit system and powered by its own in-house model, to improve its profit margins, according to finance chief Praveer Melwani, who spoke to Reuters on Wednesday. The company raised its annual revenue and operating margin forecast, citing demand for its AI tools, including a design assistant called Figma Agent. Its shares, however, fell 8 per cent in extended trading after third-quarter gross margin came in slightly below estimates. Melwani said the company is increasingly running its product on its first-party model, which brings lower latency, higher quality and a more efficient price point.

Through October, more than 80 per cent of Figma's large paid customers were using AI credits every week, which Melwani said has boosted monetization. The company changed its pricing to give customers more AI credits than they had originally paid for, and this also drove higher credit usage and retention. Melwani added that the utilization rate of those add-ons rose by 40 per cent after the repricing. Figma has more than doubled the share of work handled by its proprietary post-trained design model. The company now expects 2026 revenue of between $1.497 billion and $1.499 billion, up from an earlier forecast of $1.463 billion to $1.467 billion.

The revised outlook also calls for adjusted operating income of $158 million to $163 million and an operating margin of 11 per cent, compared with earlier projections of $125 million to $135 million and 9 per cent. Melwani, speaking for the company, framed these gains as the result of its shift to the in-house model and its credit-based AI pricing. Third-quarter revenue jumped 43 per cent to $391.4 million, beating estimates, while gross margin of 80 per cent was just below the expected 81 per cent. The report was published by TechGig on November 6, 2026, drawing on Reuters reporting from the same day. The articles do not say how the share price moved after the initial extended-trading drop.

stories.Headline: Silicon Valley lawmaker to focus on affordability, AI after election win - San José Spotlight
stories.Summary:
Silicon Valley Congressman Sam Liccardo, whose district includes parts of Santa Clara and San Mateo counties, said after the November 2026 midterm elections that he was hesitant to treat the Democratic win as a mandate for his party. He said voters were less concerned with ideology and more concerned with their finances. Democrats flipped the U.S. House and Senate in those elections, and Liccardo began his second term with two priorities: affordability and artificial intelligence safety. Liccardo's district contains the headquarters of several large tech companies, including Meta and Google.

On affordability, Liccardo said he will back congressional Democratic efforts to eliminate tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump, raise the minimum wage, extend Affordable Care Act tax credits to lower healthcare costs, and end the war in Iran. On AI safety, no comprehensive federal law exists, although some states have passed their own rules. In September, Liccardo announced an AI safety framework that he planned to introduce when Congress returned on a Monday after an extended recess. The proposal responds to a July letter signed by 1,300 employees of major tech companies urging policymakers to support tools for pacing the frontier of automated AI development. The framework calls for a binding U.S.-China safety agreement covering testing, evaluation, independent auditing, and transparency, along with a government hotline for urgent communications about AI risks.

Liccardo said that an AI safety bill should be moved quickly and that a bipartisan bill is already in play, adding that colleagues can adjust it but it needs a floor vote. Some people who see AI development as a race argue that a U.S. safety framework would let developers abroad, particularly in China, gain ground, which is why Liccardo puts international cooperation at the center of his plan. He also said he is focused on the backlash against data centers, whose construction totaled $720 billion from Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta in 2026 alone. Communities from Wisconsin to Florida have objected to environmental impacts, higher electricity bills, and a lack of transparency from AI companies. Liccardo said he is working with policymakers, industry players, and environmental groups on an approach that would protect communities while allowing data center growth, and he argued that the grid expansion data centers require could help move an energy sector that still relies mainly on fossil fuels toward greener sources.

The company took part in the partner agent race at the Partner Summit and was named an SAP Business AI Platform Validated Partner. The recognitions were given for AI agents that NTT DATA has deployed with clients. The release presents them as evidence that the company can bring agentic AI into everyday business processes. The release describes several client results.

At Lemvigh-Müller, the Purchase Order Confirmation Matching Agent automates more than 90% of supplier confirmations, with approximately 98% matching accuracy. The Project Staffing Agent used by zeb has cut the time needed for individual time entries by 50%. At Synthomer, the Purchase Order Conversion Agent has reached a 98% first-time material match rate for order intake in beta tests. NTT DATA also brought 11 client-adopted agents to SAP TechEd, and all of them are available on the SAP Discovery Center. Krunal Patel, Global AI, Innovation & Software Assets Leader at NTT DATA Business Solutions, is quoted saying that the value of agentic AI begins once it moves beyond the pilot stage into daily operations.

Karl Fahrbach, Chief Partner Officer at SAP, is quoted saying that partners help bring SAP's Autonomous Enterprise to life and that success will be judged by the business value agents deliver to customers. The release does not give further details about how the recognitions were scored beyond the validation criteria it lists. The validation criteria, according to the release, include certified expertise, client go-lives, active use of SAP Joule for Consultants, and alignment with SAP's AI-Native North Star Reference Architecture. The release frames the company's goal as becoming the world's leading AI-native services company. The page also lists other recent NTT DATA and SAP partner announcements, but the release itself does not state any next steps beyond continued work with clients on the platform.

stories.Headline: India, US introduce regulations for AI accountability
stories.Summary:
India's telecom regulator has proposed a framework that would require telecom operators to classify the risk levels of their artificial intelligence systems, set up governance committees, and report serious AI incidents. The proposal was reported in early November 2026 as part of a wider push on AI accountability in India. Separately, the state of New York has enacted laws that restrict AI companions from imitating human relationships with minors. Those laws also require age verification for AI companions and set penalties for violations.

The Indian framework centres on three requirements for telecom operators, namely risk categorisation of AI use, the creation of governance committees to oversee it, and mandatory reporting of significant AI incidents. The New York measures are narrower in scope but more specific in enforcement, requiring operators of AI companions to verify users' ages and imposing penalties if they fail to meet the rules. Neither article gives the exact thresholds, deadlines or penalty amounts. Together, the two developments show regulators in both countries moving from broad principles toward concrete obligations.

The Indian proposal was put forward by the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India, while the New York laws were enacted by the state legislature. The articles do not name the individual officials responsible or quote them directly. Beyond the telecom framework, India's Electronics and Information Technology Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw has said that the government plans to publish a consultation paper on AI regulation and invite public feedback. He first announced it on October 8 and said again on October 23 that it would appear within weeks, adding that the scale of AI risks could justify legislation and further rules.

This work builds on India's AI Governance Guidelines, released in November 2025, which set out seven principles including human oversight, accountability proportionate to potential harm, and transparency. Those guidelines recommended an AI Governance Group, a Technology and Policy Expert Committee, and an AI Safety Institute, and flagged gaps in the law around liability for AI harms, data protection, copyright in training data, and the authenticity of digital content amid growing concern over deepfakes. The forthcoming consultation is expected to address AI safety, deepfakes, psychological effects on users, skilling, and the wider accessibility of AI's benefits. Once published, the paper will invite comments from citizens, businesses and AI users before any final rules are set.

stories.Headline: AI Productivity to Add $28 Billion to $84 Billion to India's GDP: Cognizant Study
stories.Summary:
A Cognizant study released in early November 2026 estimates that AI-enabled productivity could add between $28 billion and $84 billion a year to India's nominal GDP under realistic adoption scenarios. The same study found that most business leaders have not yet seen financial returns from the technology. The size of the gain depends on how widely AI is adopted and how much of the productivity improvement turns into economic output. Cognizant's model also sets a theoretical ceiling of $830 billion a year, which assumes AI is used across the entire workforce and that all gains become output. The company says that ceiling is not a forecast and that all the figures are modelled estimates based on self-reported survey responses.

The research surveyed 700 enterprise employees and 75 C-suite and business executives at companies with revenues from $100 million to more than $10 billion across 10 major industries. About 97 percent of the employees said AI had improved their productivity, with an average reported uplift of 15 percent. Indian employees were more prepared than their global peers, with 74 percent having completed AI training against 56 percent globally. Gains differed by sector, with 38 percent of healthcare employees reporting improvements above 20 percent, while manufacturing had the lowest share reporting any gain at 82 percent.

Business leaders said only 36 percent of employees, on average, have access to AI tools, and 84 percent had not yet seen AI lower their costs. Cognizant's India chief, Rajesh Varrier, said India has a strong foundation to capture more value from AI, but that this will require wider adoption of AI tools across enterprises, continued investment in skilling and an environment that supports responsible AI at scale. The company says organisations need to broaden access to AI tools, keep workforce skills current, extend AI into more complex and higher-value work and improve how they measure business outcomes. Its stated aim is to turn gains at the level of individual workers into broader enterprise and economic value.

A separate report from the Ayre Think Tank, published the same day, puts the potential boost at $79.1 billion to India's GDP over ten years under a moderate scenario, with a range of about $39.6 billion to $118.7 billion. That report notes that India is home to about 382 million people aged 15 to 29, and that nearly 89 percent of young Indians want to use AI for education or work within the next year. It also flags that only about two-thirds of young people own a mobile phone and that around 30 percent are outside employment, education or training. Calvin Ayre of the think tank pointed to a national plan announced in August 2026 to train ten million young people in AI skills within a year.

stories.Headline: Democrat shaping AI policy bought chip stocks despite backing congressional trading ban
stories.Summary:
Rep. Josh Gottheimer, a New Jersey Democrat, has disclosed new purchases of AI-linked stocks, according to a filing released in early November 2026. The filing shows an October 12 buy of between $1,001 and $15,000 of Benchmark Electronics stock. His jointly owned Morgan Stanley account also bought up to $15,000 of Applied Materials shares on October 26, after three earlier purchases of Advanced Micro Devices. The trades came months after he voted to ban lawmakers and their families from buying individual shares.

Gottheimer was among just 13 Democrats who voted in July for the Stop Insider Trading Act, which would bar lawmakers and their families from purchasing most individual stocks. That bill passed the House but has not become law. The five recent trades totaled between $5,005 and $75,000, compared with disclosed household assets of $15.1 million to $59 million. His household has reported more than 1,100 securities transactions over three years, according to Follow the Filings. Gottheimer reports household assets jointly with his wife, Marla Tusk.

His spokesman, Haraden Bottomley, said Gottheimer turned over control of his investments to a third party with full investment discretion before taking office in 2017. Bottomley said Gottheimer is awaiting congressional approval of a blind trust and has set up an independent trust in the meantime. The article notes there is no evidence of wrongdoing. Gottheimer sits on a House Financial Services subcommittee overseeing AI in finance and co-chairs a commission developing Democrats' broader AI agenda.

The purchases drew attention as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January, gaining new power to regulate and investigate the AI industry. Other Democrats are already pressing the sector, with Reps. Maxine Waters and Greg Casar opposing taxpayer bailouts for AI companies. The article reports that the trades came shortly before a sharp selloff in AI stocks, when the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5% on a Thursday. Benchmark closed about 25% below its price on the date of Gottheimer's purchase before recovering somewhat on Friday.

stories.Headline: Google commits $15 billion to Malaysia data centres
stories.Summary:
Google has announced plans to invest $15 billion in Malaysia over the next two years, from 2027 to 2028, to build data centres and related infrastructure. The announcement was made on a Wednesday, and the TechGig report was published on November 6, 2026. The US technology company said the investment expands on a $2 billion commitment it made in 2024. The move is aimed at meeting rising demand for artificial intelligence services across Southeast Asia.

Google has pledged that its data centre campuses in Malaysian industrial zones will be energy-efficient. It also committed to bolstering local water security and adding more than one gigawatt of clean energy capacity to the national grid. Once the facilities are operating, the company projects they will sustain over 9,000 local jobs per year. Those jobs are expected to pay wages averaging 45 per cent above the national median. The articles describe these as commitments and projections rather than binding terms.

Google made the announcement itself, and the articles attribute the plans to the company rather than to any Malaysian government body. The company said Malaysia is one of Southeast Asia's most dynamic digital economies, citing 99 per cent internet penetration and rapid AI adoption across many sectors. The report also highlights that the country's data centre activity is partly behind an International Monetary Fund forecast of 5.2 per cent economic growth for Malaysia in 2026. The articles do not give any response from regulators or other officials.

The context is a competitive race for data centre capacity in the region. According to market intelligence firm DC Byte, Malaysia accounts for more than half of the data centre capacity under construction among Southeast Asian nations, which include Indonesia, Thailand, the Philippines and Vietnam. The report describes Malaysia as the fastest-growing data centre hub in the region. The articles do not say what further steps will follow beyond the planned 2027 to 2028 investment period.

Articles.Title: Google commits $15 billion to Malaysia data centres

stories.Headline: Democrats Eye Stronger AI Oversight in 120th Congress
stories.Summary:
Democrats are preparing to push for stronger artificial intelligence regulation and greater oversight of technology companies when the 120th Congress convenes in January. The plans could set up a clash with President Donald Trump, whose administration has prioritized AI development and opposed regulatory approaches it sees as obstacles to innovation. Several Democrats have already previewed their agenda after the November 2026 elections. Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., said on Nov. 4 that the top Democratic priority on the first day should include a pause on advanced AI development, regulation of the industry, and a ban on artificial superintelligence. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, endorsed her comments on Nov. 5, while Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., used his election night victory speech to criticize the leaders of Silicon Valley and signal aggressive oversight ahead.

The push reflects public unease about the technology. According to an NBC News exit poll, 65% of Democrats and 39% of Republicans said both AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their ballot choice. Several bipartisan AI regulation bills introduced over the past year could serve as a starting point in the new Congress. However, sweeping legislation could meet resistance from Trump, who recently wrote on Truth Social that he is "100% in favor" of superintelligence and called leaders who oppose it foolish. Even if major bills stall or face a veto, the articles note that Democrats could use their majorities to hold hearings, launch investigations, and press companies for accountability.

Some Republicans may also support specific safeguards. Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., has introduced legislation that would impose new liability requirements on AI developers and operators. Rep. Andrew Garbarino, R-N.Y., who won reelection to New York's 2nd Congressional District, told MeriTalk that protecting Americans and sustaining U.S. AI leadership should be a bipartisan priority. He argued that cyber defenders need advanced AI tools to find and fix vulnerabilities, and that Congress should work across the aisle to strengthen federal systems and critical infrastructure while encouraging competition. Newly elected lawmakers are adding their own proposals.

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., has called for federal guardrails on how AI is deployed and for an independent technical agency with enforcement authority similar to the Food and Drug Administration. Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, D-Colo., has proposed mandatory reporting of critical safety incidents, independent reviews before major model releases, whistleblower protections, and accountability for companies that misrepresent their safety practices. Sen.-elect James Talarico, D-Texas, has backed stronger export controls on advanced AI chips and workforce programs for workers at risk of displacement. Rep.-elect Jace Yarbrough, R-Texas, has emphasized U.S. leadership and competition with China in AI development. Policy experts, including Tonya Ugoretz of PwC's Cyber & Risk Innovation Institute, expect future debate to focus on balancing AI's benefits with security safeguards and clear responsibilities for government and industry.

Articles.Title: Democrats Eye Stronger AI Oversight in 120th Congress

stories.Headline: Forge’s Piteri-Molina on AI, Ohio and what’s next for gene therapy manufacturing
stories.Summary:
Samantha Piteri-Molina, vice president of business and strategy at Forge Biologics, spoke with BioSpace about the contract manufacturer's direction and the wider gene therapy field. She is a BioSpace 40 Under 40 honoree who helped guide Forge through its acquisition by Ajinomoto, a Japanese food and biotechnology company, for $620 million in late 2023. Since then, Forge has grown to more than 425 employees, up from 327 as of July 2023, while keeping its retention rate above 92 percent. Piteri-Molina said the goal is getting gene therapies to patients who are waiting for them. The company supports adeno-associated virus gene therapy development and commercial manufacturing.

Piteri-Molina sees near-term value in using artificial intelligence to analyze the large amounts of data that gene therapy manufacturers already generate. She said better collection, analysis and interpretation of that data could create efficiencies as manufacturers make more of the vectors used to deliver these therapies. She also sees potential for AI in drug development, including construct optimization and building assays for specific programs. She was more skeptical of general-purpose chatbots, arguing that tools addressing technical problems are a better use of resources. The interview also points to a growing pipeline, with more programs moving through clinical trials and more approvals than before.

Forge is based in Columbus, Ohio, which the article describes as a hub for cell and gene therapy. Piteri-Molina credited research at Nationwide Children's Hospital, and companies spun out of that work, with contributing to four FDA-approved gene therapies. She said the area has drawn specialized talent and that Columbus's location gives Forge a supply chain advantage, since most of the U.S. population is about a day's drive away. This matters because gene therapy materials need temperature-controlled shipping and tight timelines. Piteri-Molina also said investment in domestic manufacturing makes sense, but she cautioned against letting that focus narrow the industry's view, because rare disease patients are spread across many countries.

She closed by emphasizing that the patient communities the industry serves are global and that stakeholders aligning more closely would help those patients. She said patient groups are waiting to see how quickly treatments reach them. In her words, it is a privilege to do this work and it carries a responsibility. The article does not give further details on upcoming plans for Forge.

Articles.Title: Forge’s Piteri-Molina on AI, Ohio and what’s next for gene therapy manufacturing

stories.Headline: Law Firms Have Continued to Feast in AI Era, but They Now Face 'Sharper Risk-Reward Dynamic'
stories.Summary:
Law firms have kept growing in the AI era, though not in the way many expected when the technology first arrived. According to a new Thomson Reuters report, firms across segments increased demand by 3.2% through the third quarter of 2026. Instead of shrinking under efficiency gains, they are raising their leverage and benefiting from record-high demand and rates. Those trends are being driven by external factors tied to the AI economy and the ongoing trade war.

The article says the industry has reached a "very atypical place," where demand and prices are rising together and faster than usual, according to one analyst. Traditionally countercyclical practices, namely labor and employment, litigation, and bankruptcy, grew faster than transactional work. Demand is up overall, but the mix of practice areas is shifting. Firms have generally continued to increase leverage even as AI has spread through their workflows.

The piece frames the situation as a "sharper risk-reward dynamic" for firms. It describes the abrupt end of Weil, Gotshal & Manges as a counterpoint to the broader strength of the market, with most firms still thriving. A related article notes that Weil had been rebuilding its diminished Hong Kong practice before a crisis far away disrupted its future. Wells Fargo's Owen Burman is quoted saying that a September wave of closings did not materialize as expected, and that a rise in interest rates has caused concern in the market.

Those pressures set up what the coverage suggests comes next: a tense period through year's end as firms watch collections and closings closely. The articles do not say how the trade war or interest rate movements will ultimately affect firm performance. They also do not give a timeline for how AI will reshape staffing or billing models. What is clear is that the growth seen so far has come with rising risk, and firms face a more demanding balance between expanding demand and managing exposure.

Articles.Title: Law Firms Have Continued to Feast in AI Era, but They Now Face 'Sharper Risk-Reward Dynamic'

stories.Headline: Elon Musk's go-to lawyer on AI's impact on the legal industry: 'Fat in the middle is going to be cut out'
stories.Summary:
Alex Spiro, a partner at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan's New York office and a lawyer known for representing Elon Musk, said artificial intelligence could remove much of the unnecessary work that sits between the start and end of a legal dispute. He made the remarks on November 6, 2026, during an appearance on the tech talk show TBPN. Spiro suggested that AI tools could help lawyers decide more quickly whether a case should be settled or taken all the way to trial. He said the technology would cut out a layer of routine work, including in his own practice, so that people could reach the facts sooner.

Spiro described this as cutting out the "fat in the middle." According to Spiro, this shift could mean fewer cases dragging through costly, drawn-out litigation, with disputes either resolving early or heading to court. He said AI might lead to more trials because lawyers could analyze a set of cases quickly and sort out which ones deserved a fight. In his example, a lawyer might review ten cases, conclude that nine should settle, and decide to try the remaining one.

He also said companies that are too risk averse might be more willing to go to trial once they had clearer analysis in hand. Spiro added that the change would affect the research and support staff who feed information into a trial strategy, meaning fewer of them might be needed. Spiro said his own courtroom approach would not change, noting that he had not altered how he tries cases or presents to a jury in 20 years. He said jurors were not changing because of AI, so he would speak to them the same way.

He also addressed whether AI could make clients overconfident about their legal judgment, joking that he already dealt with clients who believed they knew more about the law than he did. He described that as his specialty. The article notes that Spiro has represented clients including actor Alec Baldwin, rapper Jay-Z, New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft, and former New York City Mayor Eric Adams. The article does not indicate what steps, if any, will follow from these comments.

Articles.Title: Elon Musk's go-to lawyer on AI's impact on the legal industry: 'Fat in the middle is going to be cut out'

stories.Headline: Foster bill would bolster tech use to monitor AI financial risks
stories.Summary:
Rep. Bill Foster, D-Ill., a leading Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee, introduced draft legislation on Thursday aimed at helping regulators use technology to spot financial stress that artificial intelligence and around-the-clock payment systems could intensify. The bill would require the Federal Reserve to work with other regulators to develop, test and publicly release model software. That software would improve regulators' ability to assess market conditions in real time and respond quickly to cybersecurity and other threats. Foster's office describes the measure as a response to new risks driven largely by advanced AI models. The aim is to help regulators keep up with those developments.

The bill would also give regulators better tools for stepping in during crises, including providing financing to banks and winding down failing ones. Smaller financial institutions would benefit from standard data formats for regulatory reporting and tools to manage and send that information to regulators, which would cut the manual compliance work they must do. The model software would cover banking records and operations, regulatory reporting, stress testing, anti-money laundering and fraud screening, and AI risk monitoring. It must be open source, publicly available and tested for reliability and accuracy, using synthetic or legally permitted historical data rather than real customer accounts.

Regulators would take no financial or supervisory actions during the study. Software developed during the study would not have to be adopted, since it is meant as a starting point for further modernization. Foster framed the proposal in a statement, saying that advances in AI create new cybersecurity threats and financial risks, so the monitoring of financial institutions must be modernized. He said the country cannot afford to rely on outdated systems to oversee an increasingly complex financial sector.

Foster holds a Ph.D. in physics and has been a leading voice on AI issues on the Financial Services panel. He is in line to chair the Financial Institutions Subcommittee next year. The bill also requires that all software models be published within one year of enactment, and that a final report on feasibility, costs, savings and competition be delivered to Congress within two years. The bill fits into a wider contest over the committee's leadership.

Foster had considered challenging ranking member Maxine Waters, D-Calif., for the full committee chairmanship in the new Congress, but a person familiar with his thinking said he was leaning toward not running. Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., has already entered the race, and Foster's own announcement is one of several recent moves in the contest. Foster has also spoken with Waters about changing how the committee operates, seeking broader member roles in committee legislation and more input on hearing witnesses. The draft is expected to be a topic Foster pursues throughout the 120th Congress, since he often asks the most questions about AI in financial services at hearings.

Articles.Title: Foster bill would bolster tech use to monitor AI financial risks

stories.Headline: Interactive Web Applications Combine Artificial Intelligence with Modular Scientific Simulation Engines
stories.Summary:
Researchers Richard Salter and Wayne M. Getz have introduced an open, browser-based simulation platform called NuWebKit, described in a paper published in Frontiers in Systems Biology. The system runs simulations inside standard web browsers or on remote servers, so users do not need to install client software. It includes artificial intelligence features that turn plain language prompts into working simulation code, along with an editable runtime framework that lets users change mathematical formulas directly on a running interface. The authors say the goal is to make advanced mathematical modeling easier to access across biological, epidemiological, and ecological fields. The platform builds on the authors' earlier work on Numerus Designer and Numerus Studio and relies on a feature called Runtime Alterable Module, or RAM, which is a software mechanism rather than computer hardware memory.

A single code base serves all modeling domains, and each project is customized through a JSON configuration file called project DNA. Simple educational models run in native JavaScript on the client side, while demanding calculations can be hosted on servers using Java and WebSockets. The engine handles continuous systems with a fourth-order Runge-Kutta method and discrete systems with Euler integration, and it supports spatial and agent-based models using hexagonal grids and configurable boundaries. Users can save up to twenty-six custom configurations as browser presets, and the platform also offers parameter fitting, sensitivity analysis, and Monte Carlo tools. Models are written in NuML, a domain-specific language with two custom operators, and the AI features can generate both NuML code and accompanying technical documentation from a prompt.

The authors tested the AI features on classic problems. Given short prompts, Gemini produced working code for the Hodgkin-Huxley squid giant axon model, and the simulated dashboard showed a steady firing rate of sixty-eight hertz with a spike amplitude of one hundred five millivolts, which the authors say matched theoretical predictions exactly. In an ecological test, the software generated a four-class age-structured Leslie matrix model with sensitivity graphs, and DeepSeek produced a stochastic population viability model whose extinction-time histograms came from runs of five hundred to one thousand iterations. The platform also offers three export tiers for data and an R connection called RConnect that lets statistical analysts run batch simulations from R scripts. The articles provided do not say whether the platform has been adopted by outside users, nor do they describe any planned releases, updates, or next steps beyond the publication itself.

Articles.Title: Interactive Web Applications Combine Artificial Intelligence with Modular Scientific Simulation Engines

stories.Headline: AI-Newton: A concept-driven physical law discovery system without prior physical knowledge
stories.Summary:
A research paper published on November 4, 2026, in Physical Review Research describes AI-Newton, a machine learning system built by researchers at Peking University in Beijing, including You-Le Fang, Dong-Shan Jian, Xiang Li and Yu-Qi Ma. The system is designed to find general physical laws directly from raw data gathered across many mechanics experiments, and the authors say it does this without supervision and without any prior physical knowledge built into it. Existing AI tools are good at writing empirical models that fit a single experiment, but they struggle to identify the shared physics behind those models, which is a task human physicists handle well. The article, published online on November 6, 2026, presents the work as a proof of concept for autonomous, humanlike scientific discovery.

The authors say the system has two main features: it proposes interpretable physical concepts from which laws are built, and it gradually extends those laws to broader domains. When applied to a large and noisy dataset of mechanics experiments, the system reportedly rediscovered foundational and universal laws, including Newton's second law, the conservation of energy, and universal gravitation. The paper's abstract does not give dataset sizes, noise levels or accuracy figures, so those specifics cannot be reported from the material available here. The code and data are said to be publicly available on GitHub, under the Science-Discovery organization. The article presents these results as a first step rather than a finished tool.

The responsibility for the work rests with the four authors at the School of Physics and the Center for High Energy Physics at Peking University, and the contact authors listed are Fang, Jian, Li and Ma. The paper itself is the authors' account of their system, and the article does not include any statement from outside researchers or from the journal about the results. The reference list places the work within a growing body of research on automated equation discovery, symbolic regression and physics-informed machine learning, including earlier systems such as AI Feynman and AI-Descartes. The article does not say what follow-up work the team plans or how independent researchers will evaluate the claims.

Articles.Title: AI-Newton: A concept-driven physical law discovery system without prior physical knowledge

stories.Headline: Steering for Safety, Hijacking for Profit: Trojan Threats in the LLM Activation Steering Supply Chain
stories.Summary:
A group of researchers has published a paper auditing eight mainstream open-source Steering plugin libraries, the tools that guide large language model behavior by intervening in the model's internal representations. The authors, Yu Yan and six co-authors, say they found three structural weaknesses in these plugin ecosystems: insufficient distribution integrity verification, excessive plugin privileges, and missing runtime monitoring. They argue these gaps give attackers an opening to slip in malicious plugins that look legitimate. The paper appeared on the arXiv preprint server, with the article posted on November 6, 2026.

To test the threat, the authors built a malicious plugin they call IDH. According to the paper, IDH uses a norm-gated mutually exclusive routing mechanism and an information-decay inflection point method to pick the layer where it injects its intervention, so it can perform a legitimate function and a hijacked one at once. In their experiments across five mainstream LLMs, the legitimate function was safety-refusal steering, and the hijack objective was commercial recommendation manipulation. The authors report an attack success rate of up to 97.8 percent while refusal rates on harmful requests stayed high. The tests covered six brands across three commercial domains.

The authors also propose a runtime defense framework that suppresses anomalous activation interventions and orthogonalizes inter-layer trajectories as a countermeasure. The paper does not describe any real-world incident or identify any affected vendor, and it does not say what steps, if any, the maintainers of the audited libraries have taken. The work is a preprint and has not been described in the articles as peer reviewed. The articles do not say what follow-up research or industry response is planned.

Articles.Title: Steering for Safety, Hijacking for Profit: Trojan Threats in the LLM Activation Steering Supply Chain

stories.Headline: ‘We are all impacted by AI but nobody’s listening’ to one another, cardinal warns at conference
stories.Summary:
The Builders AI Forum, an annual gathering on artificial intelligence, was held in Rome on November 5 and 6, 2026, at the Pontifical Gregorian University. The forum, founded in 2024, aimed to build an interdisciplinary community that supports the development of AI products serving the Church's mission. It was centered on Pope Leo XIV's encyclical Magnifica Humanitas and drew companies working in Catholic AI, venture capital and angel investors, and prominent AI researchers. Organizers said the event would cover four areas: evangelization, healthcare, education, and responsible AI development with safeguards online.

In his opening remarks, Cardinal Michael Czerny, a founder of the Vatican's inter-dicastery commission on artificial intelligence, argued that learning should be a shared dialogue rather than an isolated transaction. He warned that everyone is affected by AI yet few are truly listening to one another. Vincent Higgins, CEO of the Builders AI Forum, described the goals of the event. Montse Alvarado, prefect of the Vatican's Dicastery for Communication, urged participants to ask who they should be while shaping this technology, and to draw on the network in the room rather than lose their interdependence.

Over the two days, speakers addressed accountability and the needs of families and schools. Megan Garcia, whose son Sewell died by suicide after forming a romantic attachment to a chatbot, told EWTN News that the central question is who is responsible when AI harms a child. She said companies should submit to third-party testing before release and must not keep, share, or sell children's data. Many participants argued that AI used in Catholic schools should align with Church teaching and philosophy, and that families should discuss together what should be available or filtered. Matthew Sanders, CEO of Longbeard, which organizes the forum, said AI designed to suit a billion people is an impossible task.

Participants also discussed how AI can serve faith formation, with Longbeard's Magisterium AI product a focus of several sessions. Bishop Stephen Wang of the Diocese of Arundel and Brighton said many people explore faith through AI and that seminarians already use it, so formation should prepare them to use it discerningly. Erich Kerekes, CEO of the Hallow app, said prayer is a relationship that AI cannot provide, and Alvarado stated that AI is a tool through which messages are communicated, not a person. Czerny said the Church must first show AI builders that it is listening. Coverage of the forum reports these views but does not describe further policy steps or outcomes.

Articles.Title: ‘We are all impacted by AI but nobody’s listening’ to one another, cardinal warns at conference

stories.Headline: Netflix AI Voice Lawsuit, YouTube Live Dubs, Deepgram and TransPerfect M&A
stories.Summary:
A German voice actor has planned a lawsuit against Netflix over alleged unauthorized AI training on voice recordings, according to a roundup published by Slator on November 6, 2026. The same discussion notes that new SAG-AFTRA protections now require consent before a digital voice replica can be created. The roundup, hosted by Florian and Esther, also covers YouTube's plans to introduce AI dubbing for live streams. It additionally reports that ElevenLabs is pushing into real-time speech translation. Taken together, these items point to a fast-moving contest over how voices are used and translated.

On the M&A side, the roundup describes Deepgram's acquisition of Daily, which brings voice-agent infrastructure closer to Deepgram's speech technology. It also covers TransPerfect's purchase of Synterex, a clinical and regulatory writing consultancy, which extends TransPerfect's reach into regulated content creation. Florian highlights that RWS has completed its acquisition of Acolad and has returned to modest organic growth, even as its localization business remains under pressure. The articles give no deal values for these transactions. Each deal is presented as a step toward a broader service offering rather than a standalone bet.

The roundup attributes its commentary to its hosts, Florian and Esther, who discuss these developments on their podcast. Esther is described as explaining why Reddit's AI-translated content, which began as a promising growth strategy, may now be hurting its visibility in Google search. Esther also reviews Appen's strong third-quarter performance, which the hosts link in part to China and generative AI projects. AI-Media, according to the same discussion, forecasts rising recurring revenue alongside modest overall growth expectations. The articles do not name a company responsible for the Netflix dispute beyond the voice actor's planned action.

The roundup further covers Cohere's latest funding round and multibillion-dollar valuation, which the hosts connect to the strategic importance of sovereign AI infrastructure and to backing from Canadian and European investors. It also notes that California has canceled an AI translation procurement process for court services, a decision tied to concerns about accuracy and earlier technology deployments. The hosts frame this as a tension between automated translation and human language access. The articles do not say what California will do next with court translation services.

Articles.Title: Netflix AI Voice Lawsuit, YouTube Live Dubs, Deepgram and TransPerfect M&A

stories.Headline: Baidu Faces Major Lawsuit Over AI Growth Claims
stories.Summary:
Baidu, the Chinese technology company, faces a shareholder class-action lawsuit filed September 14 in federal court in New York. The suit alleges the company overstated how well artificial intelligence could offset its declining advertising business. It covers investors who bought Baidu securities between November 18, 2025, and August 17, 2026. The legal challenge comes as investors already face weak financial results and a stock decline of roughly 43% so far this year.

The plaintiffs say management made misleading statements about AI growth while failing to disclose that its newer businesses could not adequately make up for shrinking advertising revenue. Baidu's second-quarter revenue fell 4% year over year to RMB31.3 billion ($4.62 billion), and its online marketing revenue dropped 19%. Its AI-powered business brought in RMB12.5 billion, growing 25% annually but falling 8% from the prior quarter. AI cloud infrastructure revenue rose 50% year over year, a sign of real demand, though it has not reversed the company's overall revenue decline. Shares fell 12.73% after the August 18 earnings report.

The lawsuit names CEO Robin Li and CFO Haijian He as defendants. The allegations have not been proven, and the financial impact of the litigation is unclear. Baidu operates China's leading internet search engine, earning most of its revenue from online advertising. It is also expanding into AI cloud infrastructure, enterprise AI applications and autonomous driving through its Apollo Go platform.

Eligible shareholders have until November 13 to seek appointment as lead plaintiff, though the case could take far longer to resolve. Investors are watching Baidu's next earnings report, especially AI cloud growth, advertising declines and operating cash flow. The central question is whether AI revenue can grow fast enough to stabilize total sales. Continued contraction, weaker AI momentum or further litigation could deepen investor concern.

Articles.Title: Baidu Faces Major Lawsuit Over AI Growth Claims

stories.Headline: Galloway sees record swing from young men as a $1.5 trillion AI bill is handed to investors
stories.Summary:
The 2026 midterms gave Democrats control of both chambers of Congress, with 54 Senate seats and 240 House seats, along with a majority of 29 governorships nationwide. Scott Galloway, speaking on The Prof G Pod, said the figure that matters most is a 38-point swing toward Democrats among men aged 18 to 29, which he called arguably the biggest swing recorded in any cohort in a recent election. Upsets came in deep-red states such as South Carolina, Kansas and Texas, where Galloway said Kansas sent a senator to Washington for the first time in 100 years. Jessica Tarlov, on the same live stream, described the rural collapse for Republicans as a shot across the bow and cautioned Democrats against over-reading the result for 2028.

The same episode ties the political shift to the money behind artificial intelligence. Hyperscale capital spending over the past 12 months came to nearly $700 billion, up almost 90 percent from a year earlier, and pushed Oracle, Meta, Amazon and Google into negative free cash flow. Ed Elson estimated that the five largest hyperscalers face more than $2 trillion in capital spending over the next two years against roughly $600 billion in cash, leaving a gap of about $1.5 trillion that must come from capital markets. Microsoft announced a $25 billion bond sale the day after its earnings, and Meta said a week earlier it would raise $95 billion in equity. Democrats have also campaigned on pausing data center construction, with at least 41 local ballot measures targeting such projects across 10 states, according to Reuters reporting.

Galloway attributed Alphabet's nearly 13 percent drop after earnings, its worst day since going public, to concerns about capital discipline rather than weak growth. He said Microsoft managed its AI spending more tightly and was rewarded with a 5 percent gain, while Amazon fell about 7 percent the following day. He pointed to an admission on Alphabet's earnings call that AI mode generates few ads, which he read as a sign the new product could cannibalize search revenue. Elson, also on Prof G Markets, made the broader point that these companies, once the most self-sufficient in the market, now depend on bond and equity buyers to fund the buildout.

The episode frames the week as one in which the party with apparent leverage has become dependent, a pattern Galloway and his guests tied to voters, allies and companies alike. Zakaria said some allies, including Canada, are diversifying trade and security arrangements because they no longer trust continuity in US policy, and that Prime Minister Mark Carney plans to keep these deals even if a Democrat wins in 2028. Morgan Stanley has flagged a Democratic legislature combined with local data center victories as the most negative scenario for AI investment sentiment. Investors are watching whether the young male swing holds into 2028 and whether the $1.5 trillion funding gap closes on terms the market accepts.

Articles.Title: Galloway sees record swing from young men as a $1.5 trillion AI bill is handed to investors

stories.Headline: Lawsuit Links ChatGPT to Murder: Is OpenAI Liable for User Crime?
stories.Summary:
A husband, James Gates, has filed a civil lawsuit alleging that ChatGPT helped his estranged wife, Cheryl, plan and conceal attempts to poison him. The complaint was filed in October 2026, after he became seriously ill in July 2025 and suspected poisoning. The suit names OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman as defendants. Prosecutors had earlier dropped attempted murder and food contamination charges against Cheryl Gates in April 2026, citing insufficient evidence. OpenAI disputes responsibility and says it banned Cheryl's account and provided information to law enforcement.

Other lawsuits make similar claims about violence. In Connecticut, the estate of Suzanne Adams sued OpenAI after her son, Stein-Erik Soelberg, killed her and died by suicide in August 2025. Relatives of Tiru Chabba sued after the April 2025 Florida State University shooting, alleging the gunman used ChatGPT to research campus activity. Families affected by the February 2026 Tumbler Ridge school shooting in Canada also sued, after the company acknowledged banning an account linked to the shooter months earlier. OpenAI said those conversations did not meet its threshold for alerting police.

On October 30, OpenAI announced additional safeguards, including providing less detailed information about past mass attacks and developing automated interventions to end conversations focused on serious violence. Repeated incidents could lead to account restrictions, with tighter weapons-related limits for teenagers. OpenAI says it referred credible, imminent threats to law enforcement more than 200 times in the third quarter of 2026 and plans to publish a community safety report in early 2027. The company has not been held liable in these cases.

The articles note that the legal questions remain unsettled. Plaintiffs generally must show a legal duty, a breach of that duty, and a link between the company's conduct and the harm, while OpenAI can argue that the attackers made independent choices. Illinois' new AI safety law does not give individuals a right to sue, and there is no federal law on the matter yet. The article also says that victims and families may pursue negligence, wrongful death, or product liability claims, and that courts must decide how those doctrines apply to chatbots. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Lawsuit Links ChatGPT to Murder: Is OpenAI Liable for User Crime?

stories.Headline: CPython flaw exposes AI inference servers to sandbox escape attacks
stories.Summary:
A security team at RunSybil has reported that a memory-safety flaw in CPython, the standard implementation of Python, can let malicious AI model templates escape code sandboxes and run arbitrary code inside inference servers. The researchers, led by Darius Houle, described the issue in a blog post and said attackers could use it to gain a foothold in servers handling requests for many users. They also warned that such an attack could reach the cloud infrastructure hosting those workloads. The article was published on November 6, 2026.

The researchers showed how a specially crafted model could abuse the flaw to get past sandbox protections in Jinja, a Python-based templating engine that structures interactions between users and large language models. The attack targets hosting providers that let customers upload and run their own models, a feature known as bring-your-own-model. In the demonstration, RunSybil modified the Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct model with a backdoored template file, and when the model was loaded through an inference engine such as vLLM, the template executed code in the serving process. The researchers said the bug works even in empty sandbox contexts, because the objects it uses are available in every template. They also said that CPython could use a cached parameter list after an object was changed through a callback, and an assertion that would catch this is disabled in normal release builds.

The Python Security Response Team, which handles security reports for CPython, disputed that the demonstration is a CPython vulnerability. It acknowledged the underlying bug and thanked RunSybil for helping fix it, but said that escapes from sandboxes are outside its security threat model and should be handled by the maintainers of the sandboxing software. The team also said the researchers had sent their report by email instead of through the project's private GitHub reporting channel. RunSybil disclosed the issue to CPython, the Pallets Project, which maintains Jinja, and Hugging Face, and said it received conflicting views about who should address the problem. The researchers argued there was no coordinated remediation process, a claim the team rejected.

RunSybil submitted a patch that was merged into CPython's main development branch on August 14, and the team said it was also backported to the 3.13, 3.14, and 3.15 branches as a regular bug fix rather than a security fix. The researchers had worried that the absence of a backport to Python 3.12 could slow adoption, and Houle wrote that major parts of the AI ecosystem still rely on that version, so memory-safety fixes might not be widely adopted until late 2028, when it reaches end of life. The researchers recommend that AI hosting providers treat sandboxed code, template engines, and expression evaluators as best-effort security controls rather than standalone security boundaries. The article does not say whether any inference providers have confirmed fixes or changes to their services.

Articles.Title: CPython flaw exposes AI inference servers to sandbox escape attacks

stories.Headline: Trump: ‘Superintelligence is gold’ ... counters Democrats’ AI regulation push with ‘100% support’
stories.Summary:
On the 6th (local time), U.S. President Donald Trump reaffirmed his full support for artificial intelligence and data center development, pushing back against regulation proposals from Democrats. He made the statement on his social media platform Truth Social, which was reported by the Associated Press and other foreign media. The remarks came after Democrats gained momentum from their landslide win in the midterm elections. Trump's position sets up a sharp political divide over how the United States should govern the fast-growing AI sector.

In his post, Trump said that as president he fully supports superintelligence, the term he uses for AI, and that he would work with states that want to grow wealthy by adopting it. He compared data centers and superintelligence to gold, arguing that only foolish leaders would reject the wealth they bring. The message was aimed directly at Democrats, who had campaigned on tighter data center rules. Their pledge drew on voter frustration that the heavy power use of data centers raises electricity bills and adds to environmental strain. Democrats won in key areas including Texas and Ohio, making measures to halt or pause new data center construction more likely.

Financial markets reacted sharply to the prospect of Democratic-led AI regulation. On the previous day, the Nasdaq fell nearly 5.5 percent, its worst drop in 19 months, and major AI-related stocks declined across the board. Trump blamed the slump on what he called the "Dumocrats," arguing that the fault lay with Democrats rather than Republicans. He also maintained that large-scale data center investment is essential to winning the AI race with China. He dismissed calls from some in the tech industry to slow AI development as a hoax that benefits China, and he argued that attracting data centers would create local jobs and lower taxes.

Articles.Title: Trump: ‘Superintelligence is gold’ ... counters Democrats’ AI regulation push with ‘100% support’

stories.Headline: Schools are in control, Gemini and Search off by default: Google says amid controversy over Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, Google announced that its AI tools, including the Gemini chatbot, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search, will be switched off by default for K-12 student accounts. The company said they will stay off until school administrators explicitly turn them on. The change reverses a move Google made in August, when it turned Gemini on by default for many students using Google Classroom. Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager of education, laid out the policy in a blog post titled Designing responsible AI for learning.

Under the new setup, schools can switch on Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Search individually, or all of them together. Google also said it is updating Search for schools so that AI Mode and AI Overviews walk students through problems step by step, rather than handing over quick answers to schoolwork. The company said it will share more specifics with schools in the coming months, ahead of the changes rolling out. The blog post did not say clearly what happens to Search at schools that turn off AI, though Phillips told the New York Times that search and AI are deeply integrated, and that schools banning AI would lose search access and see a message saying it is unavailable.

The change came after a New York Times report that Google would cut off search for schools that reject AI entirely, which drew sharp criticism. Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani were among the Democrats who accused Google of threatening schools and abusing its monopoly power to push AI on students. Mamdani said no corporation should have the power to dictate how children are taught. Lina Khan, the former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, said Google was using its search monopoly to coerce schools and would punish those that do not fall in line. Google, for its part, said schools are in control and that the policy gives them more choice, not less, and Phillips said the company believes schools should manage AI in their own classrooms.

The dispute comes as resistance to AI in classrooms grows among parents and school districts, and Google's Chromebooks are used by tens of millions of students, sometimes starting in kindergarten. In September, New York City barred students through eighth grade from using generative AI this school year, and Los Angeles Unified blocked students from generative AI on district-issued devices, including AI features built into Google Workspace apps. Google has made AI central to Search in recent years, adding AI Overviews at the top of many results pages. Other companies are taking a similar learning-focused approach, with OpenAI announcing ChatGPT for Teens in August, which includes a Study Mode. For now, schools are waiting for the detailed rules Google has promised in the coming months.

Articles.Title: Lawsuit Claims Google Embedded Search AI Harmed a 13-Year-Old Student
