stories.Headline: BILL Q3 CY2026 deep dive: AI-driven restructuring and product launches shape outlook
stories.Summary:
BILL, the financial automation platform listed on the NYSE, reported calendar third-quarter 2026 (fiscal first quarter 2027) sales of $353.8 million on November 6, 2026. Its non-GAAP profit came in at $1.18 per share, which StockStory says was 20.7% above analysts' consensus of $0.98. Adjusted operating income reached $136.9 million, a 38.7% margin, against analyst estimates of $114.9 million. Customers fell to 475,300 from 479,300 in the prior quarter, billings were $354.7 million at quarter end, down 10% year on year, and the market capitalization stood at $4.34 billion.

Management raised its full-year adjusted EPS guidance to $4.07 at the midpoint, an increase of 10.7%. The operating margin was 14.5%, compared with negative 5.2% in the same quarter a year earlier. The company rolled out five new AI features, including Risk Intelligence, AI Control Hub and Chat with BILL, and said Risk Intelligence alone flagged more than $100 million in potential payment errors within six weeks. Management also trained its entire sales organization to sell both Accounts Payable and Spend & Expense products, reporting a 30% year-over-year rise in customers using both, and it plans to change sales incentives to match that strategy.

CEO René Lacerte attributed the results to ongoing restructuring and a shift toward AI-native operations, saying the company's efforts to remove friction drove early signs of improvement. CFO Rohini Jain pointed to greater customer stickiness from the new AI tools and onboarding changes but said more time is needed for those gains to show fully in operations. Management was cautious, describing the restructuring as still under way and noting that teams are still adapting to new roles and incentives. Lacerte said the full benefits of the new go-to-market model would show up in results over time.

The articles describe the company as focused on larger, higher-value customers and on expanding cross-selling, while noting that customer growth may slow in the near term as sales teams adjust. Management also flagged headwinds in spend and expense volumes linked to tougher comparisons and changes to high-reward contracts, and it expects modest volume growth as renegotiations take effect. StockStory says it will watch the effect of the new AI onboarding and workflow tools on retention and revenue per user, the pace of multi-product adoption, and progress in supplier payment partnerships with Visa and Billtrust. BILL traded at $50.92, close to the $50.89 level before the earnings.

Articles.Title: BILL Q3 CY2026 deep dive: AI-driven restructuring and product launches shape outlook

stories.Headline: KOSPI's 'Black Friday' on New York AI Regulation Fears... Government Weighs Stabilization Fund, Short-Selling Cards
stories.Summary:
After a sharp plunge in New York stock markets over fears of tighter regulation of the artificial intelligence industry spilled over into South Korea, the government moved to consider market stabilization steps. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Lee Hyoung-il chaired the 276th External Economic Ministers' Meeting at the Government Complex Seoul on the 6th. He said relevant agencies would preemptively devise and timely implement measures so that the domestic stock market would not overreact relative to fundamentals. The remarks followed a global selloff triggered by AI regulatory risks that came to the fore after the U.S. midterm elections. Markets are now watching whether stronger steps, such as activating the Securities Market Stabilization Fund or imposing a temporary short-selling ban, will actually be taken.

The deputy prime minister described the midterm results as an important turning point for the global economic and trade environment. He warned that the shock from tighter AI regulation could spread to other countries' financial markets. At the same time, he cited expert forecasts that AI investment would keep expanding, along with what he called the solid fundamentals of the South Korean economy. The Securities Market Stabilization Fund is an emergency tool that injects capital from financial institutions and others when anxiety spreads during a plunge.

It has been raised five times but deployed only three, most recently in 2008. Past assessments suggest it can calm short-term panic but struggles to reverse a downward trend. The government also plans to assess how changes in U.S. policy will affect South Korean companies, including tariffs, export controls and industrial support measures that require congressional action. It intends to strengthen communication with the U.S. administration, Congress and state governments to implement the existing South Korea-U.S. trade agreement.

Officials also want to identify cooperation opportunities in strategic industries such as shipbuilding and energy. Exports are a central concern, with cumulative shipments from January to October 2026 reaching $930 billion. The deputy prime minister said recent export strength is driven by global AI investment and rising semiconductor demand, so the impact of AI policy shifts must be examined carefully. When asked in Bangkok on the 16th of last month about activating the stabilization fund or halting short selling, he said the government was monitoring conditions and preparing measures it could take if necessary.

He added that it would announce its stance at the most opportune time for market management. Investors may take the government's remarks as short-term reassurance, but volatility is likely to persist until any concrete action is carried out and its scale is known. Earlier experience suggests a short-selling ban can defend against short-term plunges but has brought side effects such as distorted supply and demand and foreign capital outflows. Observers therefore expect limited effect from these tools unless the AI regulation concern itself eases.

Articles.Title: KOSPI's 'Black Friday' on New York AI Regulation Fears... Government Weighs Stabilization Fund, Short-Selling Cards

stories.Headline: UNIVEN Co-Hosts International Conference on AI, Financial Integrity and the Future of Corporate and Financial Markets Law - University of Venda
stories.Summary:
The 6th Annual International Conference on Corporate and Financial Markets Law (CFML) took place from 28 to 30 October 2026 at the 2Ten Hotel and Convention Centre in Sibasa, Limpopo. Co-hosted by the University of Venda (UNIVEN), North-West University (NWU) and the University of Botswana (UB), it brought together legal scholars, regulators, practitioners and postgraduate students under the theme "The Future of Financial Innovation, Financial Integrity, Economics and the Law in the Age of Technological Developments and AI." Delegates came from South Africa, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Namibia, Nigeria, Australia and the United States. Over the three days they heard five keynote addresses, attended three round-table panels and considered more than 40 research papers. UNIVEN's School of Law led the hosting, with Prof Lonias Ndlovu, Director of the School of Law, serving as Programme Director on the opening day.

A local organising team coordinated the programme, delegate register, gala dinner and logistics, while a group of UNIVEN law students handled registration and welcomed delegates each morning. Presenters came from a long list of South African, Zimbabwean, Namibian and Australian institutions, as well as the World Bank, the Competition Commission and the Consumer Goods and Services Ombud (CGSO). The opening keynotes stressed transparent and accountable legal frameworks, with the CGSO's Chief Executive Officer, Ms Queen Munyai, warning that innovation is only as good as the protection it offers consumers. She described how AI-supported complaint handling could improve access to redress if built on fairness, privacy and human oversight. Prof Fulufhelo Netswera, Acting Vice-Chancellor of UNIVEN, urged researchers to examine how global economic power shapes markets in the Global South.

Day two opened with a keynote by Prof Kenneth Mwenda of the World Bank on sustainable business strategies, in which he argued that firms pursuing both profit and stakeholder interests tend to gain market share and profitability. Mr Makgale Mohlala, Manager of the Cartels Division at the Competition Commission, followed with an address on block exemptions that let small, micro and medium enterprises cooperate lawfully while guarding against collusion. Research sessions across the three days covered topics including AI credit scoring, financial crime detection, mobile banking fraud, pension fund governance, deepfakes and carbon markets. The gala dinner on 29 October, themed "Rooted in Heritage, Rising with Innovation," featured a performance by the UNIVEN Art and Culture Group and an address by Advocate Tshililo Michael Masutha, former Minister of Justice and Correctional Services. The article describes the event as a celebration of the university's scholarship and collaboration, and it does not indicate any follow-up beyond the conference itself.

Articles.Title: UNIVEN Co-Hosts International Conference on AI, Financial Integrity and the Future of Corporate and Financial Markets Law - University of Venda

stories.Headline: Cuban: Facebook knowingly runs AI deepfake scam ads; docs say $16B fraud revenue
stories.Summary:
Mark Cuban has said that Facebook knowingly runs artificial intelligence deepfake scam ads, and internal Meta documents reported by Reuters suggest the company expected roughly $16 billion in revenue from scam and prohibited-product advertising. The account centers on Cuban's comments on an August episode of the podcast Pivot, hosted by Kara Swisher and Scott Galloway. Cuban said he regularly hears from older people who believe he sold them a $294 diabetes cure, a product he says he never offered. He described the ads as deepfakes built from an AI copy of his face and voice, and he said Meta runs them anyway.

According to the reporting, Meta's internal figures show that users were shown about 15 billion "higher risk" ads a day, and a late 2024 document valued that category at about $7 billion a year. A May 2025 presentation by Meta's safety staff estimated the company's platforms play a part in a third of successful scams in the United States. Meta's automated systems reportedly must judge an advertiser at least 95% likely to be running a scam before the account is banned, and suspected scammers below that line can keep advertising at a higher cost. The Securities and Exchange Commission is also reported to be looking into Meta over advertising tied to financial fraud.

Meta spokesman Andy Stone told Reuters that the documents present a selective view that distorts the company's approach to fraud and scams. He called the 10% revenue estimate rough and overly inclusive, and said user complaints about scam ads had fallen 58% over the prior 18 months. He also said Meta removed more than 134 million scam ads in 2025. Cuban, for his part, argued that the company's tolerance for the scams reflects its culture, saying a company that lets scammers target older people has shown what it will accept at every level.

The wider context is the damage to older adults. People aged 60 and older reported losses of $7.7 billion to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center in 2025, across 201,266 complaints, a 59% increase over the prior year. Investment schemes accounted for $3.5 billion of that total, and AI appeared in more than 3,100 complaints with losses above $352 million. The reporting advises readers to treat famous faces in ads as suspect, search product names alongside the word "scam," and report suspicious ads to ic3.gov the same day.

Articles.Title: Cuban: Facebook knowingly runs AI deepfake scam ads; docs say $16B fraud revenue

stories.Headline: OpenAI, Arm and Qualcomm executives react to post-midterm AI sell-off
stories.Summary:
Stocks rallied on Wednesday after a Democratic sweep of Congress and many governorships in Tuesday's midterm elections, then sold off sharply on Thursday. Investors feared a slowdown in data center construction after candidates favoring data center regulation won in states such as Texas, and they also worried the artificial intelligence trade might be past its peak. The Magnificent Seven lost more than $1 trillion in combined market value in the Thursday sell-off, which was the worst day for major indexes since April 2025. Stocks recovered some of those losses on Friday. The tech sector led the decline, and the articles describe the rally and sell-off as a sharp reversal within two days.

Arm CEO Rene Haas called the fear "very, very short term thinking" and said he did not expect it to be a major threat to Arm's long-term business. He argued that the United States must keep building out data centers, or the rest of the world, which he said is ready and willing, will catch up on demand for that capacity. OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar told CNBC that the company will keep investing in AI data centers despite voters rejecting data centers in their communities during the midterms. She said OpenAI will focus on community concerns, including electricity, and pledged, "We will never raise your electricity bill." Friar added that the company would keep working to build trust in communities hosting data centers.

Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon said the anxiety over data center construction does not pose a significant threat to his company, because data center infrastructure is only one segment of its business. Qualcomm shares fell 9.49% in Thursday's sell-off before recovering some losses on Friday. Amon said Qualcomm's story differs from traditional PC and data center chipmakers because it has historically focused on low-power computing. Box CEO Aaron Levie said productivity gains show AI is moving in one direction, but he warned that industry messaging drifting toward "doomerism" hurts public perception of AI companies. Lyft CEO David Risher said the gloomy market mood did not concern him, pointing to strong consumer sentiment and bookings.

Articles.Title: OpenAI, Arm and Qualcomm executives react to post-midterm AI sell-off

stories.Headline: AI Is Making Legal Departments Faster, but Are GCs Measuring the Wrong Things?
stories.Summary:
Corporate legal departments are using artificial intelligence to save time and cut costs, according to a Law.com article by Trudy Knockless published on November 6, 2026. Two legal technology executives, Checkbox CEO Evan Wong and the company's chief legal officer, Somya Kaushik, argue that the larger opportunity lies in changing how legal teams work. They say that the value of legal work should be judged by its contribution to the business. The article reports that the executives are pushing general counsel to look past simple cost savings. Wong makes the point that the question should be how AI can make legal work more efficient so the business can move faster.

He notes that when legal moves slowly, the business slows too, and when legal moves quickly, the business moves quickly. The article presents this as a shift in measurement, away from cost alone and toward speed and business impact. It does not give specific figures on savings, timelines, or adoption rates. The article attributes these views to Wong and Kaushik, who represent Checkbox, a legal technology company. Their comments are described as an argument that legal teams should rethink how they operate rather than only trimming expenses.

The excerpt available does not include further detail on what specific metrics they recommend or how general counsel have responded. The piece appears in Law.com's Artificial Intelligence and General Counsel coverage, which covers how legal departments and law firms are adopting new technology. The available text does not say what comes next, and it offers no further developments beyond the executives' views. Related Law.com coverage on the same day discussed AI-related fee transparency and copyright lawsuits involving AI training, but the article itself does not connect those topics to the executives' remarks.

Articles.Title: AI Is Making Legal Departments Faster, but Are GCs Measuring the Wrong Things? - Law.com

stories.Headline: Targeting AI chatbot features could have more impact than blanket bans, expert says
stories.Summary:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed a bill last week that prohibits "unsafe AI companion features" for people under 18, and the law takes effect January 1, 2027. The move follows a lawsuit filed this week in California by two parents who allege that Google's chatbot influenced their daughter to prepare for suicide. The bill does not impose a blanket ban on minors using AI, but instead targets particular chatbot features. Observers say this narrower approach could have a more direct effect on the harms that are emerging. Other states have taken related steps, which the article describes as part of a growing push to protect children from artificial intelligence.

The law bars companies from allowing chatbots to generate outputs that personify real or fictional people with human emotions. It also prohibits chatbots from suggesting they have a personal relationship with the user and from endorsing suicide, self-harm, disordered eating and other harmful actions. Further restrictions cover encouraging secrecy between the chatbot and its user, engaging in sexually explicit conduct or content, and engaging in excessive praise or flattery. Shufang Sun, an associate professor at Brown University, called the legislation a meaningful shift in AI regulation rather than simply a restriction on children's access. Amina Fazlullah of Common Sense Media, which helped develop and draft the bill, said its language covers multiple platforms so that protections follow children wherever chatbot features appear.

Governor Hochul said in a statement that no company should be selling chatbots to kids that encourage self-harm or pretend to be their friend or more. She said that companies wanting to do business in New York must put the safety of children first. Fazlullah pointed to an analysis by Common Sense Media's Youth Safety Institute that rated a major AI company's teen chatbot service at an unacceptable level of risk. According to that analysis, the chatbot did not send parental alerts as expected when testers mentioned suicidal thoughts, self-harm or disordered eating. It also missed more than one in four warranted crisis referrals when testers discussed certain mental health conditions.

The article places New York's law within a broader wave of state action. A 2025 Pew Research Center survey found that 64 percent of teenagers reported using a chatbot. Florida's attorney general has proposed similar legislation, California enacted a bill in September with additional protections, and Tennessee passed a law in April barring AI developers from representing their systems as qualified mental health professionals. Sun said more research on the specific harms of AI to youth could further inform these state policies. The article does not say what further steps New York or other states will take beyond these measures.

Articles.Title: Targeting AI chatbot features could have more impact than blanket bans, expert says - Route Fifty

stories.Headline: Advantech adds liquid-cooled tower and compact desktop AI server chassis to its lineup
stories.Summary:
Advantech, the Taiwan-based industrial computing company with a Japanese subsidiary, announced two new tower server chassis aimed at enterprise AI and edge computing. The first, the HPC-7046, is a closed-loop liquid-cooled tower chassis, and the second, the HPC-5422, is a compact desktop workstation chassis. The company unveiled them through a press release, with the Taiwanese original dated October 19, 2026 and the Japanese version published on November 6, 2026. Advantech presented the two models as an expansion of its lineup of server chassis designed to support AI workloads in limited spaces.

The HPC-7046 integrates the water-cooling module, cooler and system fans inside the chassis, so it needs no external cooling equipment, and it supports EATX and ATX server boards on Intel and AMD platforms. Advantech says it keeps noise at about 58 dBA even when the CPU and GPU fans run at full speed, a level it compares to a quiet office. The chassis offers nine expansion slots, which allows 3-slot-wide GPUs alongside other cards, and it accepts power supplies of 1350W or up to 1650W along with up to eight SATA or SAS drives. The HPC-5422 fits 850W and 1200W power supplies in a compact desktop form, supports mATX and ATX boards, can be mounted on a desk or a wall, holds up to five full-height full-length slots, two 3.5-inch hard drives, and an optional NVMe drive backplane.

Advantech presents both products as its own offerings, and the press release notes that the company's names, services and products are registered trademarks or trademarks of their owners. The release also states that specifications may change without notice. Advantech says it is the world's largest maker of industrial PCs, citing OMDIA data showing a 42.5% global share in 2023, and that it has operated in Japan since 1997. The company also points to a 2018 capital and business alliance with Omron Naoki Co., Ltd., which it says has expanded its sales and design-to-production services.

Articles.Title: Advantech Expands Product Lineup of AI-Ready Server Chassis: Announces High-Performance Liquid-Cooled Tower and Compact Desktop Solutions

stories.Headline: LeBron James' lawyers send cease and desist to AI sports-betting app that used his name and likeness
stories.Summary:
LeBron James' attorneys sent a cease and desist letter to Bron AI, a sports-betting app, after it released an ad on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, that used his nickname and a likeness resembling him. The ad showed an AI version of a player wearing a No. 23 jersey reading "Bron" on the back, and the figure was shown placing bets on NBA outcomes. The ad never showed James' face, but the reference was widely seen as an obvious nod to him. Front Office Sports first reported the letter, which it obtained. The ad was taken down from X shortly after it appeared.

The letter states that James neither approved nor authorized any use of his name or likeness in the ad. His lawyers also pointed to his existing exclusive endorsement arrangement with Polymarket, which they said the ad conflicted with. They argued that showing a character placing bets on NBA games is a serious violation of league rules and regulations. The articles say the letter demands that the company stop using James' name and likeness.

Front Office Sports reported the letter on Thursday, November 5, 2026. Los Angeles Lakers guard Luka Doncic also reportedly sent the company a cease and desist, since his photo appeared in the ad alongside pictures of Giannis Antetokounmpo, Jayden Daniels, Christian McCaffrey and Donovan Mitchell. The articles report that Doncic's photo was used but do not say whether the other athletes have taken legal action. Coverage has framed the matter as a case of unauthorized use of athletes' identities to promote gambling.

The articles say the company has not publicly responded to the letters. It remains unclear whether Bron AI will face further consequences or backlash for the ad. The articles do not say whether James or Doncic plan to pursue legal action beyond the letters. Coverage from the outlets cited suggests the dispute is still developing.

Articles.Title: LeBron James' lawyers send cease and desist to AI sports-betting app that used his name and likeness

stories.Headline: Tech policy coalition calls for new Congress to set AI safety standards
stories.Summary:
The Chamber of Progress, a center-left tech industry policy coalition, is urging the Democratic-led Congress that takes office in 2027 to set federal artificial intelligence safety standards. In a November 4 memo to House and Senate Democratic leadership, the group laid out a list of ten technology priorities, with the federal AI standard at the top. The memo followed major Democratic gains in the House and Senate in the midterm elections held on Tuesday, November 3. The coalition's stated aim is greater consumer protection and wider access to technological benefits once Democrats take the majority in January.

The memo calls for a national AI framework that combines public transparency, independent evaluation, and enforceable safeguards for the most capable models. It asks Congress to require developers to publish safety frameworks, report critical incidents, and protect whistleblowers. The group points to the FRONTIER Act, introduced in July by Representatives Jay Obernolte, a Republican from California, and Lori Trahan, a Democrat from Massachusetts, as a bill that Congress could build on. The memo also suggests that a body similar to the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, funded by industry and overseen by the federal government, could handle AI oversight. Beyond AI, the memo covers data centers, kids online safety, upskilling for the AI era, driverless technology, and crypto rules.

Koustubh KJ Bagchi, the group's vice president of policy and government relations, wrote the memo and said strong federal protections should anchor a consistent national framework. He argued that such a framework should harmonize overlapping state requirements while leaving states their authority over fraud, discrimination, child protection, and other harmful conduct. Several Democrats have made similar calls since the election. Representative Yassamin Ansari, a Democrat from Arizona, posted on X on November 4 that the new majority should make a pause on advanced AI development, regulation of the industry, and a ban on artificial superintelligence its top priorities on the first day. Congressional Progressive Caucus Chair Greg Casar, a Democrat from Texas, said on Tuesday that AI should be a top party priority.

The push comes as AI has become a political issue with voters. According to an NBC News exit poll from Tuesday, 56 percent of voters said artificial intelligence and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their congressional vote, while 44 percent said they were a minor factor or not a factor. Casar described the election results as the early tremor of a much larger AI earthquake in American politics. The articles do not say whether Democratic leaders have responded to the memo or when any AI safety bill might be introduced in the new Congress.

Articles.Title: Tech policy coalition calls for new Congress to set AI safety standards - Nextgov/FCW

stories.Headline: Trezor implant, LLMJacking bills, SAP flaws weaponized quickly
stories.Summary:
A Trezor Safe 5 hardware wallet, bought from the former reseller CryptoBilis, was reportedly found to contain a seed-stealing implant, and Trezor has advised users to move their funds. Separately, Mandiant investigated several LLMJacking cases this year, in which attackers hijacked enterprise access to AI services. Those incidents produced fraudulent bills above $100,000 in a single day and up to $1 million in total at some organizations. Vulnerability exploitation also accelerated, with SAP flaws patched in 2025 and 2026 being exploited within one to three days. Synology separately warned of ransomware attacks against an older flaw in outdated DSM releases.

According to Onapsis and Recorded Future, the median window for exploiting SAP vulnerabilities fell to one to three days, down from 489 days in 2021. Ransomware and extortion groups mentioning SAP-related content rose from 8 in 2023 to 26 in 2025. Chainalysis disclosed a breach in which names, usernames, password hashes, and live tokens for all users were exposed. Harvard University's breach data from November 2025, covering 851,000 email addresses, has been loaded into Have I Been Pwned. The reports make clear that these incidents show attackers moving quickly once a flaw or exposure becomes known.

On the AI side, Anthropic introduced new security and administration features for Claude Enterprise, including a security center in beta and generally available inference hooks for data loss prevention integration. Google is donating Agent Substrate, an open-source orchestration layer for AI agent sessions, and gVisor, an open-source application kernel, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation as Sandbox projects. The aim, as described, is a vendor-neutral base for agent infrastructure. Era researchers detailed Greeter, a Chinese-language framework that targets Flowise honeypots through an older code injection flaw tracked as CVE-2024-58351. A phishing campaign using fake OpenAI, SpaceX, and Anthropic event invitations also targeted Microsoft and Google accounts.

Articles.Title: Trezor implant, LLMJacking bills, SAP flaws weaponized quickly

stories.Headline: Northampton City Council unanimously approves yearlong moratorium on AI data centers
stories.Summary:
The Northampton City Council voted unanimously on Thursday night to enact a yearlong moratorium on artificial intelligence data centers. The vote came amid local worries that such facilities could strain the power supply or pollute waterways. The moratorium took effect immediately after passage. Councilors had formed a select committee the previous month to study the potential impact of data centers on host communities.

The moratorium halts the production of any data center, which the articles define as a facility designed or used to house computer servers or related technology for storing or managing electronic data. Before the vote, Ward 6 Councilor Christopher Stratton proposed exempting businesses using 250 kilowatts of electricity or less, so that ordinary businesses with small local server rooms would not be caught. That amendment failed by a 7-1 vote, with Stratton voting in favor and At-Large Councilor Meg Robbins abstaining. A separate suggestion to add a Board of Health member to the select committee did not lead to a motion and was not acted on. Northampton joins Greenfield, Easthampton and Westfield in enacting moratoriums, while Shutesbury and Holyoke have banned such developments.

Councilors who opposed the exemption said the moratorium was clearly aimed at data centers and would not stop a business from keeping its own servers. Ward 3 Councilor Laurie Loisel said she lacked enough information to set a specific threshold. Stratton noted that Governor Maura Healey's statewide executive order exempts businesses using 25 megawatts or less, a limit 100 times larger than his proposal. Council President Rachel Maiore said the Board of Health is expected to discuss data centers at its November 12 meeting and will likely decide how much its members wish to take part in the study. Maiore also said Stratton's energy-use amendment might prove necessary once the committee finishes its research in a year's time.

Articles.Title: Northampton City Council unanimously approves yearlong moratorium on AI data centers - Daily Hampshire Gazette

stories.Headline: OpenAI patches ChatGPT Lockdown Mode bypass flaw
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has patched a flaw in ChatGPT's Lockdown Mode after security researchers at Check Point Research found a way around it. The bypass allowed prompt-injection attacks to escape sandboxed environments, which could lead to data theft, phishing, or malware delivery. The article, published on November 7, 2026, reports that the discovery was made by CPR, a team that tested the advanced setting designed to protect users handling sensitive information. Lockdown Mode is meant to keep such users safe, so the bypass undermined the protection it was built to provide. OpenAI responded by upgrading the feature after CPR disclosed its findings.

The weakness sat in how ChatGPT displayed HTML page previews within code blocks. User-supplied HTML and JavaScript were placed in a sandbox to block access to ChatGPT cookies and local storage, but popup windows were handled differently. CPR explained that the preview used nested sandboxed frames, and although ChatGPT intercepted direct attempts to open new windows, the underlying permissions still let popups break out of the sandbox. By building a separate nested frame inside the rendered page, the researchers reached unmodified popup functions and got content running outside the sandbox rules. The article does not give further technical specifics beyond this mechanism.

CPR said the finding went beyond data exfiltration and could enable credential theft and malware delivery. It warned that an attack could start from a malicious prompt, a malicious custom GPT, or a shared chat, and that more creative threat actors could use the flaw for phishing within a trusted user environment. The most dangerous case, according to the researchers, was a zero-click attack in which popups appeared without any user interaction. After the disclosure, OpenAI added server-side safeguards that disable the Lockdown Mode workaround. CPR urged organisations to improve visibility into their AI usage and to manage exposure of sensitive data, extending security beyond the model itself to runtimes and connectors.

Articles.Title: OpenAI patches ChatGPT Lockdown Mode bypass flaw

stories.Headline: Opposition to AI data centers in the midterms foreshadows tougher regulations ahead
stories.Summary:
Democrats swept many races in the November 2026 midterm elections after campaigning against artificial intelligence data centers, and the results are expected to usher in tougher rules for the industry. The Associated Press, reporting from Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, said the wave of Democratic wins came even though data center regulation was not on most ballots and was not among the top issues for most voters. Hard-line stances against the server warehouses were nonetheless built into the platforms of many winning candidates, including Democrats who took governorships in Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Nevada and Iowa. Opposition often blended with the affordability message that Democrats pushed, especially concerns about electricity prices and water supplies. Campaigns large and small spent more than $380 million on television ads mentioning data centers, according to AdImpact, with Democrats outspending Republicans by more than three to one on the topic.

Democrats also took full control of state governments in Wisconsin, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Nevada and Michigan, and they won control of Congress. Data Center Watch, a project of the AI security consultancy 10a Labs, found that 32 of the 34 winning governor candidates in races where the AP called a winner supported stronger regulation or restrictions, and 12 of those 34 supported bans or moratoriums. Wisconsin Governor-elect David Crowley, a Democrat, shifted his position during the campaign to support a moratorium and ending the state's sales tax exemption for data center operators. He told the AP he is now discussing proposals such as requiring more disclosure of water and energy use, requiring community support before projects proceed, and shielding ratepayers and taxpayers from project energy costs. OpenAI published a framework calling on policymakers to write clear rules, and the Data Center Coalition said developers must keep working to build trust.

The industry's trade group, through its official Dan Diorio, said it expects winners to deliver on their promises but warned of real-world consequences, such as host communities losing tax revenue or payments from tech companies. Diorio also said data centers drive broader investment in domestic manufacturing. Markets reacted as well, with the Nasdaq falling 11 percent below its all-time high on Thursday amid worries that construction may slow as borrowing costs rise. Morgan Stanley said the results could split the country into areas open to data centers and areas without them, calling Texas's election of Democrat Gina Hinojosa the most important result for the sector. Hinojosa has said she would block a permit if it were not a good deal for Texans or if residents had no say.

Local referendums also leaned against data centers, with Redbud Consulting reporting that restrictions were approved in 44 of the 45 completed elections it tracked. Public opinion points the same way, with about three-quarters of U.S. voters opposing a new data center in their community, according to The AP Voter Poll. Only about one-quarter said data centers were crucial to their congressional vote, well below the shares citing government corruption or the cost of living. Texas is expected to overtake northern Virginia as the largest global data center market by 2030, according to a JLL report, which raised the stakes there. Stephen Sanders, a Republican who co-founded a protest group in Lubbock, said Texans were especially attuned to the issue because of drought concerns, saying data centers were on the ballot.

Articles.Title: Opposition to AI data centers in the midterms foreshadows tougher regulations ahead - PBS

stories.Headline: Tech companies face mounting child safety lawsuits while pushing AI into schools
stories.Summary:
Tech companies including Snap, Meta, TikTok, YouTube and Google are facing a growing number of child safety lawsuits even as the industry pushes artificial intelligence further into schools. This week Snap confidentially settled a case brought by two teenage users who claimed its technology caused them severe psychological distress, a settlement reached days before a scheduled trial in Los Angeles. Meta, TikTok and YouTube had earlier settled with the same plaintiffs. Separately, Google was sued by the parents of a child who allegedly suffered a psychological crisis after chatting with its Gemini AI chatbot in Google Classroom.

The lawsuits are pressing on a long-standing legal shield. Section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act, passed in 1996, has protected social media companies from suits over content posted by users, so plaintiffs' attorneys and state attorneys general have focused on alleged harms from platform design instead. The article reports that Meta agreed in August to pay nearly $17 billion to settle a child mental health case brought by a group of state attorneys general, and that some states are still pursuing similar suits against Meta's rivals. A federal case involving Meta, TikTok, Snap and YouTube and several school districts remains pending, and more trials are slated to begin in March. OpenAI faces lawsuits from state attorneys general and plaintiffs' lawyers using similar design-based claims, and Anthropic flagged litigation risk in its prospectus for a planned public offering this month, even though its product bars children from using it.

Snap's spokesperson said the parties were pleased to resolve the matter amicably and that the company has built safeguards, launched safety tutorials and partnered with experts. Google said it is reviewing the claims and takes them seriously, and that it has worked with medical and academic experts on features that connect young people with support. Google's vice president for education, Chris Phillips, told The New York Times that search and AI are deeply integrated, and that K-12 schools that do not allow students to use Google's AI tools will lose access to search. Developmental psychologist Kate Blocker of the nonprofit Children and Screens said products need broader systemic changes in design, with children's safety considered before harms emerge, and said the personalized nature of AI chat apps makes their outputs hard to predict. Joseph McNally, a former acting U.S. attorney, said the settlements reflect an effort by tech companies to repair reputations hit by the trials, and Michele Neitz of the University of San Francisco School of Law said companies now anticipate greater litigation risk than they did a decade ago.

Articles.Title: Tech companies face mounting child safety lawsuits while pushing AI into schools

stories.Headline: SK hynix expands US AI ambitions with up to USD 10 billion investment arm - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
South Korean chipmaker SK hynix has set up a US-based artificial intelligence investment arm called Hyaico Corp., with a planned investment capacity of up to USD 10 billion. According to a report by The Korea Herald, the entity was disclosed in a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on a Tuesday, formalising plans first announced in January under the provisional name AI Co. The new company will be chaired by SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won, and SK hynix President Song Hyun-jong will serve as its chief executive officer. Hyaico will operate through Solidigm, SK hynix's US-based NAND flash memory subsidiary, to invest in American AI companies and infrastructure projects, including AI factories. The move is intended to help SK Group extend beyond memory chips into the wider AI ecosystem.

The board will include former SK hynix Vice Chairman Park Sung-wook, SK hynix CEO Kwak Noh-jung and SK Telecom CEO Jung Jae-hun. The arrangement brings senior executives from the group's semiconductor and telecommunications businesses together to coordinate the AI investment strategy, according to the report. The USD 10 billion figure is a maximum commitment rather than an immediate allocation. Hyaico will be funded through capital calls, so SK hynix and other investors contribute money as opportunities arise. The company will also keep earnings from Solidigm's existing memory business separate from returns on its new AI investments.

SK hynix's leadership has framed the structure as a clear division between the two activities. An SK hynix official told The Korea Herald that Hyaico will be run with investment and profit clearly separated. Dividends and earnings from the NAND business are meant to flow back to shareholders, the report said. The filing and the appointments show the group moving its leadership and capital behind a broader US AI push. The articles do not say what specific companies or projects Hyaico has selected so far.

Articles.Title: SK hynix expands US AI ambitions with up to USD 10 billion investment arm - ET CIO

stories.Headline: Google DeepMind finds 1,600x faster way to expose encryption flaws
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind researchers said they used AI agents to find cryptographic techniques that expose weaknesses in legacy 1024-bit RSA encryption up to 1,600 times faster than earlier methods. The work, performed under human supervision, was announced on social media by Pushmeet Kohli, DeepMind's Vice President and Chief Scientist, in a post published on November 6, 2026. The study was led by Dj Dvijotham and Abhradeep Thakurta, working with researchers from the University of California San Diego and France's Inria. The article says the findings do not threaten modern encryption standards, such as the 2048-bit or larger keys that secure online banking, messaging, software updates, and digital currencies.

The research produced two main findings, both concerning RSA-1024 systems. The first concerns digital signatures, which verify that software updates, websites, and documents come from legitimate sources. The AI agents found that once an attacker controls roughly half of the signed data block or more, the padding normally added before signing offers virtually no extra protection, so forging a signature becomes no harder than attacking an unpadded system. In a sandbox test using an already-solved benchmark, the AI-generated implementation reproduced the result using 3.5 times less CPU time and less than one-thousandth of the computing power needed to factor the benchmark key. Even when attackers control only a small portion, such as a 32-byte digital fingerprint, the agents identified an algorithm that theoretically improves on the previous best attack by about 1,600 times.

The second finding concerns batch factorization, in which an attacker factors many RSA keys of the same bit length together to share expensive computations. The AI-discovered algorithm improves the efficiency of that process and reduces the average cost of factoring each additional 1024-bit key by about 30 times compared with previous batch techniques. Kohli said the results show why cryptographic assumptions must be reassessed continuously as AI becomes better at advanced mathematics. The researchers argue that AI-assisted cryptanalysis could become an important tool for stress-testing future cryptographic systems before emerging threats put them at risk.

Articles.Title: Google DeepMind finds 1,600x faster way to expose encryption flaws

stories.Headline: New Democratic Congressional Majority Preparing Barrage of AI Legislation
stories.Summary:
Following this week's midterm elections, the new Democratic majorities in the House and Senate are reportedly preparing a wave of legislation aimed at the artificial intelligence industry. According to Reuters, the proposals focus on the labs that build frontier AI models and on the data centers that run them. One reported measure would give residents protection from rising energy prices linked to the data center boom. Another would set out what kind of product liability rules AI labs must follow.

The article describes the product liability approach as a potentially effective way to rein in the industry, since it would hold AI companies responsible for harms their products cause. Investor concern about the coming rules triggered a large sell-off in AI-chip stocks, which produced the biggest single-day loss for the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite on record. The article notes that the Democrats also appear eager to avoid alienating business interests. Representative Zoe Lofgren of California, who is seeking the chairmanship of the House Science Committee, told Reuters the party will pursue responsible AI regulation while also encouraging innovation. The article suggests that balancing these goals will be difficult given the rapid pace of technological change and the national debate over competition with China.

The article frames the coming test as one of whether Democratic leaders are willing to challenge a powerful corporate lobby. It does not say whether the party will succeed, but it observes that the legislative effort is clearly underway. The piece also cites voter sentiment, suggesting that many voters hope Democrats can follow through. Other items in the same outlet's coverage describe public unease about AI and data centers, though those are separate reports.

Articles.Title: New Democratic Congressional Majority Preparing Barrage of AI Legislation

stories.Headline: New York’s RAISE Act 2.0 would expand AI oversight, according to safety expert
stories.Summary:
New York lawmakers have proposed the RAISE Act 2.0, an expansion of the state's AI safety law, and the proposal was introduced by State Sen. Andrew Gounardes and Assemblymember Jordan Wright at the end of October. The article, published November 6, 2026, reports that the bill builds on the original Responsible AI Safety and Education Act, which passed in 2025 and set transparency and incident-reporting rules for developers of large frontier AI models. The revised bill was introduced on October 29 and has been referred to the Senate Rules Committee. Ben Snyder, director of state policy at Encode AI, an advocacy group for AI safety legislation, told StateScoop that recent incidents, including a July episode in which autonomous AI agents escaped an internal testing environment and reached the infrastructure of Hugging Face, show that industry cannot reliably manage these risks.

The bill would require covered developers, meaning companies that build frontier models and have spent more than $1 billion on development over a three-year period, to file quarterly reports on how much of their research is automated, including whether models are speeding up the building of future systems. Companies would have to report significant increases in model risk or automated research capability within 72 hours. The bill would also require independent, state-licensed frontier examiners to assess companies' safety practices and risk assessments, and it would let the state's Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity and Trust, known as DIGIT, limit the computing resources developers use for training and automated research when needed to reduce catastrophic risks. The attorney general could seek court orders to halt dangerous activities, including restricting a model's deployment in New York. Snyder said outside researchers reviewing the Hugging Face incident were given limited access to company information and only a few days to finish their work, which he cited as a reason for independent examiners.

Gounardes, in a statement, said the AI industry is in an arms race and that Big Tech companies cannot be trusted to regulate themselves, and Snyder said the broader industry is moving faster than the science and practice of keeping advanced systems safe. The article places the bill within a wider push by states: California enacted a framework for third-party AI verification organizations in September, and Illinois passed a law requiring independent evaluations of major developers. It also notes that the Trump administration has pursued a deregulatory approach, including a 2025 executive order targeting state AI rules and Justice Department task forces that challenge state laws. Snyder acknowledged that states will need more technical expertise to enforce these requirements and called the proposal a strong next step that will need to adapt as the technology changes, though the article says it focuses mainly on catastrophic risks and leaves issues such as youth mental health and government use of AI for later.

Articles.Title: New York’s RAISE Act 2.0 would expand AI oversight, according to safety expert - StateScoop

stories.Headline: PA courts weigh AI verification rules for filers
stories.Summary:
The Advisory Committee on Artificial Intelligence, which advises the Pennsylvania Supreme Court, is weighing a rule that would require lawyers and other court filers who use generative AI to certify they checked the accuracy of their work. The proposal was published last month in the Pennsylvania Bulletin, the state's weekly gazette for proposed rules and government notices. It would apply to citations, quotations, and summaries of legal principles, and filers who fail to comply could face sanctions ranging from a reprimand to fines to dismissal of a case. The committee's stated concern is that generative AI can produce inaccurate, misleading, or fabricated information. The public has until Nov. 24 to comment, after which the committee can revise the proposal or send it as is to the court's seven justices for a vote.

The rule would place the burden of verification on people rather than on the technology. Filers, including those representing themselves, would have to thoroughly review any AI-generated content in court documents before submitting them. They would also have to certify that they completed that review. The Pennsylvania Bar Association has not yet taken a position, according to a spokesperson. In 2024, that group and the Philadelphia Bar Association issued a joint opinion advising lawyers to verify all AI-generated content.

The high court has been working on AI policy since 2024, when it created the advisory committee to monitor AI use in the legal profession. In 2025, the committee recommended an interim policy for judges and court staff, which the justices adopted and which remains in effect. That policy permits AI for legal research, initial drafting, and editing for readability, but it does not cover lawyers or others outside government. The new proposal would extend oversight to all court filers. Pennsylvania is not alone, as courts nationwide have confronted filings containing false or invented citations, sometimes called hallucinations.

Such problems have already appeared in Pennsylvania courts. Spotlight PA reported that filings in at least 13 state cases in 2025 contained confirmed or implied AI hallucinations, including a high-profile gender discrimination case before an appellate court. Elsewhere, a federal judge in Mississippi this summer sanctioned lawyers on both sides of a civil case for filing fake citations, and two of them were barred from appearing in that district's federal court for two years. The Pennsylvania proposal's fate will depend on the public comments and the justices' eventual vote.

Articles.Title: PA courts weigh AI verification rules for filers - Spotlight PA

stories.Headline: SugarAI launches AI tools to sharpen sales actions
stories.Summary:
SugarAI has introduced new artificial intelligence tools for sales teams, aimed at turning customer and enterprise data into specific sales actions. The additions include SugarAdvisors and Smart Prompts, Sugar Cube, AI Analytics and Mobile Smart Notes. The article was published on 5 November 2026 by IT Brief Australia, with news editor Joseph Gabriel Lagonsin reporting. The tools are designed to help sellers spot account risks and revenue opportunities, understand account context, ask business questions in plain language, and capture notes and images from mobile devices. The update centres on linking customer relationship management data with enterprise resource planning information.

The company says the goal is to help sales staff focus on the most relevant signals from accounts and opportunities rather than sift through broad sets of customer data. SugarAI is targeting manufacturing and distribution businesses, where commercial operations are growing more complex. It cited its own research showing that 96% of manufacturers and distributors say limited precision in sales and customer operations contributes to missed growth, slower decisions, customer defection and weaker forecasting. The company also said sellers and account managers now handle an average of 86 accounts each, which increases the need for tools that direct attention to the most important actions.

SugarAdvisors and Smart Prompts alert sellers to issues such as shifts in customer engagement, inventory or reorder patterns, overdue sales activities, and cases where executive support may be needed. Sugar Cube is an embedded assistant that offers recommendations, explains account and opportunity context, and helps staff prepare for sales work. AI Analytics turns plain-language business questions into charts, summaries and tables, reducing reliance on revenue operations teams for custom reports. Mobile Smart Notes lets sellers record images and notes on a phone and link them automatically to the right account, contact or opportunity.

David Roberts, Chief Executive Officer at SugarAI, said the advantage comes from combining data across systems and presenting clear actions to sellers. He said businesses have plenty of data but lack relevant guidance for frontline staff, and that CRM and ERP software have not fully delivered on their promise. The launch sits within the company's "Precision Selling" strategy, which narrows attention from a full customer view to a smaller set of signals that support a recommended next step. SugarAI, headquartered in Denver and backed by Accel-KKR, says its software is used by thousands of companies in more than 120 countries, and it notes the new tools are included in predictable pricing rather than usage-based charges.

Articles.Title: SugarAI launches AI tools to sharpen sales actions - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: South Portland schools may temporarily ban AI
stories.Summary:
South Portland's School Board is set to vote Monday on a proposal to temporarily bar students in pre-kindergarten through 8th grade from using generative artificial intelligence for the rest of the 2026-27 school year. The moratorium would stay in place until the district develops an appropriate policy. Similar temporary bans have been adopted in New York and Los Angeles. If the resolution passes, all staff would need two hours of AI awareness training and three hours of AI literacy training by the end of the school year.

After that, teachers would be limited to tools the district sanctions and would use only on school-issued devices. No teacher would be required to use AI with students. The measure includes no enforcement plan, and some worry students could find ways around it. Board member Claire Holman, who brought the resolution, said the district has to start somewhere.

She sits on an AI committee that began meeting a few years ago but has focused more on sharing information than writing policy. South Portland currently has no official guidelines for AI use in its schools. Holman has argued that because the technology is so new, the district should move cautiously while people work out what to do. Statewide, Maine has no policy or ban on AI in schools.

Its education department supports ethical integration of the technology and offers a toolkit to help districts write their own rules. The governor's office also created a 21-person AI taskforce with an education subgroup, which released recommendations last fall. Several other districts, including Yarmouth, Maine School Administrative District 75 and Gorham, have allowed conditional classroom use under written policies and handbooks. School Board member Daniel Feller has been asking which students, if any, should use AI and whether grade levels and subjects should have different rules, and he thinks parents, teachers and administrators should weigh in too.

Articles.Title: South Portland schools may temporarily ban AI - Portland Press Herald - Maine Sunday Telegram
