stories.Headline: Learning a Prior-Data Fitted Network for Graph Foundation Models via Structural Causal Model Priors
stories.Summary:
A research team led by Ziwei Zhang and nine co-authors has posted a paper on arXiv describing GSCM-PFN, a graph prior-data fitted network for graph foundation models. The article was indexed on doi.org on November 6, 2026, at 06:00 UTC. The authors built on the idea that prior-data fitted networks, which learn from large synthetic datasets, could support prediction across many domains. Their work proposes a model that is pre-trained on synthetic graphs rather than on real-world graph data.

The authors say existing graph foundation models face limits, including small pre-training scale and reliance on aligning with text used by large language models. Existing graph prior-data fitted networks, they add, struggle to model causal relationships among nodes and edges, to generate diverse graph structures, and to design architectures that can learn from complex synthetic data. To address this, the paper introduces a joint feature-edge-label structural causal model that guides synthetic graph generation. It also describes prior-guided node-edge dependency modeling, which the authors use to produce varied graph generation strategies. A third component is a feature-permutation-invariant dual-path graph network, which the authors say comes with theoretical guarantees.

The paper's authors, Ziwei Zhang, Tianyin Liao, Chunyu Hu, Ge Lan, Nuo Xu, Yi Huang, Qingyun Sun, Xingxuan Zhang, Peng Cui and Jianxin Li, report that GSCM-PFN outperformed both conventional graph foundation models and prior-data fitted network-based models across 23 real-world benchmarks. They state that this result was achieved without using real-world graph data for pre-training. The authors also say they prove their structural causal model-based generation prior is more expressive than existing priors. The article includes a link to the code, but the indexed text does not describe any further steps, release plans or independent review.

The company noted that earlier that week it had described how it was scaling Git with Pando, its in-house source control backend for engineers and agents. OpenAI said it wanted to set a standard for modern software development, from the first branch an agent creates to the moment code is deployed. The company also said it wants Codex to link the code a company releases with the decisions its people make. stories.Headline: Why $2.5 Trillion Vanished from Nasdaq 100 After Democrats' 'Blue Tsunami' Spooked AI Investors

Nasdaq 100 companies lost about $2.5 trillion in combined market value on Thursday, 5 November 2026, two days after Democrats won both chambers of Congress. Reuters put the Nasdaq 100 drop at 6.4%, while the broader Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5%. The S&P 500 dropped 4.4% and the Dow lost more than 1,800 points. By Friday morning South Korea's main index fell so fast that its exchange paused trading for 20 minutes.

The sell-off followed a rising worry that new limits could slow the data centres that AI companies depend on. Texas stands at the centre of that concern, because incoming Democratic Governor Gina Hinojosa campaigned on halting new data-centre projects until stronger safeguards exist. Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican, had already ordered a review of grid connections and a pause on permits. Senator Bernie Sanders has proposed a national moratorium on new AI data centres, though that proposal would still need to become law. Projects still waiting on approvals or grid links face the greatest risk of delay or higher costs.

Companies that rent out AI computing were among the hardest hit because they borrow heavily to buy equipment before customers pay. CoreWeave shares fell 10% on Thursday, and the cost of insuring its debt against default hit a record, according to Reuters citing S&P Global Market Intelligence. IREN moved its revenue target from December to January 2027, citing a customer design change and supplier timing, though it said the capacity was already contracted and funded. OpenAI said on 5 November that for future campuses it owns and operates, it would cover the electricity and infrastructure costs those campuses create and provide financial assurances before major spending begins.

The selling spread beyond the United States to Asia's chip supply chain, since Korean memory makers and Taiwanese chipmakers depend on US AI orders. Japan's Nikkei fell more than 6% early Friday, and in Seoul the Korea Exchange's circuit breaker halted trading at 9:03 a.m. local time when the KOSPI fell 8%. After trading resumed at 9:26 a.m., the index was still down 8.6%. stories.Headline: Rank Data Problems, PageSpeed Scores & AI Training Opt-Out – SEO Pulse
stories.Summary:
Two separate stories this week show how hard it is to trust reported numbers in search and AI. Search tracking tools have been producing misleading rankings, with one SE Ranking review of 10,000 Google US desktop keywords published Nov. 3 finding that 84 percent of flagged cases were unrelated listings matching a single word from the query. Separately, DataForSEO and Serper reported that Google limited how many goto links could be resolved from one results page, starting around Oct. 30, while SerpApi logged a related incident opened Nov. 3. Those problems can hide where a page actually ranked, so reports from those tools deserve a closer look before anyone acts on them.

PageSpeed Insights moved to Lighthouse 13.6.0, which changes how it simulates First Contentful Paint and Largest Contentful Paint in lab scores. Barry Pollard of Google said on Bluesky that the new approach should be more accurate and will generally give better results, with JavaScript-heavy sites most affected. The simulation now uses Chrome's render-blocking label for each request and falls back to fetch priority when that label is missing. Scores from before and after the switch come from different simulations, so a rise on an optimized page may come from the update rather than the work. Field data from real users, which appears in the same report, is the better check before claiming improvement.

Google, Microsoft and OpenAI said on Oct. 30 that they plan to honor a shared robots.txt control for AI training preferences, based on an Internet-Draft by Anthropic's Kevin Kelley. The control is a normal robots.txt group under a policy token called __usage_ai-training with Allow and Disallow rules, and none of the three companies supports it yet according to their announced timelines. Google said it would treat a shared opt-out as an opt-out from Google-Extended where that is not set, and its documentation says Google-Extended also covers grounding in Gemini Apps. Microsoft will use the shared control for training, add a separate page-level AI Grounding preference, and stop treating NoArchive and NoCache as training or grounding preferences after March 1, 2027.

Google's John Mueller told David Iwanow in an interview posted Oct. 29 that AI systems "build on SEO" and that technical SEO will stay relevant. He said AI crawlers request pages with different intent, such as training versus fetching recent content, which he called another flavor of technical SEO. ChatGPT product lead Adam Fry told Big Technology that its search-like query volume is about one-fifth of Google's, but no period or market was given for that comparison. Ahrefs referral data across 118,671 sites in October put Google at 24.74 percent of tracked traffic and ChatGPT at 0.36 percent, so the measure behind any size figure should be named.

stories.Headline: Enterprises struggle to link AI spending to business value
stories.Summary:
Enterprises are getting better at tracking what they spend on artificial intelligence, yet many still cannot prove the return on that money. According to a recent survey, only 9 per cent of respondents felt confident showing value from their AI spending, even though they understood their costs. J.R. Storment of the Tokenomics Foundation described a "whiplash" this year, as early enthusiasm gave way to spending caps. Companies could see their total AI bills but struggled to tie that spending to results.

Attribution remains the core problem, because firms often cannot assign AI costs to specific activities or cost centres. Enterprises typically draw AI from four to six separate sources, each reporting data differently. Shawn Alpay of the Linux Foundation is working through the FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification to unify billing data across providers. The effort plans to work with OpenTelemetry during its 1.6 development cycle to link telemetry data with cost data. Storment also warned that simply moving work to cheaper models can break cached tokens and raise uncached costs.

Jerod Johnson of CData Software argued that AI spend is now driven by agent behaviour in production, making it largely a data and architecture problem. In CData's tests of 27 models, only one in 400 runs succeeded without business context, while 12 models achieved 15 out of 15 successful runs with context. Runs without context averaged 29 turns compared with seven with context, and 37 per cent hit a 40-turn cap versus 2 per cent. Johnson urged firms to measure cost per correct answer rather than raw spending.

Separately, ISG, a global AI-focused research and advisory firm, reports that European enterprises face similar pressure, with AI adoption exceeding expectations but financial returns lagging. ISG will hold its AI Impact Summit Paris on November 9 and 10 at the Pullman Paris Tour Eiffel, bringing together leaders from companies including Pfizer, Thales and WPP. The summit will focus on moving AI beyond isolated experiments, with sessions on measuring business value, sovereign AI, and governance. Its organisers say the goal is to help firms capture returns while keeping control of their data and managing risk.

On November 5, 2026, RJ Lee Group, a Monroeville, Pennsylvania scientific and technical firm, and Carahsoft Technology Corp., a Reston, Virginia government IT provider, announced a partnership to bring RJ Lee's quantum-resilient cybersecurity products to public sector buyers. Under the agreement, Carahsoft will act as RJ Lee's Master Government Aggregator, making the products available through Carahsoft's reseller partners and its NASA SEWP V and E&I Cooperative Services contracts. A later version of the same announcement, dated November 6, 2026, was published with the word "update" added to its headline and with one technical detail changed. The earlier version said Quantum Shroud protects data in motion in six independent layers, while the later version drops that count and describes the protection in general terms.

The partnership centers on two products. Greenlight is a passwordless, image-based sign-in tool that does not rely on passwords, one-time codes or push approvals, which the announcement says attackers can steal or replay. It completes authentication on the device, so users can log in even in denied, disconnected, intermittent or low-bandwidth environments, and it integrates with Microsoft Entra ID and CAC/PIV credentials. Quantum Shroud and Quantum Guard use NIST-standardized post-quantum cryptography, specifically FIPS 203 ML-KEM and FIPS 204 ML-DSA, to protect data in motion at enclave boundaries and data on devices, respectively. The release says these tools are meant to help agencies move toward Zero Trust and CNSA 2.0 timelines without modifying existing systems.

Scott Monfredo, Vice President of Government Programs at RJ Lee Group, said the partnership would put the company's security portfolio in front of agencies that need it, and he pointed to federal mandates, including the DoW Zero Trust Strategy and OMB memoranda M-22-09 and M-26-15, that require phishing-resistant authentication and post-quantum cryptography on tight schedules. Rob Pickle, Sales Director overseeing RJ Lee Group at Carahsoft, said the products complement Carahsoft's cybersecurity offerings and will be made more accessible to government agencies through reseller partners and contract vehicles. The release says RJ Lee Group is a small business with four decades of service to government and commercial clients, and that it maintains a NIST SP 800-171-aligned program with CMMC Level 2 posture. stories.Headline: Incoming Democratic majorities put AI giants on notice
stories.Summary:
Following the 2026 midterm elections, Democrats flipped control of both the House and Senate, and incoming leaders have signaled they will end the hands-off approach Republican-led Washington took toward artificial intelligence. Voters across the country chose Democratic candidates who campaigned on AI guardrails and approved dozens of state and local ballot measures limiting the construction of new data centers. Exit polling by SSRS found that 56 percent of voters said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their votes for Congress. The reporting describes this as a clear mandate from the electorate.

At a post-election press conference on Wednesday, Representative Ted Lieu of California, vice chair of the House Democratic Caucus, outlined the plan. He said the new Congress will hold public hearings on AI and pass reasonable guardrails for the industry. Lieu also said that the Trump administration and House Republicans had made a poor political and policy choice last year by allowing the AI industry to operate without restraint. He co-chairs a House Democratic commission on AI formed last year by Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, and he said he and his colleagues will release a document outlining policy priorities for the new Congress. Several Democratic candidates who won in the midterms ran on AI regulation, including Annie Andrews of South Carolina, who backed a two-year moratorium on data centers, and Roy Cooper of North Carolina, who called for data centers to cover the full costs of their energy use.

OpenAI responded less than 48 hours after Election Day by announcing new data center commitments, including covering energy costs and investing in jobs. The company said voluntary commitments are a starting point and called for federal, state, and local policymakers to set clear rules for how the industry builds. The articles note that Democrats are likely to push for policies requiring OpenAI and other AI giants to go further than their voluntary standards. However, Democrats did not win large enough majorities to override a presidential veto. President Donald Trump has strongly opposed AI regulation and supports data centers, but the articles suggest that voters' rejection of Republican policies may push him toward compromise.

stories.Headline: Authorities tighten restrictions on data centres amid AI boom
stories.Summary:
Governments across several countries have tightened restrictions on data centres, citing concerns about electricity demand, water use and environmental harm tied to the AI boom, according to a Reuters report published on November 5, 2026. In the United States, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed an executive order that requires companies building AI data centres to meet environmental and transparency safeguards and to secure local community approval. The order also removes all data centres from the state's Fast Track permit program and bars state offices from signing non-disclosure agreements with developers. Texas Governor Greg Abbott paused approvals of new projects through the state's grid interconnection process, and developers must now disclose more about power demand, water use, tax incentives and ownership.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul imposed a one-year construction moratorium on data centres using 50 megawatts or more of power, making New York the first U.S. state to enact a full moratorium. During that freeze, the state's Department of Environmental Conservation will not issue new discretionary permits while officials develop standards to assess environmental impact. In Maine, Governor Janet Mills vetoed bipartisan legislation that would have enacted an 18-month moratorium on new data centres using more than 20 megawatts. Mills said she supported a moratorium in principle but objected that the bill lacked an exception for a specific project in the Town of Jay. Residents of Monterey Park, California, voted in June 2026 to permanently ban data centres, the first U.S. city to do so at the ballot box.

Outside the United States, Amsterdam imposed a one-year moratorium on new data centre developments in 2019 and in April 2025 barred new facilities or expansions until at least 2030. Ireland's grid operator effectively blocked new connections around Dublin from 2021 until the freeze ended in December 2025, and new connections must now bring their own on-site power generation. Denmark adopted legislation, effective October 2026, that gives new data centres the lowest priority for grid connections, placing households, healthcare, industry, transport and renewable projects ahead of them. Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the government will create an "Office of AI" to set standards, including rules for large data centres on location, power and water use, with legislation due early next year. Portugal's Environment Minister Maria da Graca Carvalho said new rules are coming that would require data centres to run on renewable energy and use cooling systems that do not compete with household and business water supplies, even as the country promotes large projects such as the 1.2-gigawatt Start Campus in Sines.

stories.Headline: Trump official who wants data centers on public lands has tens of millions invested in AI industry
stories.Summary:
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who leads the Trump administration's push for AI infrastructure, has substantial personal investments in the AI industry, according to a November 2026 investigation by ProPublica that was republished by the North Dakota Monitor. The reporting found that Burgum's 2026 financial disclosure shows much of his wealth sits in Arthur Ventures, an investment firm he co-founded, and that between $18.1 million and $64.4 million of those holdings are in AI companies, based on an analysis by the public lands group Save Our Parks. The articles say that in the year before he joined the administration, while he was North Dakota's governor, he realized between $2.1 million and $11 million in capital gains from AI-related investments, and in 2025 he sold AI stocks and equity that produced between $2.5 million and $15.1 million. Under his Senate confirmation ethics agreement, he resigned from positions at Arthur but kept his financial interests there.

The administration has also offered federally managed public lands for data centers, which the articles say could be built on as much as 91.3 million acres, an area comparable to Montana, according to a U.S. Geological Survey report released earlier in the year. Public opposition to data centers has grown, and the articles note that local and state processes have slowed projects in ways federal property may not allow. The Bureau of Land Management is reviewing permit applications for about 15 data centers and 17 associated infrastructure projects across six Western states, and the articles say the rent charged for data centers on public land, described by an Interior spokesperson as an annual fair-market-value rent, may be low enough that the public's economic benefit is unclear until projects are permitted. A federal land law from 1976 that predates data centers is being used to permit them, according to the reporting. The Boulder City, Nevada, project was paused by an Interior appeals board and sent back for further review after the BLM approved a change in plans in June without studying its environmental implications.

The Interior Department says Burgum has met his federal ethics and financial disclosure obligations and that claims his decisions are driven by personal investments are false and unsupported. The department added that his work requires engaging industry leaders and international partners. Ethics experts quoted in the articles said his investments appear to be legal under a criminal statute with a high burden of proof, but Cynthia Brown of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington said non-criminal ethics rules bar officials from acting in ways that create the appearance of a conflict, and Richard Painter, a former Bush administration ethics lawyer, said Burgum should stay away from decisions benefiting an industry in which he is heavily invested. Democratic senators wrote to Burgum in October demanding he stop efforts to use public lands for data centers and disclose his role. The articles also report that Steve Pearce, the BLM director, and Michael Boren, a Forest Service overseer, hold AI investments of their own, and that hundreds of Trump appointees have financial ties to major AI-linked companies, though the articles do not say what action, if any, will follow.

stories.Headline: Democratic victories cloud outlook for AI data center rollout
stories.Summary:
Strong wins for Democratic candidates in the US midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, threaten the prospects for energy-hungry data centers in key states and could slow the AI rollout that has carried Wall Street forward over the past four years. Republicans lost strongholds such as Texas, where both the Senate and the governorship went to Democrats who back greater data center regulation. President Donald Trump, who has supported hands-off regulation for what he calls "super intelligence," suffered a stinging rebuke of his Republican party after a campaign marked by growing concerns about the environmental effects of data centers. The prospect of stricter regulation weighed on stocks in AI heavyweights such as Elon Musk's SpaceX ahead of the US markets open, after drops for key chipmakers in Asia including Samsung in South Korea.

In Texas, Gina Hinojosa, a lawyer who defeated outgoing governor Greg Abbott, called during the campaign for an immediate moratorium on data centers until the legislature can meet to put real protections in place. She has also urged an end to tax exemptions granted to the sector, as has fellow Democrat James Talarico, who was elected on Tuesday as a Texas senator. Abbott had wanted to make the state the "nerve center" of artificial intelligence and data center development, but he noticeably shifted his stance amid a public backlash over energy and water provision. Texas is expected to account for nearly 30 percent of national demand for electricity dedicated to AI operations by 2028, according to calculations by Bloom Energy. Alphabet, the parent of Google, has announced plans to build several data centers in Texas, and Musk has moved the headquarters of Tesla, SpaceX and X to the state.

Musk, who spent hundreds of millions of dollars supporting the Republican camp, joked after the vote that "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," referring to his goal of a satellite computing network. Patrick Munnelly, market strategist at the brokerage Tickmill Group, said Democratic opposition to rapid data-center expansion could focus on power use, environmental constraints, local infrastructure strain, competition policy and the social consequences of AI deployment. He said none of this necessarily breaks the long-term AI theme, but it can raise the hurdle rate for investment. Veteran financial analyst Jim Bianco posted on X that given the size of the Democrats' victory, including the Texas governorship and a 29 to 1 lead to restrict data centers, politicians who want to remain employed are going to heed these messages.

The regulatory impact will be greatest at state level, highlighting the role of governors in responding to voter concerns. In Georgia, another state with a heavy slate of data center projects, the new Democratic governor Keisha Lance Bottoms has advocated a temporary statewide pause on new data centers, alongside requirements intended to ensure that large customers bear the costs of their infrastructure, according to Stephen Innes at SPI Asset Management. Amy Acton, elected Democratic governor of Ohio, is also committing to a tougher regulatory framework on the data center buildout. Data centers require substantial amounts of fresh water to help cool servers, raising fears of localized shortages.

Nooks, an AI sales automation startup, has secured a $500 million commitment from General Catalyst's Customer Value Fund to finance its sales and marketing push and the launch of new products. Nooks is positioning sales as the next profession to be reshaped by AI, following coding, legal work and customer support.

Unlike a traditional investor that buys a stake in a company, General Catalyst's arrangement involves taking a share of the returns its capital helps generate, according to Nooks CEO Dan Lee. Lee declined to disclose the terms of the deal. He said that transforming an industry requires a great deal of capital, and that the company saw this structure as the best way to fund aggressive growth alongside new product launches. Nooks also said it is on track to nearly triple its annual recurring revenue by the end of the year, though it did not reveal its current figure.

The company formally launched its Revenue Agent Platform the same day, covering tasks from first customer contact through to renewal. The company reports more than 2,000 customers, including Cursor, Notion, Replit, Glean and HubSpot, and a net revenue retention rate of 135 per cent. Pranav Singhvi, partner and co-head of the Customer Value Fund at General Catalyst, said the platform has shown a highly predictable revenue engine and strong unit economics, qualities the fund looks for in companies it backs. He described the traction as impressive given how early it is.

The figures and characterizations come from Nooks and General Catalyst, and the articles do not provide independent verification of them. The articles do not say what products Nooks plans to introduce beyond the Revenue Agent Platform, nor do they give a timeline for the expansion. stories.Headline: 3 deliberate moves for businesses to maintain trust in AI decisions
stories.Summary:
Gartner's 2026 CEO and Senior Business Executive Survey found that 76% of leaders expect AI to be the technology most likely to disrupt their industry within three years. The same survey found that 59% of AI pilots never reach production, mostly because of problems inside organizations rather than the technology itself. Incorta, a company that provides a governed data and AI platform, has published guidance on how businesses can keep trust in their AI systems. Its advice centers on three deliberate steps that address why so many pilots stall and why AI outputs can be unreliable. The article appeared on November 6, 2026, and was produced by Incorta and distributed by Stacker.

Gartner notes that AI only pays off when the organization around it changes as well, which means redesigning processes, clarifying who makes which decisions, and aligning incentives. Without those changes, AI simply speeds up and amplifies whatever inputs already exist, whether they are good or bad. The article also says that AI can only give trusted answers when a business can say who has access to its data, how fresh that data is, where it came from, and what agents may do with it. Gartner predicts that through 2026, organizations will drop 60% of AI projects that lack AI-ready data. A separate IBM study from 2025 reportedly found that only 16% of AI programs have scaled across companies.

Incorta's first recommendation is to centralize AI models, tooling, and infrastructure so that spending is controlled and visible, letting a chief financial officer see the full cost in one place. Its second is to govern data so that teams can build what they need without creating security risks. The article cites IBM's 2025 Cost of a Data Breach report, which found that one in five organizations had a breach tied to shadow AI, adding an average of $670,000 to breach costs. Of organizations that suffered an AI-related breach, 97% lacked AI access controls. Incorta's third recommendation is to build systems flexible enough to swap AI models, using adaptable interfaces and portable data so that businesses do not have to rebuild when better models arrive.

The article argues that once these foundations are in place, a business can rely on its AI responses and draw on a competitive edge that others cannot easily copy. Because competitors can access the same public models, the company's own governed data becomes the differentiator, including years of customer conversations, support tickets, contracts, and product and financial records. Incorta says that clear data governance, visible spending, and defined lines of ownership together let businesses trust the AI outcomes they generate. The piece is presented as sponsored content and was reviewed and distributed by Stacker.

stories.Headline: Hong Kong police to enable AI facial recognition on CCTV network this month
stories.Summary:
Hong Kong police will switch on artificial intelligence facial recognition across their expanding smart surveillance network this month, according to the force. The aim is to speed up the tracking of missing persons and suspects, and the data the system generates may be kept for up to 180 days. Police say the technology is widely used by law enforcement agencies worldwide and that residents' privacy rights will be protected. Eric Leung Ming-leung, senior superintendent of the force's operations wing, said the tool would cut the time officers spend reviewing CCTV footage.

Under the SmartView programme, officers can enter a suspect's facial features to see whether that person appeared in particular footage or on certain cameras within a set period. A real-time function can also send alerts when a person entered in the system, such as a missing elderly person, appears on camera. Any search must be approved by an officer at inspector level or above and must serve national security, crime prevention or public safety. Officers must also justify the scope of each search, and the approving officer will check whether it has gone beyond that scope. Footage itself will be kept for no more than 31 days because storage is costly, while the facial recognition data may be held for no more than 180 days.

Leung said police had to comply with the relevant ordinance and that the longer retention period would help with older cases, some of which occurred six months or a year earlier. The force said all cameras under SmartView capture only public areas and that its procedures were based on independent privacy impact assessments and discussions with the Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data. The privacy commissioner, in response to questions, said it would not comment on individual cases but that all data users must comply with the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance whether or not facial recognition is involved. The SmartView project, first rolled out in 2024, plans to install 60,000 cameras across the city by 2028, and it has already helped solve 2,192 criminal cases and lead to 2,831 arrests as of the end of October.

The project is now moving into a second phase that will bring private organisations into the network, beginning with busy locations such as shopping centres and transitional housing. Leung said several shopping centres had responded positively to linking their cameras, and the first batch could be connected as early as the end of this year. Security Secretary Chris Tang Ping-keung earlier said authorities were still weighing whether shopping centres should post extra notices about the link, arguing such notices "may not be necessary" since many malls already display recording notices. Leung said police nonetheless encouraged such notices because they could reassure the public and even benefit business.

stories.Headline: Longbridge Group and Cyberport announce strategic partnership to advance responsible agentic AI innovation in Hong Kong
stories.Summary:
Longbridge Group, an AI-native financial technology company, announced on November 5, 2026 that its AI arm, Longbridge AI Technologies Limited, has signed a three-year strategic partnership with Hong Kong Cyberport Management Company Limited to advance the responsible development and adoption of agentic artificial intelligence in Hong Kong. The partnership will support the establishment of a Hong Kong AI Lab that brings together fintech expertise, research talent and technology innovation. It sets out a framework for collaboration across AI research, industry engagement, talent development and innovation. The AI Lab is meant to gather financial institutions, technology companies, academic institutions and start-ups to explore practical uses of AI. Longbridge says closer ties between the fintech and research communities should foster growth and mutual trust in AI-enabled financial solutions.

Under the arrangement, Longbridge AI will contribute its fintech expertise, AI capabilities and industry experience, while Cyberport will connect the partners to its technology and innovation ecosystem. The organisations plan to explore work in four areas: responsible AI research and innovation, the Hong Kong AI Lab as a platform for research and experimentation, industry engagement through roundtables, seminars and publications, and talent development through hackathons, workshops and mentorship programmes. The partnership also aims to turn research into proof-of-concept initiatives. The partners describe these steps as a way to support Hong Kong's development as an international financial centre and AI innovation hub.

The companies have not stated in these articles a budget or any figures beyond the three-year term. Nowa Zhu, Co-founder and CEO of Longbridge, said that agentic AI could change how people interact with financial information but that realising this requires trust, accountability and close collaboration across the financial ecosystem. Ir Eric Chan, Chief Public Mission Officer of Cyberport, said that agentic AI offers significant potential for financial services and that the AI Lab should help test, validate and deploy solutions in the real world. Zhu added that Longbridge sees Hong Kong as an important market for shaping how AI is adopted responsibly.

Longbridge describes itself as a group that operates licensed financial businesses across several jurisdictions and holds 22 financial regulatory licences or qualifications, and it was founded in 2019. The announcement comes as AI systems move beyond providing insights toward supporting complex financial decisions, which raises questions about transparency and accountability, according to the release. The articles do not describe any specific next steps or timelines beyond the planned establishment of the AI Lab and the partnership's stated areas of work. A separate CIO commentary in the same period, not tied to the partnership, notes that autonomous agents require governance built in from the outset and that human oversight matters most in high-stakes areas such as financial transactions and regulatory compliance.

SpaceX, which went public in June and now calls its AI business Super Intelligence, reported third-quarter revenue up 161% year over year to $14.6 billion. Tesla is presented as an AI company that uses the technology for its self-driving vehicles, robotaxi plans and Optimus humanoid robots, rather than selling compute capacity. stories.Headline: Scaling Up Metasurfaces: Accuracy, Computational Cost, and Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Researchers from Hanyang University and Korea University Sejong Campus published a review article examining how to design large metasurfaces without excessive computing costs. The paper, titled "Scaling Metasurface Design: From Reusable Unit Cells to Full-Metasurface Inverse Design," was made available online on October 25, 2026, and appears in Volume 5, Issue 10 of the journal Opto-Electronic Science. Metasurfaces are thin optical layers of subwavelength structures that control the phase, amplitude, and polarization of light. The authors, Prof. Haejun Chung and Prof. Sunae So, reviewed strategies for scaling these devices to large apertures. The review was based on the research teams' analysis of existing methods rather than a new experiment.

The review organizes design approaches by how much of the device is treated jointly during calculation. Unit-cell methods reuse a library of meta-atom responses computed under periodic boundary conditions, which avoids repeated full-wave optimization of the whole device. Supercell methods treat several interacting elements as one composite unit, while full-metasurface inverse design treats the entire aperture as a coupled system. The authors note that the full-aperture approach improves physical accuracy but demands far more computing resources. Neural-network methods are examined across all these scales as surrogates, candidate generators, and learned components within solvers.

The authors cite a hardware-aware FDTD analysis that estimates a one-centimeter square aperture would require approximately 3.1 petabytes of resident memory under the stated assumptions. They also report that, in an ideal axisymmetric metalens, the reuse ratio of reduced radial phase patterns falls from 71.4% to 3.0% as segment width grows from one to six wavelengths. The paper does not claim these figures describe electromagnetic equivalence, optical performance, or computational savings. The authors stress that the choice of design method depends on required accuracy, interaction range, reuse potential, and available computing resources. They also recommend full-wave verification of final structures and assessment of experimental results under the relevant fabrication and operating conditions.

The article identifies several directions for further work, including coupling-aware local models, adaptive overlapping domains, and distributed full-wave solvers with lower memory requirements. It also suggests that neural operators could assist repeated field calculations, provided their predictions are validated against reference simulations. The authors call for consistent reporting of simulation dimensionality, numerical accuracy, memory, runtime, fabrication constraints, and experimental performance so that methods can be compared under defined conditions. The funding statement lists support from the National Research Foundation of Korea, the Ministry of Education, and other Korean agencies, and the authors declare no competing financial interests.

stories.Headline: Kansas Board of Education set to vote on artificial intelligence policy, discuss elementary recess policies
stories.Summary:
The Kansas State Board of Education is preparing to vote on a new policy covering artificial intelligence and student technology use, according to a report from KSNT. The board will meet Monday and Tuesday, November 9 and 10, 2026, in its November session. The vote concerns instructional technology policy for school districts and nonpublic accredited schools across the state. The board will also take up guidance on elementary recess during that same meeting.

The draft policy, which Kansas Education Commissioner Jake Steel will present, covers several areas of student technology use. Among the topics listed are the purpose and intended use of technology in elementary and secondary settings, student technology access, digital citizenship and student well-being, and artificial intelligence. It also addresses privacy and security, along with expectations for technology use and the consequences of violations. Board members will receive and discuss the recess guidance, but the recess policy itself is expected to come up for a vote at the December meeting.

The announcement came from the Kansas State Department of Education, which issued a press release about the meeting. Commissioner Steel is responsible for presenting the draft to the board. The report does not include any direct statements from the commissioner or board members about their positions on the proposals. It also notes that the board's decision on the technology policy will follow the discussion scheduled for the coming meeting.

The schedule suggests the state is moving on two fronts at once, with technology rules voted on in November and recess rules expected to follow in December. The articles do not say what the board will do if it fails to approve either measure at these sessions. They also do not indicate how the policies would take effect in local classrooms once adopted. Readers who want to follow the outcome can watch for the board's decisions after the November meeting and the December recess vote.

stories.Headline: iQIYI Revives 90-Year-Old Lost Film with NadouPro, Shortlisted for the AI Unit at the Golden Rooster Awards
stories.Summary:
Chinese streaming platform iQIYI has used its NadouPro AI platform to recreate "Visiting Shanghai after Sixty Years," a short film from 1938 that has been lost for nearly 90 years. Because no physical prints, reels or scripts survived, an eight-person team built the film from scratch in just two months at the iQIYI-XMU Joint Laboratory of Film Restoration. The team relied only on production still photos, posters and newspaper clippings as guides. The project has been shortlisted for the "2026 Future Images AI Unit" at the 39th Golden Rooster Awards, one of China's most prestigious film honors.

The film, one of China's earliest science-fiction works, used comedy to imagine life sixty years into the future. Recreating it required solving two difficult problems in generative video: keeping characters looking the same from shot to shot and controlling the camera precisely. NadouPro addressed the first by locking in permanent digital assets for each character's face, proportions and costumes before shooting. The team used the platform's 3D Director Studio to control positioning, composition and movement. The 1938 sequences follow the look of early black-and-white cinema, while the 1998 scenes use a documentary style with natural light and handheld camera work.

Enji YANG, the film's director, said NadouPro helped the team move from random image generation toward shots with clear directorial intent. He said the team still followed traditional methods, including script analysis, character design and storyboarding, before deciding how AI would realize the audiovisual design. Aigong ZHANG, the film's chief planner and director of the joint laboratory, said the project shows how AI can fit into a professional filmmaking workflow. Zidong JIANG, iQIYI's director of AI restoration technology, said the platform let the team move beyond the conventional restoration mindset and reconstruct the film creatively from historical materials.

The project builds on iQIYI's AI restoration work, which began in 2017 and includes its proprietary ZoomAI tools for scratch repair, super-resolution, noise reduction and frame interpolation. Through its joint lab with Xiamen University, the company has already returned several 4K classics to screens. The article presents the reconstruction as an extension of that work into recreating lost films rather than only repairing surviving ones. No further release dates or screening plans for the restored film are given in the article.

stories.Headline: Amazon’s AI Spending is Pressuring Free Cash Flow. Is the Stock Still a Buy?
stories.Summary:
In early November 2026, The Motley Fool published an analysis by Adria Cimino asking whether Amazon's stock remains a buy despite heavy spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure. The piece was carried on Yahoo Finance on November 7, 2026, and on Fool.com the same day. It notes that Amazon Web Services is the world's largest cloud provider and that the company's core retail business and its AI businesses are both pushing revenue to record levels. In the third quarter, AWS reached an annual revenue run rate of $184 billion, with quarterly revenue up 39% to $46 billion, the fastest growth in almost five years.

The article explains that Amazon must make large investments to meet current demand and prepare for future demand. The company forecasts $220 billion in capital spending for the full year, which has put pressure on free cash flow. In the third quarter, Amazon reported negative free cash flow of more than $42 billion over the trailing twelve months, driven by purchases of property and equipment. The company also lifted its capex forecast by $20 billion during the second quarter, while keeping the full-year forecast unchanged in the third quarter. Amazon's chief executive, Andy Jassy, said on the second-quarter earnings call that the free cash flow headwinds would continue until the new data centers are running, and that spending occurs about two years before monetization begins.

The author argues that the spending is necessary if Amazon wants to keep its lead in AI, and points to AWS growth as evidence the investment has paid off. The article describes Amazon's e-commerce moat, including its fulfillment network and Prime subscription, and says AWS now makes up more than 60% of total operating income. It also cites Amazon Bedrock as the company's fastest-growing multi-billion-dollar service and says the stock trades at 23 times forward earnings estimates. Based on these points, the author concludes that Amazon is a stock to buy and hold for the long term. The article is an opinion piece, and the page also carries a note that the author holds a position in Amazon.

stories.Headline: XCMG Highlights International Innovation at "AI + Construction Machinery" Competition
stories.Summary:
The 15th China Innovation and Entrepreneurship Competition, "AI + Construction Machinery" Division, co-organized by XCMG, concluded in Xuzhou on October 30, 2026. The competition drew participants from more than 20 countries and regions, with international companies and universities among the winners. Its projects focused on smarter and more sustainable construction machinery and operations. The event was hosted by the Torch High Technology Industry Development Center of the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology along with other government and industry organizations. More than 2,750 teams registered, and the competition received over 1,600 project submissions.

After preliminary and semifinal rounds, 106 projects advanced to the finals, and international teams earned awards in both the Customer Co-Creation and Professional Contest tracks. Austria's VA Erzberg GmbH won first prize in the Customer Co-Creation track for an electric mining truck project. Fortescue Trading Shanghai took second prize in the same track for work optimizing the full lifecycle of zero-emission mining equipment. Urgench State University in Uzbekistan earned third prize for SmartFleet UZ, an AI platform meant to predict equipment failures for UzXCMG machinery. Indonesia's Manado State Polytechnic won third prize for TerraSight AI, a system that automatically monitors earthwork progress and volumes.

Germany's RWTH Aachen University received an Excellence Award for a solution that adapts autonomous mining trucks to multiple operating scenarios. XCMG Group and XCMG Machinery chairman Yang Dongsheng said the competition is meant to turn real industry needs into innovation challenges and bring partners together to solve technical problems in construction machinery. He named embodied intelligence as a key area for development and said XCMG would use its innovation platforms, testing resources and industry funds to bring AI innovations to worksites and serve customers worldwide. At the closing event, agreements were signed covering six projects selected through the Open Challenge track and four commercialization projects. XCMG said it will continue connecting competition teams with funding sources, industry and research partners, talent and suppliers to help bring these innovations to market.

Responsibility for the plans therefore rests with Anthropic's leadership and the advisers handling the listing, though the articles do not name them. stories.Headline: Revolut turns to self-hosted AI to cut coding costs tenfold over Claude
stories.Summary:
Revolut, the British fintech firm, says it has cut the cost of running AI coding tools by about 90 percent by moving from commercial services such as Anthropic's Claude to self-hosted AI models. The company said the change also improved coding time by 60 percent and reduced software delivery lead times by 70 percent across its rollout to about 2,000 engineers. Its operations and infrastructure lead, David Abitbol, explained the switch at the AI Engineer conference in New York last month. He said Revolut had made self-hosted models its primary option in under a year.

Revolut first tested Google's Gemini in early 2025 and then adopted Claude Code in early 2026. The company grew concerned about the expense, since some engineers were spending between $1,000 and $10,000 a month. Abitbol said Revolut first introduced strict spending limits, but these restricted how many tokens engineers could use. The company then moved to self-hosted alternatives, starting with GLM-5.1 and later switching to GLM-5.3, developed by the Chinese AI company Z.ai. Revolut said hosting GLM-5.1 cost about $0.30 per million input and output tokens, roughly a tenth of the cost of Claude Code or OpenAI's Codex.

Running the models at scale required substantial computing resources. Revolut deployed 56 Nvidia B200 graphics processing units to support GLM-5.3, but Abitbol said adding hardware was not the main source of the gains. Instead, the company tuned model settings, introduced NVFP4 quantisation, separated the stages that process prompts from those that generate responses, and adjusted context lengths. After these changes, Revolut reported a time to first token of under three seconds at context windows of about 256,000 tokens, with generation speeds of roughly 200 tokens per second. Abitbol said response times were particularly important for keeping engineers satisfied with the tools.

Revolut has not abandoned commercial AI services entirely, because GLM is text-only and less suited to visual interfaces. The company introduced a model router that sends each request to the most suitable system, using GLM for code generation and directing vision queries to models such as Google's Gemini or OpenAI's GPT. Revolut believes this approach offers a more cost-effective way to use AI without losing access to specialised capabilities. Abitbol summed up the company's position by saying that open source is now a priority at Revolut and that its economics are favourable.

stories.Headline: Intern Lumina U2: A Multi-Codebook Diffusion Large Language Model for Omni-Visual Understanding and Image Generation
stories.Summary:
Researchers including Qian Yu and 42 other authors have published a paper introducing Intern Lumina U2, a diffusion language model that the authors say is the first to represent multi-codebook visual tokens in a fully discrete space. The article's date is November 6, 2026, and it appeared on doi.org and arXiv, where the paper is listed under the identifier 2610.20818. The model is described as a unified system that handles text and visual content together within a single backbone. The authors say it supports image, video, and 3D inputs and reaches leading performance among unified models in visual understanding, image generation, and image editing.

The design works by representing each visual position as a group of codes drawn from complementary codebooks, which the authors say raises the representational capacity of visual content while keeping it compatible with discrete text modeling. At the input, the embeddings for each position are concatenated, and at the output a lightweight multi-codebook autoregressive head predicts the codes within each position in sequence. The diffusion backbone processes all positions in parallel. The authors also describe a stability-aware sampling strategy that pairs a confidence-plateau-guided unmasking approach with drift-triggered cache refreshing, which they say speeds up image generation by 4.45 times.

The paper lists Qian Yu first among its many authors, with Bin Fu and Yihao Liu also named, and the work was built on a unified four-dimensional representation called AToken. The authors state that they built a full training, inference, and evaluation system running on both Ascend and NVIDIA platforms to test whether the model works across both hardware families. The abstract frames the work as an answer to a central question about how to model high-capacity visual representations alongside text in a shared optimization space. Based on the abstract alone, the article does not describe any reaction from outside researchers or any planned release, so the reported claims rest on the authors' own evaluations.

stories.Headline: Tesla unveils AI accelerator roadmap, adopts new 'SI' branding in 'Super Intelligence' push — SI6 to bring 80X more compute performance, Dojo 3 headed to space
stories.Summary:
Tesla has unveiled a revised AI accelerator roadmap, along with a new naming scheme that replaces "artificial intelligence" with "super intelligence" in the chip labels. The disclosure, reported by Tom's Hardware and published on November 6, 2026, lays out the company's next chips and its plans for a new training accelerator. According to the article, Tesla now labels its chips SI4, SI5 and SI6 rather than AI4, AI5 and AI6, and the same branding is being applied to older parts. The article notes that Elon Musk had also confirmed SpaceXAI would be renamed SpaceXSI.

The roadmap projects that the 6th Generation inference accelerator, SI6, will deliver roughly 80 times the compute performance of the existing 4th Generation chip, SI4. The article's table lists estimated compute of 17,280 to 46,080 TOPS for SI6 and 72 TOPS for SI4, with SI6 built on TSMC 3nm or Samsung 2nm-class processes and using a multi-chiplet design with GDDR7 memory. The third-generation Dojo training accelerator, D3, is described as a chiplet-based design combining 2.5D and 3D packaging with stacked HBM, a clear departure from the wafer-scale, SRAM-centric Dojo D1. Tesla has not yet disclosed D3's compute performance, memory capacity, manufacturing process or development schedule, though it says D3 will be optimized for space, training and scaling.

The article attributes the roadmap to Tesla, which presented it in a recent company briefing, and cites Elon Musk as the figure behind the new naming. It reports that Musk canceled the wafer-level Dojo project in August 2025 and said in August 2026 that SpaceX and xAI would use Nvidia hardware exclusively in their terrestrial and extraterrestrial data centers. The article also points to a social media post noting that the renaming appears to echo a push by President Trump to replace "artificial intelligence" with "super intelligence." The article does not say how the new naming will affect Tesla's product timelines or whether Tesla will pursue wafer-scale integration for D3, and it treats that question as unresolved.

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Models Show Moderate Accuracy in Detecting Trigeminal Neuralgia Phenotypes
stories.Summary:
Researchers from The Fifth Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University published a systematic review and meta-analysis in Frontiers in Radiology finding that magnetic resonance imaging artificial intelligence models show moderate accuracy in identifying pain-related nerve phenotypes in patients with non-secondary trigeminal neuralgia. The team pooled eight eligible studies comprising 628 nerve-level observations. Using a bivariate random-effects model, they found a pooled sensitivity of 0.83, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.78 to 0.87, and a pooled specificity of 0.81, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.74 to 0.86. The summary area under the curve was 0.86, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.82 to 0.88. The authors describe these tools as potential adjunctive diagnostic instruments rather than replacements for clinical judgment.

Trigeminal neuralgia causes recurrent, brief, shock-like facial pain that is often triggered by light touch, eating, or speaking, and it can severely disrupt sleep and daily life. The authors used the term non-secondary trigeminal neuralgia to cover classical and idiopathic forms once structural causes such as tumors or multiple sclerosis plaques have been excluded. Distinguishing these forms matters because it shapes decisions about procedures such as microvascular decompression. Standard visual review of scans is limited, since vessel contact against the nerve also appears in people without symptoms. The review notes that the diagnostic criteria for classical disease require definite morphological changes, not contact alone.

Quantitative radiomic and machine-learning methods aim to detect subtle differences that the eye cannot reliably see. The reviewers searched the literature following the PRISMA 2020 statement and its diagnostic accuracy extension, and registered their protocol in PROSPERO under identifier CRD420261394456. The initial searches produced 164 citations, which became 103 unique publications after removing 61 duplicates. After screening, 38 full-text reports were assessed, and eight studies met all eligibility criteria. Six studies used 3.0-Tesla scanners, one used a 1.5-Tesla system, and one used both field strengths.

Model types ranged from logistic regression and support vector machines to neural networks and ensemble classifiers. The review found mild heterogeneity, with inconsistency values of 20.77 percent for sensitivity and 27.65 percent for specificity. Risk-of-bias assessments flagged concerns including small samples, limited external validation, and possible data leakage during feature selection. The authors caution that the evidence rests on only eight mostly single-center, retrospective studies without independent multicenter testing.

They also note that the analysis combined contralateral-nerve designs with healthy-control comparisons, two tasks they describe as biologically different. Exploratory subgroup analyses showed that radiomics-only models achieved a pooled sensitivity of 0.84 and specificity of 0.84, while models combining radiomics with morphological variables reached 0.86 and 0.78. Excluding one influential study shifted the pooled sensitivity to 0.82 and specificity to 0.78. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Models Show Moderate Accuracy in Detecting Trigeminal Neuralgia Phenotypes

stories.Headline: Global Study Maps Mounting Energy Water Material and Land Demands of Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
A systematic review of forty-six environmental studies has mapped the energy, water, material and land demands of artificial intelligence, finding that the physical infrastructure behind machine learning draws heavily on electricity, water, minerals and land. The work was carried out by researcher Sibongiseni Hlabisa and published in the journal Carbon Neutral Systems. The authors searched Web of Science, Scopus and Google Scholar for studies published from 2015 to 2025, starting from about 3,130,000 records and narrowing them through successive screenings until forty-six sources met all inclusion criteria. The corpus combined twenty-two peer-reviewed articles and proceedings, seventeen technical and government reports, four preprints and three reference volumes.

The review's central finding is that artificial intelligence cannot be judged through carbon figures or narrow efficiency measures alone, because its footprint grows as computing workloads expand. Training a single large model such as PaLM-2 or GPT-3 is reported to consume between 1.3 and 1.5 gigawatt-hours of electricity. The International Energy Agency projects that data center electricity demand will rise from 415 terawatt-hours in 2024 to 945 terawatt-hours by 2030 under its base case, approaching 1,200 terawatt-hours by 2035, with the United States accounting for nearly half of global growth. Water is needed both to cool servers and to make chips, with evaporative cooling using roughly 7,000 to 12,000 liters per megawatt-hour and each silicon wafer requiring 1.8 to 2.5 cubic meters. Hyperscale data centers typically occupy 30 to 100 hectares, and the review notes that some regulators, including authorities in Ireland and Singapore, have already moved to limit or condition new facilities.

The authors argue that policymakers should move beyond voluntary corporate efficiency metrics toward binding regional limits on cumulative electricity, water withdrawal and land conversion tied to local ecological capacity. They point to practical measures such as capturing waste heat for district heating, recycling ultrapure water in chip plants, recovering metals from retired hardware, and shifting non-urgent computing to times and places with surplus wind or solar power. The review also warns that the benefits of computing are concentrated in the Global North while extraction and e-waste burdens fall on the Global South, and it acknowledges significant empirical gaps in the underlying evidence. The articles supplied do not say how these recommendations will be taken up by governments or industry, so the outcome remains open.

Articles.Title: Global Study Maps Mounting Energy Water Material and Land Demands of Artificial Intelligence

stories.Headline: AI For People And Not For Profit – OpEd
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion piece rather than a news report, and it draws on a specific event: a 2026 pilot run by the Utah Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy with the AI health-tech company Doctronic. The pilot began in January 2026 and used an automated AI system to process renewals of refill or repeat medications for 190 chronic conditions, based on earlier prescriptions written by licensed physicians. The state office said the system would work within strict parameters and under physician oversight, and it was meant to ease the workload of doctors and widen patients' access to care. Within three months, in April 2026, the Utah Medical Licensing Board called for the immediate suspension of the pilot, which ended the first legally AI-led system to renew prescriptions for chronic non-controlled medications.

The board said the pilot compromised patient safety and put patients at risk. It also said that AI or other financial motives should not be allowed to override the duty to protect patients, and that this was what had happened in this case. The author, Bhabani Shankar Nayak, a professor of business management at London Metropolitan University, uses the episode to argue that AI companies are pressing governments worldwide to deploy AI in healthcare for profit. He argues that medical professionals and researchers are calling instead for a "human loop" covering every stage of an AI system's life, from problem formulation and data collection through model development, validation, and final decisions on how the tools are used. He also contends that the same principle applies in every sector, since people's welfare should not be sacrificed for productivity or profit.

The author's broader claim is that AI and its language models carry demographic, racial, gender, social, cultural, and class biases from the way problems are framed, data is collected, and models are built and tested. In his view, these biases can produce wrong diagnoses and wrong prescriptions, and uncritical commercial adoption threatens both human welfare and the scientific development of AI. He calls for transparent governance with sustained human oversight and accountability, so that people control the technology rather than being controlled by it. The article does not report any official response beyond the licensing board's statement, and it does not describe any further steps planned for the Utah pilot or for similar programs elsewhere.

Articles.Title: AI For People And Not For Profit – OpEd

stories.Headline: Study Evaluates Artificial Intelligence Integration in Sustainable Apparel Design and Production
stories.Summary:
A study published in the Journal of Industrial Ecology by Liu and Tang in 2026 evaluated how artificial intelligence can be used in sustainable apparel design and production. The authors reviewed AI tools used for concept generation, sewing-pattern engineering, virtual prototyping, production planning, consumer evaluation, and circular information systems. They organized the review by lifecycle stage, sustainability problem, and how well each tool had been validated. The findings were reported on November 6, 2026, by Scienmag and bioengineer.org.

The research drew on four separate sets of data covering design, specialist appraisal, consumer response, and production metrics. These included 4,200 garment-design records and assessments of 350 designs by 28 specialists. A consumer experiment tracked 858 participants who completed the study out of 864 recruited, and 426 enterprise pattern records with measured cutting-waste rates were also analyzed. In the consumer experiment, participants appeared to show higher purchase intention for co-created and labeled products, but lower intention at the higher price premium. The authors noted that the precision of one statistical reconstruction was limited by rounding in the reported inputs.

The clearest direct evidence of material savings came from manufacturing pattern engineering. Using ridge regression across the observed enterprise, quarter, and product mix, the model achieved a test root mean square error of 0.049 and a mean absolute error of 0.038, compared with a baseline root mean square error of 0.096 when predicting cutting-waste rates. To organize the results, the authors proposed an integration framework built on three pillars: data and technical integration, circular design performance, and validation and governance. It also uses four evaluation dimensions: digital plausibility, design feasibility, market viability, and verified sustainability performance. The authors themselves stated that direct sustainability verification remains limited to production-stage cutting waste and that broader lifecycle outcomes would need separate validation.

Articles.Title: Study Evaluates Artificial Intelligence Integration in Sustainable Apparel Design and Production

stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence faces rejection in American museums; visitors cling to art and human creativity
stories.Summary:
Washington, DC, has become a focal point for a growing backlash, as several American museums have faced a wave of rejection for exhibitions built on artificial intelligence. Visitors have voiced clear reservations about displaying works that rely on digital technology instead of human creativity. The reporting describes the response as a widening debate over the limits of technology in art and culture. Questions have arisen about whether algorithm-made works hold real artistic value and whether they can express human experience, emotion, and ideas. These concerns come as AI tools spread quickly and can produce images that mimic the styles of well-known artists.

Many museum visitors argue that art is not defined only by its final form but also by the creative process and the personal effort behind it. They stress that human experience matters, and they question whether works made almost entirely by AI are authentic enough for major cultural institutions. Supporters of the technology see these experiments differently, describing them as a natural extension of artistic evolution that can open new horizons and offer fresh ways to present ideas. The debate reaches beyond museums to artists, critics, and cultural bodies. It also touches on intellectual property rights, the sources of images and data used to train these systems, and who bears responsibility for works produced with algorithmic help.

Museums now face the challenge of balancing technological progress with maintaining public trust. According to the reporting, they must clarify the tools used in producing exhibited works and how much a human artist was involved. Some creators also worry that the rapid output of modern software, which can produce large volumes of work quickly and cheaply, may shrink opportunities for traditional artists. The article notes that the American museum debate shows technological development does not automatically earn public acceptance. It suggests the relationship between art and AI still needs clear guidelines that protect creators' rights and preserve the authenticity of the artistic experience without stifling innovation.

Articles.Title: Artificial intelligence faces rejection in American museums; visitors cling to art and human creativity

stories.Headline: Copyright Suits Over AI Training Continue With Latest Surge Against Meta
stories.Summary:
Meta is facing a new wave of lawsuits accusing the company of using copyrighted works to train its artificial intelligence models without the authors' permission. The suits are the latest in a series of cases testing how intellectual property law applies to AI. Reporter Brendan Pierson wrote about the filings in a Law.com article published on November 6, 2026. The article's framing is that the litigation continues to build against the company. One of the plaintiffs' lawyers, Kyle Roche of Freedman Normand Friedland, explained his firm's approach.

He said the firm chose to sue on behalf of individual authors rather than bringing a class action. According to him, a class action can be difficult because it may be hard to prove that all members of the class were affected by the AI companies' conduct in the same way. The article attributes this reasoning to Roche and does not describe any ruling on the merits. The article does not give the number of new lawsuits, the courts where they were filed, or the specific works involved. It also does not say how Meta has responded to the allegations.

Much of the text on the page is subscription material and site navigation, so the available detail is limited. Related Law.com coverage on the same site includes a November 5, 2026 piece reporting that only 31% of in-house legal professionals surveyed in a Pinsent Masons report said junior colleagues were driving AI adoption. A separate November 4, 2026 article reported that at least two AI-native law firms had bid for Weil Gotshal & Manges' data. Neither piece addresses the Meta lawsuits directly.

Articles.Title: Copyright Suits Over AI Training Continue With Latest Surge Against Meta

stories.Headline: Sysco Counts on AI Routing and Bidding for $500 Million in Savings
stories.Summary:
Sysco, the largest food service distributor in the United States, is using artificial intelligence to cut what it costs to move and buy goods, according to a November 6, 2026 report from PYMNTS. The company runs 333 distribution centers in 10 countries that serve about 670,000 customer locations. Its U.S. trucks drive more than 4.5 million miles a week. Sysco's routing software is live in pilot regions and has raised the number of cases delivered per mile by 2% to 4%.

Sysco introduced a $500 million AI efficiency program in a September 9 press release. The program has four workstreams covering supply chain productivity, automation across merchandising and procurement, indirect spend management, and customer experience with back-office simplification. The company expects $100 million in net cost savings this fiscal year and at least $500 million by the close of fiscal 2029. Sysco plans to roll the routing software out to every U.S. broadline operating location this fiscal year, with a second phase starting at the end of the year. Each 1% gain in cases per mile is worth about $3 million across the company.

Sysco CEO and Chair of the Board Kevin Hourican discussed the routing results and the program on the fiscal first-quarter 2027 earnings call on November 3. He said the company's first AI-run supplier bid finished about 30% above its savings target, with a person supervising. Sysco Chief Financial Officer Brandon Sewell said the reverse-auction tools cover more than $1 billion of annual indirect spend. Hourican also said that AI360, the company's in-house sales tool, helped raise Sysco brand mix in local accounts by 44 basis points, and that sales consultants still make the final decisions.

The article places Sysco within a wider trend. A PYMNTS Intelligence report from July found that wholesale enterprises use AI for 35 of 75 tracked business tasks, compared with 20 in retail and 22 in construction. The same research found that 85% of wholesale executives said future AI spending will prioritize margins and profitability. Sysco rival US Foods reported a 2% gain in cases delivered per mile from its own routing software, according to a PYMNTS report from October 28.

Articles.Title: Sysco Counts on AI Routing and Bidding for $500 Million in Savings

stories.Headline: AI Effects on Fees Requires Transparency With Clients, Attorneys at Harvey Event Say
stories.Summary:
Law firm attorneys and in-house counsel say that legal artificial intelligence is already shaping how legal work is priced. The discussion took place at a Harvey event, where speakers said the effects are still unsettled but agreed that frank conversations with clients are the right place to begin. The article was published by Law.com on November 6, 2026, and reported by Madeline King. Much of the available text is behind a paywall, so the full set of specifics the speakers offered cannot be confirmed from this material.

The article indicates that exactly how AI will affect fees has not been settled. Participants agreed on the need for honesty with clients about what AI is doing to the work and the bill. The reporting leaves open which fee structures are changing and by how much. No figures, dates beyond the publication date, or formal requirements appear in the portion available.

The lack of detail in the accessible text means any rule or practice change described by the speakers cannot be stated with confidence here. Desirée Moore of Venable is quoted as saying that some clients hold more extreme views about what they expect AI to do, and that she respects those views. The article attributes the broader call for transparency to the attorneys and in-house counsel who spoke at the event. Beyond Moore's remark, the accessible text does not detail the other speakers' positions or name additional responsible parties.

Readers seeking those statements will need the full article. The article sits within a wider conversation about how legal technology is changing the business of law, and related Law.com coverage describes firms building AI tools into client work. The accessible text does not describe any next steps, scheduled follow-ups, or pending decisions. The available material therefore ends with the speakers' shared view that transparency should come first.

Articles.Title: AI Effects on Fees Requires Transparency With Clients, Attorneys at Harvey Event Say

stories.Headline: Legaltech Rundown: Harvey Launches Litigation Tool, Agiloft Debuts New AI Agents, and More
stories.Summary:
Law.com's weekly Legaltech Rundown reported on the past week's legal technology news, including Harvey's launch of a litigation tool and Agiloft's debut of new AI agents. The article itself is a roundup, so the specific details of those launches are not included in the text provided to me. stories.Headline: Review Finds Artificial Intelligence Depression Detection Performance Drops In Large Studies
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence models built to detect depression perform far worse in large populations than in small benchmark tests, according to a narrative review published in Discover Mental Health. Small case-control studies with 30 to 200 participants often report accuracies between 93 and 100 percent under internal validation. In studies covering several hundred to nearly 15,000 people, language, speech, and clinical-record models reached only about 0.69 to 0.78, and neuroimaging models reached 54 to 61 percent. The review, by Younas and colleagues, covered text, speech, facial behavior, electroencephalography, and multimodal approaches. It drew on papers published from January 2015 through August 2026.

The authors found that many studies share methodological weaknesses. Most models are trained against self-report scales such as the PHQ-8 rather than diagnostic interviews. External validation on independent datasets is rare, and widely used public benchmarks show demographic and interviewer-prompt biases. No study so far has shown that using AI detection improves patient outcomes. Each technology also carries its own limits, with large language models performing inconsistently depending on the prompt, and electroencephalography results failing to hold up at scale.

The authors conclude that AI currently has plausible value for scalable pre-screening, continuous monitoring, and triage, but not as an autonomous diagnostic replacement. They say genuine clinical readiness will require larger, demographically diverse datasets, interview-based reference standards, rigorous external and prospective validation, and transparent reporting. They also call for fairness auditing and privacy-preserving designs under clinician supervision. The review's authors are listed as Younas, Paripati, Niharika, Panda, Mwita, Alghzawi, Sahu, Modi, and Aminpoor. The review was reported on November 6, 2026, and the article does not describe any follow-up steps beyond the recommendations the authors set out.

Articles.Title: Review Finds Artificial Intelligence Depression Detection Performance Drops In Large Studies

stories.Headline: Review Separates Artificial Intelligence From Robotic Execution In Total Knee Arthroplasty
stories.Summary:
Researchers published a narrative review and evidence map in the journal Arthroplasty, concluding that direct clinical evidence showing artificial intelligence gives patients benefit beyond conventional robotic assistance in total knee replacement remains limited. The team searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, along with citation searches, for peer-reviewed English-language studies published between January 2015 and January 2025, with the final search run on April 15, 2026. The authors note that robotic systems and artificial intelligence are often lumped together under the label AI-assisted robotic surgery, even though they serve different roles. A single reviewer handled screening, a limitation the authors say was partly offset by review and approval from all co-authors. They deliberately avoided pooling results across studies because the interventions were too varied.

The review separates physical surgical execution from algorithmic prediction, tracing the development of platforms such as Mako, ROSA, CORI, and NAVIO alongside optical navigation systems. These tools were introduced to improve the accuracy of bone cuts, component placement, and limb alignment, and the evidence for that technical precision is considered mature. Artificial intelligence, by contrast, operates mainly in adjacent tasks such as radiographic interpretation, implant sizing, patient selection, dissatisfaction forecasting, risk stratification, and postoperative monitoring. In studies predicting postoperative patient dissatisfaction, models reached moderate accuracy, with area-under-the-curve values between 0.70 and 0.82.
