stories.Headline: CRR Hires 2 Inspectors for Cyber, CER and AI Rules [2026] - tech-insider.org
stories.Summary:
The Commission for Railway Regulation (CRR) is hiring one senior inspector (Grade I) and one inspector (Grade II) for a new cyber security, critical infrastructure and artificial intelligence (CCIAI) division, according to a notice TechCentral.ie published on 5 November 2026. Both posts are permanent, full-time and based in Blackrock, County Dublin. The senior role covers the rail and cableway sectors within the CRR's statutory remit and carries a stated salary of €87,510 to €101,776 a year. The notice names the NIS2 Directive, the Critical Entities Resilience (CER) Regulations and the Artificial Intelligence Act as the frameworks the division will work under. The notice does not name a candidate, a manager or a spokesperson, and it contains no on-record quotation.

The pairing of a railway regulator with AI and cyber remits reflects how EU law assigns enforcement to national bodies that already know the industry. NIS2 and the CER rules both cover transport, and a rail or cableway operator may face cyber, resilience and AI obligations at once. The notice does not explain the design choice, so the view that a combined division avoids three separate inspection regimes is our analysis. Inspectors in this field must also weigh security against safety, since older operational technology often cannot be patched on demand. The CER rules add a resilience question about whether essential services keep running whatever the cause, including dependencies on a single provider.

The AI Act's safety-component rules may reach predictive maintenance and automated monitoring tools already used in transport. Two points deserve plain disclosure. The TechCentral.ie page carrying the notice is labelled as sponsored content, so readers should treat it as an advertisement for the roles. The dates also conflict: the senior listing's application deadline is given as 12 noon, Irish time, on Friday 17 July 2026, which predates the publication date, and the advert we read shows a later closing date and a higher top-of-scale salary. The material we verified does not show whether the competition was reopened, the terms updated or an older listing republished.

Applicants should check the CRR's own application page for the current closing date and pay scale. Two posts will not move the wider labour market, but they show Irish regulators competing for scarce people who combine technical depth with legal literacy against private employers in Dublin. Greater inspection capacity is likely to raise compliance spending for operators and create work for assurance and advisory firms, though we have no data on the number of applications received. The CRR's next steps beyond the posted vacancies are not stated in the notice.

Articles.Title: CRR Hires 2 Inspectors for Cyber, CER and AI Rules [2026] - tech-insider.org

stories.Headline: Who pays when AI takes from creators? Europe rethinks copyright rules
stories.Summary:
Europe is reconsidering whether its two-decade-old rules on enforcing intellectual property can cope with artificial intelligence, as disputes over creative work multiply. The European Parliament's Legal Affairs Committee has continued discussing changes to the Intellectual Property Rights Enforcement Directive, which was adopted in 2004 and sets common procedures for enforcing copyright, patents and trademarks. A European Commission study found that enforcement varies unevenly across EU countries, including in how courts assess injunctions and in the costs faced by smaller rights holders. The debate has been driven by examples such as a book used as AI training material, a song feeding a music generator, and a news article turned into a chatbot answer.

MEP Axel Voss, who reported back from a September meeting of the EU Intellectual Property Office Observatory, said generative AI, copyright licensing and fair compensation are growing concerns. He told the committee that a balance is needed between protecting creativity and cultural values and allowing technological innovation, and he pointed to the need for transparency and proper licensing. Another MEP, René Repasi, presented arguments attributed to Leire Pajín, saying that public interest should be weighed, including effects on public health, critical infrastructure and emergency response, and he favoured case-by-case assessment. The Commission's representative, Denis Dambois, said the problems may stem more from differences in national enforcement than from the directive itself. He argued that these differences call for closer dialogue with member states, judicial cooperation and sharing of best practice rather than rapid legislation, and he warned against separate criteria for different intellectual property rights.

Courts are also weighing in on AI and copyright. A day before the committee meeting, Advocate General Maciej Szpunar at the EU Court of Justice advised that AI chatbots retrieving and reusing news articles to generate answers could, under certain conditions, infringe publishers' rights, in a case brought by Hungarian publisher Like Company against Google over its Gemini tool. In France, the Paris Court of Appeal rejected Meta's challenges and required it to negotiate in good faith with French media organisations over payment for their content. Culture Action Europe has warned that the EU's voluntary AI Code of Practice does not by itself guarantee compliance with copyright law, which could leave artists reliant on costly litigation. In Germany, a case brought by the collecting society GEMA found that the AI music generator Suno had infringed six protected compositions.

The Commission is considering broader changes to digital copyright policy, and a consultation that closed on 3 November sought evidence on AI training, online piracy of live events, performers' remuneration and copyright in scientific research. A June 2026 EUIPO study estimated that monitored websites offering infringing content, goods or services generated €382 million in advertising revenue worldwide in 2025, including €28.5 million within 18 monitored EU countries. The EU already has relevant instruments, including the 2019 Copyright Directive, which sets rights for publishers and rules for certain content-sharing platforms, the Digital Services Act, which requires intermediaries to offer reporting mechanisms for illegal content, and the AI Act, which imposes copyright-compliance and transparency duties on providers of general-purpose AI models. The article does not say what specific legislative changes will follow from the consultation or the committee's discussions.

Articles.Title: Who pays when AI takes from creators? Europe rethinks copyright rules - EU Perspectives

stories.Headline: Radial Kernel Attention for Global Feature Exchange in Polymer Machine Learning Force Fields
stories.Summary:
Researchers Wenbo Fu, Chenghui Mao, Chengwen Hu, Haifeng Lv and Zhou Lu have described a new method called Radial Kernel Attention, or RKA, for modeling polymer systems with machine learning force fields. The work was posted to arXiv and indexed on November 7, 2026. The authors say that existing approaches usually depend on local neighbor graphs, which restrict how information moves across polymer chains and the environments around them. Full all-pair attention could overcome that limit, but its computational cost grows quadratically with the number of atoms.

RKA instead maps interatomic distances from the cluster centroid to learned radial features, then combines their kernelized overlap with content-dependent queries and keys. Factorized aggregation and readout allow global feature exchange at linear complexity in the number of atoms, for fixed feature dimensions. The authors insert an invariant scalar update between EquiformerV3 local blocks and derive conservative forces by differentiating the total energy, including its dependence on the radial coordinate. Models were trained for 12 epochs on the official OPoly26 training set and evaluated directly on the complete official validation set.

In a matched 5M-parameter comparison, the authors report that RKA cuts per-atom energy and force mean absolute errors by 67.4% and 36.3%, respectively. Their 20M RKA model reaches a total-energy MAE of 15.81 meV, a per-atom MAE of 0.1182 meV/atom and a force MAE of 2.619 meV/Angstrom. On the same validation structures, the paper states, this model improves all three metrics over UMA-S-1.2 and UMA-S-1.2.1. The authors conclude that RKA offers a compact way to exchange information beyond local graph connectivity in polymer machine learning force fields.

Articles.Title: Radial Kernel Attention for Global Feature Exchange in Polymer Machine Learning Force Fields

stories.Headline: Rethinking LLM Pruning via Test-Time Scaling
stories.Summary:
A research paper posted to arXiv by Mingyang Song and Mao Zheng examines whether shrinking large language models through structured pruning actually costs them reasoning ability. The authors tested expert, feed-forward network and layer pruning on four benchmarks covering mathematics and coding, comparing original and pruned models at matched sampling budgets. The paper's central finding is that the accuracy drop often seen after pruning may reflect how hard it is to sample correct answers rather than a loss of reasoning capacity. The work was listed on the arXiv site with a date of November 7, 2026.

According to the abstract, some pruned models matched or exceeded the original model's reasoning coverage, measured by pass@k, even though their single-attempt accuracy, pass@1, was lower. These pruned models also solved some problems the original model left unsolved in its samples. However, under severe pruning the models produced more repetitive and less reliable chain-of-thought traces, so correct answers became harder to obtain. The authors report that additional attempts could sharply raise total token use even when individual responses got shorter. They also found that expert-selection methods with very different pass@1 scores could solve the same problems at large budgets but needed different numbers of attempts to reach a common coverage target.

The authors argue that pruning should be judged on two measures: the range of problems a model can still solve, and the sampling cost of getting correct solutions. The abstract does not name any outside party responsible for the work or report any reaction to it. The articles provided do not say whether the paper has been peer reviewed or accepted by a journal, and they do not give the specific model sizes, pruning ratios or token counts used in the experiments. The paper is available as a PDF and in HTML form on arXiv.

Articles.Title: Rethinking LLM Pruning via Test-Time Scaling

stories.Headline: MatMoE: Matryoshka Mixture-of-Experts with Dynamic Mixed-Precision Quantization for Efficient Inference
stories.Summary:
The source is a research paper posted to arXiv, dated November 7, 2026, that introduces a method called MatMoE for running Mixture-of-Experts language models more efficiently. The authors are Renjie Wei, Haochen Huang, Chuyu Qiu, Jinqi Wen, Dehao Xu and Meng Li, and the paper is listed under the identifier 2611.01704. The work addresses a problem with Mixture-of-Experts models, which reduce computation by activating only some expert components at a time but have very large parameter counts that make them hard to run on constrained hardware. The article does not describe any event beyond the publication of this paper.

According to the abstract, MatMoE is a dynamic mixed-precision quantization framework, meaning it adjusts how many bits each expert uses while the model runs. The authors say existing mixed-precision methods are static because they fix each expert's bit-width across all decoding steps, which misses changes in expert importance and fails to respond to fluctuating system load. MatMoE is built on three parts: a Matryoshka-style post-training quantization algorithm that lets experts run at several precisions within a tight memory budget, a floor-and-compensation method that removes redundant memory accesses, and a bit-width allocation strategy that sets each expert's precision from its routing score to meet a latency requirement. The system was implemented for both CPU and GPU platforms.

The authors report that across three modern Mixture-of-Experts models and challenging benchmarks, MatMoE achieves accuracy between 4.0 and 18.3 percent higher than the leading static mixed-precision method. They also report speedups over that method of 1.3 to 3.7 times on a Raspberry Pi 5 and 1.2 to 1.3 times on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 and a Jetson AGX Orin. The paper is authored by researchers whose affiliations the article does not state, and it is presented as an arXiv preprint, which has not been described in the source as peer reviewed. The source does not say what follow-up work or adoption is planned.

Articles.Title: MatMoE: Matryoshka Mixture-of-Experts with Dynamic Mixed-Precision Quantization for Efficient Inference

stories.Headline: SpecOPD: Branch-Parallel On-Policy Distillation for Speculative Decoding
stories.Summary:
A research paper posted on arXiv under the title "SpecOPD: Branch-Parallel On-Policy Distillation for Speculative Decoding" was made available in early November 2026, with a listed date of November 7, 2026. The paper was written by fifteen authors led by Tianyu Liu, and it describes a method for speeding up how large language models generate text. Speculative decoding is a technique that reduces the cost of producing text one token at a time by having a smaller drafter propose several tokens that the main model then checks. The authors say that more advanced versions of this approach still depend on how many proposed tokens are accepted on average, which limits overall speed.

The authors propose SpecOPD, a training framework that runs draft sampling and target supervision in parallel across independent branches of a drafter. These branches are packed into proposal trees so that shared computation on the target prefix is reused, and special masks and state-replay methods are used to keep each branch's history intact across full, sparse and linear attention designs. The drafter is trained with a surrogate objective that directly targets acceptance length. The study tests this approach on target models of 8 billion, 27 billion and 125 billion parameters, three parallel draft architectures named DFlash, DSpark and DFlash V2, and four task areas: dialogue, coding, mathematics and agentic tasks. According to the abstract, SpecOPD raises mean acceptance length by up to 41.45 percent, achieves up to 16.09 times the supervised-token throughput of sequential-rollout on-policy distillation under native configurations, and reaches up to 3.56 times generation speedup over standard autoregressive decoding.

The paper credits its work to its listed authors, who include Tianyu Liu, Jun Zhang, Wenjie Huang and Mingchen Wan, along with ten others, and the article gives no further institutional or funding details in the text provided. The arXiv listing also notes that the page belongs to the arXivLabs framework, which lets outside collaborators build features for the site, but the articles do not state that arXiv itself endorsed the findings. The articles do not describe any peer review status, independent replication, or public release of code or models beyond the paper itself. The text also indicates that a PDF and an HTML version of the paper are available, though it does not say when a formal journal or conference publication might follow.

Articles.Title: SpecOPD: Branch-Parallel On-Policy Distillation for Speculative Decoding

stories.Headline: US voters lashed out at data centres. What does that mean for Australia’s AI ambitions?
stories.Summary:
Voters in the United States delivered large gains to the Democrats in this week's midterm elections, and a rising backlash against data centres played an unexpectedly important role. Candidates campaigning for local limits on data centres won across ten states, and according to exit polls, about 56% of voters said AI data centres were a crucial or major factor in their vote. The result reflects a growing tension between America's push to lead in artificial intelligence and the reluctance of local communities to host the infrastructure that supports it. The Trump administration has made data centre expansion a core pillar of its technology and economic strategy, and in July 2025 the president signed an executive order to speed their development. In June alone, US$4.4 billion was spent on building data centres, a fivefold increase from November 2022, when ChatGPT was first released.

About 75% of data centres under construction sit in Republican-led states, yet opposition grew there as well. Pew Research found American sentiment hardening against data centres between January and August this year, with most Americans believing they do more harm than good. Residents cited energy costs, environmental pressures and noise, and in areas near US data centres, wholesale electricity prices rose by as much as 267% over the past five years. Many people also questioned what they would gain from AI if they were being asked to cover those costs. Candidates from both parties shifted toward stronger regulation as the opposition spread, though Democrats moved faster to campaign for tighter oversight.

Democrat-led states including New Jersey, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Oregon have introduced local bans or are debating statewide ones. Gubernatorial races in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, all major growth areas for data centres, were won by candidates calling for pauses on new projects. The article notes that data centre stocks in the US fell as the Democratic sweep became apparent, and that Democrat-led states account for around 45% of planned US capacity. Tighter rules could bring project delays and higher costs, and investment might move to jurisdictions with more accommodating regulation.

With the 2028 presidential election approaching, the authors expect data centres and AI to become key political battlegrounds. In Australia, the market is much smaller than in the US but growing quickly, and local opposition is rising as well. A A$1.2 billion data centre project on Sydney's north shore was scrapped in September after strong community objections, and residents in West Footscray in Melbourne used bins and cars to block power line construction for a data centre. The Australian government is developing mandatory national standards for large data centres covering energy and water use, siting and community engagement, though how strict they will be and how they will fit with state and territory rules remains unclear.

Articles.Title: US voters lashed out at data centres. What does that mean for Australia’s AI ambitions? - The Conversation

stories.Headline: PaddleMaterials: An End-to-End Deep Learning Toolkit for Materials Science
stories.Summary:
A research team led by Xuwei Liu and seven co-authors has released PaddleMaterials, an open-source deep learning toolkit for materials science, described in a preprint posted to arXiv on November 7, 2026. The framework is built to bring together several materials-learning tasks that have until now been handled by separate, fragmented tools. Its authors say it keeps the specific representations and scientific meaning of each task intact while unifying data processing, training, evaluation, pretrained-model management and workflows. The toolkit covers six task classes: property prediction, structure generation, machine-learning interatomic potentials, electronic-structure fields, spectrum elucidation and microscopy image processing. Each task interface records physical quantities, units, aggregation conventions and references, which the authors say makes cross-task composition verifiable.

A shared compiler backend lets users switch from dynamic-graph to compiled execution through a single setting, using graph optimization, operator fusion and hardware-targeted code generation without altering model definitions. Across 65 model instances in 11 groups, compiled execution sped up every instance in eight groups, with group median speedups of 11% to 224%. The authors report case studies on LiMnO2 and toluene that link structure generation or spectrum elucidation, interatomic-potential relaxation, property prediction and electron-density prediction. For LiMnO2, predicted formation energies for generated and relaxed structures differed from same-geometry PBE+U reference calculations by at most 7 meV per atom. The authors state that the computational cost of the model steps was less than one-twentieth of a density functional theory single-point calculation.

They present these results as evidence that the framework can support verifiable cross-task operations and compiled execution. The paper's classification places the work under machine learning, materials science and computational engineering, finance, and science. The preprint is an arXiv posting, so its results have not been described in the article as peer-reviewed. The authors frame PaddleMaterials as an extension of unified materials workflows beyond conventional property, potential and structure-generation tasks. The articles do not say what follow-up work, releases or adoption plans the team has announced.

Articles.Title: PaddleMaterials: An End-to-End Deep Learning Toolkit for Materials Science

stories.Headline: Investigation: some Chinese companies approved by the US Commerce Department to handle Nvidia's H200 chips have empty offices and ties to firms under sanctions (New York Times)
stories.Summary:
The New York Times reported that the U.S. Commerce Department approved several Chinese companies to handle Nvidia's H200 chips, and some of those firms appear to have empty offices and links to sanctioned businesses. The reporting centers on New Matrix, a company listed at an address in a recently built industrial park on the northwest edge of Beijing, where the building stands empty. The approval came earlier this year, after President Trump allowed the sale of the chips to China late last year. Before any sale could proceed, the Commerce Department had to review the companies for national security risks.

New Matrix passed that review, but the Times found little evidence in China that the firm actually operates. The company was created about 17 months ago, and only scant information about it appears online. A company directory at the listed building does not include the firm, and staff at the industrial park's property management agency said they had no record of it. The reporters therefore raised questions about who in China is truly behind the company.

According to Chinese corporate records, New Matrix's owners have ties to a prominent Chinese private equity fund that the U.S. government placed on a trade blacklist in 2024. Two analysts who reviewed those records and other Chinese-language information told the Times they believed New Matrix may be a front for firms linked to that fund. The article describes the sale to New Matrix as part of a broader pattern that has concerned technology experts both inside and outside the government. In that pattern, the Commerce Department cleared Chinese companies with ties to firms previously hit by national-security trade restrictions to buy and handle Nvidia chips.

Articles.Title: Investigation: some Chinese companies approved by the US Commerce Department to handle Nvidia's H200 chips have empty offices and ties to firms under sanctions (New York Times)

stories.Headline: I Can't Code, But AI Let Me Fix Everything I Hated About My Favorite Games
stories.Summary:
Columnist Tchernobill, writing for PCMag Australia, describes how a non-programmer used AI to create game mods for Valheim and the Claude Code app, and the piece was published on November 7, 2026. The author says they are not interested in AI-generated "slop" games but found that AI helps build mods that fix things they disliked in games they already love. One example was a Valheim mod called Map Rings, which adds rings to the in-game map showing distance from the world's center. The author wanted a hotkey to toggle the rings, which the original mod lacked, so they used Claude to decompile the mod and add that feature. The article also covers other fixes, including a reworked gambling mechanic for Valheim's Forge of Potential and a "stay" command called StayPut that keeps tamed animals in place.

The author lays out a no-code workflow that requires a premium subscription to a frontier model such as Claude or ChatGPT, and recommends setting ground rules before starting, including lightweight code, compatibility with existing mods, and read-only access to game save files. The author favors Claude's Opus 5.5 model at its highest effort setting, and suggests having the AI write a plan, review it, build the mod, and then review the result. The article advises against using AI to generate art and assets, noting that matching an existing art style is harder and that the practice raises ethical concerns about training on other people's work. The author also says testing is essential because the modder acts as the lead playtester. The article further describes a custom Claude Code mod that stops work and creates a handoff when a session reaches 80 percent of its context limit or 95 percent of the five-hour usage limit.

The author concedes that they cannot read the code their mods produce and describes their approach as vibe coding, but says thorough testing, review policies, and the limited scope of their mods have given them confidence. The author argues that top models are more than most small mods require, and notes that GPT-6 Astra is another capable option, with new models appearing regularly. The article does not report any problems, outside incidents, or formal responses from Anthropic, Valheim's developers, or other companies. It does not say what will happen next beyond the author's continued modding.

Articles.Title: I Can't Code, But AI Let Me Fix Everything I Hated About My Favorite Games

stories.Headline: Lanarkshire AI datacentre to fully rely on National Grid despite renewables claim
stories.Summary:
DataVita, the company behind a planned AI datacentre near Chapelhall, outside Airdrie in Lanarkshire, has admitted that the scheme will now be fully served by the National Grid. The Guardian reported the change on 7 November 2026. The company had earlier said the project would draw 1GW of power from renewable sources, the equivalent output of a small nuclear reactor or Britain's largest windfarm. When questions were raised about that pledge, the company described the arrangement as subject to final commercial agreements, planning, grid and consenting processes. It has since quietly revised its plan.

The revised plan says the datacentres will be "fully grid served," with solar and windfarms possibly connecting in the future. The company says the power drawn from the grid will be largely renewable. DataVita was to build an "AI growth zone" in Lanarkshire, and the project was expected to bring 3,400 jobs by building a 500MW datacentre. The company still holds £202m in public money, provided as wealth guarantees by the National Wealth Fund. The shift could create difficulties for both the company and the government's AI strategy, which relied on large datacentres in zones across the country.

A DataVita spokesperson told the Guardian that the company had not misrepresented its renewable plans and that its commitment to renewable energy was unchanged. The spokesperson said the datacentres were being designed to be grid served, with supply coming through a renewable power purchase agreement. The company also left open the possibility of connecting to a wind and solar park it proposes to build in North Lanarkshire. Kat Jones, director of the charity Action to Protect Rural Scotland, said the change reflected exaggerated claims by datacentre developers in Scotland. She argued that hyperscale AI datacentres cannot run on renewable power alone and need a highly reliable grid supply.

The article places the change against a wider pattern. Britain's AI strategy, set out under the former prime minister Keir Starmer, offered developers incentives such as possible energy discounts and faster planning approvals, but the Guardian's investigations found that many announced plans lacked solid backing. AI datacentres are highly energy-intensive, British energy costs are higher than in most of Europe, and UK developments face a wait of several years to connect to the grid. The article also notes that other projects have faced scrutiny, including a planning suspension for new Scottish AI datacentres of up to a year.

Articles.Title: Lanarkshire AI datacentre to fully rely on National Grid despite renewables claim

stories.Headline: AI accelerates cyber threats, increases defensive spending
stories.Summary:
AI is accelerating and making cyber threats more sophisticated, according to executives, and this is straining IT departments around the world. In response, companies are increasing their investment in AI-powered security tools to help manage the growing workload. Nearly 37,000 security flaws were reported in the third quarter of 2026, according to the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures list, a figure that tripled from a year earlier. The reporting ties the surge to the growing pressure on defenders as well as the attackers.

Booking.com's chief security officer, Marnie Wilking, said hundreds of engineers at the company are now building AI-powered defence systems. Markus Noga, chief technology officer of the German web hosting company Ionos, told Reuters that the company is seeing events of a magnitude every week that used to come months apart. After a spike in vulnerabilities in July, Ionos changed its security practices by deploying AI-based monitoring systems and AI-assisted tools for round-the-clock patching. Binance, which suffered a $6.3 billion cryptocurrency theft, plans to increase its investment in AI-enhanced detection systems.

Other organizations are following a similar path. The Port of Rotterdam is developing an AI-powered "cyber shield," and Siemens is testing advanced AI models for defensive security. Researchers at Claroty used widely available AI tools to reproduce refrigeration controller flaws for $6 in 28 minutes after attacks began. Two AI-discovered flaws in the PHP programming language, disclosed in October, led governments and companies worldwide to take websites offline as a precaution. Cloudflare reported that attempts to exploit the PHP flaws rose from thousands to millions within hours of their disclosure.

Business leaders are also weighing in on the shift. Kraft Heinz chief executive Steve Cahillane said cybersecurity is becoming increasingly important to the company. Holcim chief financial officer Steffen Kindler said that both sides in the cyber battle are heavily equipped with AI. Their comments suggest that the arms race between attackers and defenders is now being fought largely with the same kind of technology.

Articles.Title: AI accelerates cyber threats, increases defensive spending

stories.Headline: Australian universities are creating AI-native graduates
stories.Summary:
Australian universities are partnering with OpenAI to give students and staff access to advanced AI tools, and the work is already taking shape on campuses. According to the article, UNSW Sydney, the University of Sydney, La Trobe University and Adelaide University are all forging these collaborations, which the piece dates to 5 November 2026. The institutions are using AI in clinical simulations, robot-assisted teacher training and student projects meant to lead into industry. Students, educators and IT teams are involved in this work. UNSW is bringing ChatGPT Edu to more than 80,000 students and staff, with access expanding in stages.

The university plans to build generative AI foundations and Codex into courses, with hackathons, industry projects, internships and startup connections. The University of Sydney will give students and staff supported access to ChatGPT Edu, with training, and access for all students is scheduled for Semester 1, 2027 after a trial. It is also setting up a $1 million AI Sustainability Research and Innovation Fund. La Trobe has given all 3,500 staff access to ChatGPT Edu, with universal access planned for its 45,000 students and staff in the first quarter of 2027, and it will launch Australia's first Bachelor of AI Engineering (Honours) in 2027. Adelaide University is using OpenAI's API and has adopted OpenAI Daybreak Blue for authorised defensive security work.

The universities themselves lead these programs, and their leaders have described their goals. Phil Laufenberg, La Trobe's Pro Vice-Chancellor AI and Chief AI Officer, said students in every discipline should be able to help shape how AI is used in their profession. Abhishek Singh, Adelaide University's Chief Technology and Security Officer, said the tools would strengthen the university's cyber security posture. The article also quotes UNSW Master of IT student Nalin Iyer, who said it matters to understand what industry wants and how AI fits into that. The article notes that the survey was commissioned by OpenAI, so its findings reflect the company's research.

The surrounding research shows that students already use AI heavily. In a Pureprofile survey of 1,018 Australian university students, conducted for OpenAI from 3 to 7 August 2026, 81% said they use AI several times a week and 28% had built an AI agent or assistant. Four in five students want more chances to use advanced AI on real projects. Universities are also setting rules for use, with UNSW's Can, Can't, Must framework for assessment and La Trobe's free Responsible and Safe AI modules. The article does not say what the outcomes of these programs will be, and it describes them only as the start of a longer rollout.

Articles.Title: Australian universities are creating AI-native graduates

stories.Headline: Cult.fit builds operational muscle with Codex
stories.Summary:
Cult.fit, an Indian fitness company, has standardized its software engineering on OpenAI's Codex and extended it across the organization, according to a customer story published by OpenAI on November 5, 2026. The company operates 708 fitness centers in 77 cities and serves nearly one million paid members. Its business mixes subscription gym and trainer-led class access with a growing line of consumer fitness products. The article describes this as a way to solve operational and product problems without adding layers of process.

Engineering was the first area to change. Before standardizing, developers used a mix of coding agents and assistants that followed different conventions for repositories, agent instructions, skills, and workflows, which made sharing knowledge harder. Cult.fit chose Codex as a shared platform so repository structures, testing, code review, and feedback loops could follow common rules across teams. The company then built specialized agents on top of it, including a Site Reliability Engineering agent that investigates incidents and often proposes a fix as a pull request, along with security and on-call agents. A recent social feed project, which the CTO estimates would previously have taken more than a year, was built and shipped in two months using this workflow.

The change has since reached non-engineering staff. Cult.fit made its company data easier for Codex to use, so teams can run routine analysis themselves instead of routing every request through a central analyst team. HR, for example, built a Codex workflow for performance reviews, scheduling, and feedback collection, and more than 20 internal applications have been built by non-engineering teams in recent months. When the cost of its internal dashboard software rose sharply, one engineer rebuilt that capability with Codex over a weekend, which the company says avoids more than $100,000 in annual software costs. Support for this shift included an employee hackathon, a one-day session in which management built relevant tools, and twice-weekly engineering office hours.

Santhosh Kumar, the company's CTO, said the company wanted to become more AI-native in how it runs operations and what customer experiences it offers. He said Codex has been the company's biggest step toward data democratization and that software has been democratized so employees can build what their teams need. Cult.fit is also using the OpenAI API for its AI Trainer, which about 20 percent of its gym users currently use and which over 45 percent of members, who are first-time gym goers, rely on for guidance. The newest version is voice-first and uses GPT Realtime to give coaching cues and support workout logging. The company also uses AI agents in customer support to decide whether to waive penalties for missed classes, and the article says it plans to move toward an "autopilot operations org" and a "trainer in your pocket."

Articles.Title: Cult.fit builds operational muscle with Codex

stories.Headline: GPT‑6 Cyber: Advancing the frontier of aligned cybersecurity agents
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced GPT-6 Cyber on November 5, 2026, a cybersecurity model designed to find and validate exploitable vulnerabilities while staying within the scope that researchers set. The company says the model delivers major gains over its predecessor, GPT-5.6 Cyber, scoring 48.5% on the ExploitGym benchmark against 32.1% for the earlier model, a relative improvement of about 51%. On an alignment test measuring whether the model avoids attacking out-of-scope services, GPT-6 Cyber stayed within bounds in 99.93% of cases without its deployment prompt and 100% with it, up from 94.49% for GPT-5.6 Cyber without the prompt. The model is already in use on real software, and OpenAI's researchers used it to develop 948 privilege escalation exploits in Linux and identify 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox, for which Mozilla has released fixes for many issues.

OpenAI says the model is classified as Critical in cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework, up from High for GPT-5.6 Cyber. The company also describes a tiered access program called Daybreak, which includes Daybreak Blue for verified defenders who need validation of vulnerabilities and fixes with fewer refusals, and Daybreak Red for deeper exploit development and authorized security testing with GPT-6 Cyber. On a new benchmark called RemoteExploitBench, the company reports that GPT-6 Astra running with Daybreak Blue refused all tasks, while GPT-6 Cyber completed 95%. The company also says it plans to expand Daybreak to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers, and that it sees a limited window to use frontier models to secure software.

OpenAI is responsible for the announcement and is the source of all the performance figures, which come from its own evaluations and system card. Several security firms, including Cisco, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks, SentinelOne, and CodeRabbit, along with Mozilla and the developer Calif, provided testimonials praising the model's usefulness for vulnerability research and code review. The announcement also notes that OpenAI used the model to harden its own infrastructure, where agents chaining vulnerabilities in controlled red-team campaigns were found to escape microVMs, prompting patches and network restrictions. The articles provided do not describe independent verification of these results or any regulatory response.

Articles.Title: GPT‑6 Cyber: Advancing the frontier of aligned cybersecurity agents

stories.Headline: Flipsnack grows product signups with conversion optimization
stories.Summary:
Flipsnack, a company that helps teams turn static documents into interactive digital experiences, reported on OpenAI's site that it grew product signups by shifting its ChatGPT Ads campaigns to a conversion focus. The company had previously run click-focused campaigns with fixed bids, and in November 2026 it described the change and the results it saw. Its tests ran across five US campaign pairs, comparing late August with early September 2026. The company said it had relied heavily on search advertising before trying ChatGPT Ads.

The change required Flipsnack to rebuild existing campaigns with a conversions objective and bidding set to maximize conversions. It created conversion-focused versions of five US campaigns that had used a clicks objective with fixed bids. Its landing pages sent people into a signup flow, so completed registration became the main measure the team optimized for. The company also split its broad Flipbook campaign into narrower campaigns for Magazine, Catalog, and Brochure, plus campaigns for Sales Enablement, Employee Benefits, Real Estate, and Hospitality.

Flipsnack said the results were encouraging. Across the five campaigns, registrations rose about 310 percent while cost per registration fell about 75 percent, with daily budget limits unchanged and spend up roughly 1.3 percent. The article attributes the figures to Flipsnack's ChatGPT Ads Manager data, measured with 30-day clicks and excluding views, and notes that objectives and bidding changed together. The company's marketing team said the lower cost per signup gave it confidence to make conversion optimization the focus of its campaigns. The article presents these numbers as company-reported results rather than independently verified outcomes.

The article describes the results as a foundation for continued growth with ChatGPT Ads rather than a finished outcome. Flipsnack's team said it aims to bring more prospective customers into the product and help them see how it can support their business. The article does not say how long the campaigns will run or whether the same gains will hold at larger budgets. It also does not report any figures beyond the five campaign pairs.

Articles.Title: Flipsnack grows product signups with conversion optimization

stories.Headline: Franklin Templeton uses OpenAI to support investment research
stories.Summary:
Franklin Templeton, a North American asset manager, has been using OpenAI tools, including Codex, to support its investment research, starting with equity research. The firm is building AI workflows meant to help portfolio managers compare different research views and examine the risks behind an investment idea. Franklin Templeton's account, published by OpenAI on November 5, 2026, describes the work as a shift from using AI to automate a human-led process to using it to surface insights. The firm says the change lets it combine what it calls continuous intelligence with human judgment.

According to the article, Franklin Templeton first connected AI models to a database, but the results were poor because the models did not understand how the data fit together. The team then added agents and a semantic layer, a structured model of what the firm's data means and how it is connected, and the results improved. The firm says it is building a governed, reusable intelligence foundation that links trusted connectors, portfolio and workflow context, and agentic capabilities. Research, risk, compliance, and trading each offer a different view of an investment, and the firm wants to bring those inputs together for its portfolio managers. The earlier equity-research process was sequential, with analysts doing first-pass stock analysis, reviewing earnings calls, and studying competitors.

Katrina Dudley, Senior Vice President of Public Market Investments at Franklin Templeton, is quoted as the main voice on the project. She says the firm's use of OpenAI's tools has made it possible to merge continuous intelligence with human judgment. Dudley says the firm wants its AI to surface a range of research views rather than only more of what a user already prefers, since a narrowing tool could bias the investment process. She also says a strong investment idea should include an analysis of its risks, which she describes as a help to informed decisions. Her message from leadership, as she describes it, is to encourage experimentation with AI within defined risk guardrails.

The article presents Franklin Templeton's experience as a set of practices: bringing new tools to teams quickly, helping staff learn them, and building with security review, expert support, and data agreements before production use. The firm has used Codex in hackathons, pairing experts with investment practitioners, and its Investment AI champions are working to turn experiments into production-ready workflows. Dudley's longer-term goal is to make the connected intelligence available across investment teams, and she wants analysts to spend more time in the field speaking with experts and executives at private companies. The article does not give figures on results, costs, or a timeline for full rollout.

Articles.Title: Franklin Templeton uses OpenAI to support investment research

stories.Headline: ‘Shock absorbers’: Korn Ferry says managers are carrying AI change that executives aren’t ready to lead
stories.Summary:
Korn Ferry published its Talent Trends 2027 report on October 22, based on a survey of more than 1,300 talent and senior leaders, from CHROs to CEOs and board members, in more than 75 countries. The findings show that just 6% of those leaders believe their organizations' top executives are fully prepared to lead AI-driven transformation. Two-thirds of respondents, or 66%, expect middle managers to spend more time helping their teams through change than overseeing day-to-day work. The firm also found that 77% of respondents see capability gaps as a bigger challenge than talent shortages, and 78% believe too few people are ready for how work will be done in the future. Together, these results suggest that managers are being asked to absorb a large share of the pressure created by AI adoption.

The added burden is sitting on managers who already have little spare capacity, and many now oversee larger teams after years of cuts to management layers. Cathi Rittelmann, a senior client partner at Korn Ferry, described managers as the shock absorbers of the organization, whose job is to keep teams moving even when they cannot say exactly where things are heading. Susan De La Vega, senior vice president of global tech market and client experience at Korn Ferry, told Fortune that AI transformation requires redesigning the workforce, not just rolling out new technology. She said managers often must defend and communicate AI mandates they had no say in and little context to explain. She also warned that when leadership later changes course, employees end up redoing work, and that poor communication can erode trust and drive away valuable people.

De La Vega placed much of the responsibility for getting this right on senior leaders, arguing that they should learn the tools themselves so they can speak credibly about what AI changes and what it does not. She recommended job-specific training, since a finance analyst and a data scientist have different needs, and time and room for employees to experiment. She also said managers should be briefed on the reasoning behind leadership decisions before those decisions reach their teams. Rather than waiting for a flawless master plan, she urged leaders to share what they know, acknowledge what remains uncertain, and lay out the broader roadmap. Her view is that middle managers need a system behind them to do this work effectively.

The communication gap is not unique to Korn Ferry's research, according to Gallup data cited in the article. As of May, only 25% of U.S. employees said their organizations had communicated a clear plan for integrating AI, even though 47% said their employers had begun using AI tools. A July Gallup analysis found that 43% of employees whose employers had communicated a clear integration plan were engaged at work, compared with 28% of those whose employers had not or who were unaware of one. Employees whose manager actively supported their team's use of AI were engaged at 48%, compared with 30% among those without that support. The article does not describe specific steps companies have announced beyond these recommendations.

Articles.Title: ‘Shock absorbers’: Korn Ferry says managers are carrying AI change that executives aren’t ready to lead

stories.Headline: A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.
stories.Summary:
Gradium, the team behind Phonon, released a new on-device text-to-speech model family on November 5, 2026, after a two-week launch window that began with the first public release. Phonon is designed to run on the user's own device without a server or network connection, so text stays on the device. The company released two sizes, about 65 MB and 75 MB, that together speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese, with more than 100 built-in voices. Phonon 31m, the English-only model, is licensed under Apache 2.0 and may be used freely, including in commercial products, while Phonon 40m, which covers all five languages, is available under a non-commercial CC BY-NC license.

The company says the models use flow matching to generate audio, a technique that let it keep quality high in a small model but made training numerically unstable and required several workarounds. Phonon handles phone numbers, dates and codes, and it runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab. Users can clone a voice from a short recording with the speaker's consent, or describe a new voice in plain text in Gradium Studio, and the resulting voice file then runs on the device. The release also includes an inference framework called ptts with more than 10 hardware backends, plus a PyTorch implementation added to Hugging Face Transformers from version 5.21.

Gradium's authors, including Olesia Krizhevich, Laurent Mazare, Eric Bezzam and Eustache Le Bihan, presented the launch and the results. They said the company tested Phonon on the Open TTS Leaderboard, which compares open speech models across 23 languages on intelligibility, speed and naturalness. According to the post, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish on intelligibility, is in the top three in every language evaluated, and tops the CPU streaming benchmark for time-to-first audio. The authors also said the model was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks and is still trending on Hugging Face.

The articles say Gradium offers custom Phonon models to design partners, including smaller models for tight memory budgets and training for additional languages such as Korean, Arabic and Japanese. They also say the team will fine-tune on a product's own vocabulary on request. Developers have already built on the release, with an ExecuTorch conversion that runs Phonon in a browser on a visitor's GPU, a Node.js library called Micdrop, and Hugging Face Spaces that use it. The company describes this as its first open release and invites users to try it and share what they build.

Articles.Title: A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

stories.Headline: Le Chonk brings the brains. Studio puts it to work.
stories.Summary:
Mistral AI has released Mistral Large 4, which it calls Le Chonk, along with an expanded version of its enterprise platform, Mistral Studio, on November 5, 2026. The company says the model is stronger at coding, defensive cybersecurity, and reasoning over complex documents and business tasks. Studio lets companies deploy agents, workflows, and apps connected to their own data and systems. It can run in the cloud, in a customer's own virtual private cloud, on-premises, or across a mix of these.

The update adds managed agents and apps, along with new features for workflows, enterprise context, agent observability, and evaluations. Managed agents can carry out multi-step tasks using skills, sandboxes for running code, and subagents, while Studio handles the runtime. Workflows can now be triggered by events from enterprise systems and include a visual graph of their logic. Developers can also use a new Mistral MCP server to build locally and deploy to Studio with one command.

Mistral named several customers already using Studio in production, including ABANCA, Accenture, Alten, BNP Paribas, Capgemini, CMA CGM, and Tata Consultancy Services. Executives quoted in the announcement said the platform lets them keep control of sensitive data and infrastructure, with BNP Paribas running Studio on its own infrastructure. Accenture's representative described the platform as a foundation for building and scaling solutions, and TCS's chief officer said the partnership supports sovereignty, governance, and deployment flexibility. Capgemini's executive said the platform helps move AI projects beyond pilots to systems that can be measured and relied upon.

Customers described specific results in the announcement. An engineering team built an agent that investigates production incidents and posts findings in Slack, which the company says saves hundreds of hours each month. A product operations team built a workflow that sorts internal and customer feedback and routes it to the right teams, saving about 35 hours a week. Mistral also said Studio gives customers control over where AI runs, which models they use, and which actions need human approval, with OpenTelemetry traces and evaluations kept under their own control.

Articles.Title: Le Chonk brings the brains. Studio puts it to work.

stories.Headline: Grid Dynamics (GDYN) Stock May Be 11% Undervalued After Record AI Led Results
stories.Summary:
Grid Dynamics Holdings, which trades under the ticker GDYN, has had a strong run recently, and its share price jump has raised questions about whether its valuation matches its cash flows. A Simply Wall St analysis published on November 7, 2026 argues that the stock may be about 11% undervalued after record results led by AI-related work. The article notes that the shares have climbed 70.8% over the past month. Its central question is how much of the recent optimism is already reflected in the market price.

The article's discounted cash flow model estimates intrinsic value using the cash the company could return to shareholders over time. It cites latest twelve-month free cash flow of about $25.7 million and assumes that cash generation keeps growing rather than shrinking. On that basis, the model places intrinsic value modestly above the current $13.10 share price. The analysis also points to record third-quarter 2026 revenue and stronger AI-related work as factors already built into the projections. The article describes the model as not extreme or aggressive.

The article attributes its analysis to Simply Wall St, which says the piece was produced with the assistance of AI automation using its data and analyst forecasts. Its commentary is written by Bailey Pemberton, and the publisher states that it is not financial advice and not a recommendation to buy or sell the stock. The article also notes that Simply Wall St has no position in the stocks it mentions. Community views cited in the piece are split, with some seeing AI-driven execution as underappreciated and others believing the good news is largely priced in.

The article presents some risks alongside its valuation case. It cites rising customer concentration, with the top five accounts contributing 43.5% of revenue and the top ten contributing 61.5% in the most recent quarter. It also notes that the stock trades at a 134.1x price-to-earnings ratio. The publisher says its analysis may not factor in the latest company announcements or qualitative material. The article does not describe any specific next steps for the company.

Articles.Title: Grid Dynamics (GDYN) Stock May Be 11% Undervalued After Record AI Led Results

stories.Headline: What this AI spotted under the desert changes how we read an entire civilization_22705
stories.Summary:
An AI system has helped archaeologists find a 72-foot killer whale etched into the Peruvian desert roughly 1,500 years ago, a figure that a century of human scholarship had missed. Researchers at Yamagata University, led by project leader Masato Sakai, trained an object detection model on thousands of high-resolution photographs of the Nazca Pampa. With AI assistance, the team has now recorded 463 new geoglyphs in under three years, a total that exceeds every figure found by people since the 1920s. The initial findings of 303 figurative geoglyphs were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, a sixteenfold rise in the discovery rate compared with earlier manual surveys. By mid 2025, the team announced 248 more finds at Expo 2025 Osaka, bringing the confirmed total to 893, of which 781 came from the AI-human partnership.

The newly confirmed figures include humanoids, birds, felines, domesticated camelids, and complex scenes, among them a priest holding a severed head. The killer whale holds a knife, a motif that also appears on Nazca pottery and links the figure to human sacrifice. The team visited about a quarter of the 1,309 candidate locations the model flagged during the 2022 to 2023 field season, and the remaining 968 sites have not yet been assessed. Based on the confirmed success rate, the researchers estimate that hundreds more geoglyphs may still lie beneath the desert surface. Sakai said the traditional visual method was slow and risked overlooking figures, and the AI compressed what would have been generations of fieldwork into less than three years.

The model supplies leads, but people still walk each site to confirm it. The expanded dataset also supports a theory about how the Nazca people used the desert floor. Large line-type geoglyphs, often hundreds of meters long and showing wild animals, cluster around Cahuachi, the ceremonial adobe center of Nazca culture, and the PNAS paper argues they served as community-level spiritual landmarks. Smaller relief-type geoglyphs sit along ancient winding trails within viewing distance of a single traveler and depict human motifs, including decapitation and sacrifice. The researchers read this split as a coordinated spiritual landscape built for two scales of participants.

The work also validates the earlier observations of mathematician Maria Reiche, who had anticipated structured intent, though the full pattern became visible only once the AI produced a large enough dataset. The Nazca project is part of a wider shift in archaeological survey, with AI systems now locating burial sites in Europe, settlements under forest canopy in Central America, and artifact concentrations at desert sites in the UAE. The team holds a permit extending through 2026 and is moving into the final unmapped stretches of the Pampa. Hundreds of flagged sites remain unassessed, and the researchers expect that more significant discoveries are still ahead.

Articles.Title: What this AI spotted under the desert changes how we read an entire civilization
